item.title: Winter rains threaten 1,000 Gaza shelter sites, councils warn
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Winter rains threaten 1,000 Gaza shelter sites, councils warn

About 200,000 tents need replacing, Gaza’s municipalities say, as the European Union urges Israel to reopen all crossings into the territory to aid.

Gaza’s municipalities have warned that winter rains could flood about 1,000 camps and other sites hosting displaced Palestinians in the war-torn enclave, adding that damage to drains and sewers, and a shortage of pumps, have left their crews with little means to clear the water.

After a meeting in Gaza City on Wednesday, the Union of Gaza Strip Municipalities singled out al-Mughraqa and al-Zahra in central Gaza, where water levels in Wadi Gaza could rise suddenly. Across the territory, about 200,000 tents need replacing, and more than 2,000 damaged buildings are at risk of collapse, the union said. Gaza’s Government Media Office had warned on Tuesday that it expected another storm within days.

This is Gaza’s fourth winter since Israel launched its war in October 2023. The union said storms in early November flooded about 70,000 tents and affected more than 350,000 displaced people. During a winter storm this November, families piled sand at tent entrances to keep out the rain. Others carried their children out and salvaged what belongings they could.

One displaced mother said she had cut up the burial shroud she had bought for her son and used it to patch her tent. She wanted to keep the family’s bedding and clothes dry. “I couldn’t get a tarpaulin,” she said.

When the first rains hit, Gaza’s civil defence crews reached only a minority of those who called for help. Most of the other callers received advice by phone, Al Jazeera reported.

Tents waiting at the border

In Brussels on Wednesday, the European Commission called on Israel to reopen all Gaza crossings to humanitarian aid. Commission spokesperson Eva Hrncirova said tents were waiting on trucks outside Gaza because Israel had not allowed them or the equipment needed to put them up to enter.

The UN said earlier this month that more than 150,000 tents were awaiting entry into Gaza.

Al Jazeera’s open-source unit (Ar.) measured a queue of trucks stretching about 1.1km (0.7 miles) along the Egyptian road to the Rafah crossing in a November 17 satellite image, up from about 460 metres (1,510 feet) on October 6. The images do not establish what the trucks carried. Freight from Egypt is routed through the Karem Abu Salem crossing, known as Kerem Shalom in Israel, for inspection rather than entering Gaza through Rafah.

COGAT, the Israeli military body that coordinates aid, said that nearly 100,000 tents had entered Gaza since the start of a winter aid programme. It said Israel would allow reconstruction equipment into Gaza only after Hamas had fully disarmed.

Inside Gaza, aid workers have cleared drains, installed flood barriers and reinforced shelters. The UN’s humanitarian affairs office reported on November 20 that teams had recorded such work at 162 of the 356 flood-prone locations they had identified. Gaza’s municipalities are asking for pumps, backup generators and fuel before the next storm, as well as 10,000 tonnes of cement for emergency repairs and mobile homes that can withstand wind and rain.

Source: Al Jazeera | Published: 2026-11-25 21:03 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/25/winter-rains-threaten-1000-gaza-shelter-sites-councils-warn?traffic_source=rss

Decorations for Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade and the holidays are installed outside Macy's Herald Square, as the Empire State Building rises in the background, in New York City, U.S., Nov. 24, 2025.

Macy's on Wednesday announced it's postponing the annual Thanksgiving Day Parade due to severe weather.

The parade, held each year on Thursday morning, will now take place on Saturday at 8:30 a.m. ET, according to the company. The New York City area is expected to have heavy rain and thunderstorms on Thanksgiving.

"The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our city and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year's celebration," Macy's said in a statement.

This year's event marks the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. The annual event has never been canceled due to weather, though it was suspended between 1942 and 1944 for World War II.

item.title: US Education Department probes Virginia schools after sexual abuse scandal
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

US Education Department probes Virginia schools after sexual abuse scandal

Virginia schools face scrutiny after revelations of abuse and widespread failures in mandatory staff background checks.

The United States Department of Education says it is launching an investigation and withholding funding from a district in the state of Virginia after local officials shut down all of its schools in the wake of a child sexual abuse scandal involving its employees.

“Parents should never have to question whether their child’s school is aiding and abetting child predators,” US Secretary of Education Linda McMahon said in a statement on Tuesday. “The Trump Administration is taking decisive enforcement action to hold those responsible accountable and ensure Virginia schools are safe places for children to learn.”

Officials in Albemarle County, Virginia, announced they were closing all 29 schools in the district last week, after learning that more than 500 staff had not been subjected to a routine background screening for a history of child sexual abuse. The school system has about 2,800 employees, and only a fraction of its $284m budget comes from the federal government.

Local officials emphasised that none of the 524 employees is suspected of abuse.

Approximately 14,000 students attend the schools, and parents have scrambled to find childcare, while many who depend on free school meals for their children have had to look for other sources of food.

Bob Beard, a member of the Albemarle school board, told Al Jazeera that families were struggling to deal with the shutdown, but schools would reopen on Monday.

The child abuse allegations have shaken the county and caught the attention of the Trump administration.

A former elementary school teacher was arrested for possession of child sexual abuse material earlier this year, while a counsellor at another school was put on leave and later indicted on 20 counts of sexual crimes involving seven different children, according to the Albemarle County Police Department.

Two county school officials and a school principal were later charged with failure to report child abuse, and the county’s superintendent of schools resigned.

‘Processes not followed’

Jason Grant, a spokesman for Albemarle County Public Schools, told Al Jazeera that none of the individuals implicated in those cases was among the 524 employees who were hired without the proper screening required to check for a history of child sexual abuse.

“This was not about having the policies in place, this was about processes that were not followed,” Grant said. He said officials were working with the state to “make sure the processes are in place to make sure this doesn’t happen again.”

Grant said all employees in the district undergo several stages of vetting, including a criminal background check and an attestation that they have no history of child abuse or neglect. Then the school system submits their information to the Virginia Department of Social Services to verify that they are not part of the agency’s abuse and neglect database.

For three years, it appears that vetting procedures were not consistently applied. Putting employees hired over that period on leave to carry out background checks meant schools would not be able to run, so officials decided to close them until next week.

“Those were for every range of employee, from teachers to bus drivers to substitutes and across the division, so we couldn’t get coverage for that amount of people,” Grant said.

All but three of the 524 employees have now been properly vetted, and none had background issues, Grant said, adding that the county will reopen schools on Monday.

The Trump administration has long called for the dismantling of the Department of Education. The US president signed an executive order last year that tried to set that in motion.

The department, which distributes federal funding to states for use in schools, also traditionally investigates whether local officials are complying with civil rights laws banning discrimination against minorities and marginalised groups.

Since returning to office in 2025, the Trump administration has cut more than half of the department’s staff and subjected it to wider changes it says are aimed at rooting out “diversity, equity, and inclusion” (DEI) policies.

Source: Al Jazeera | Published: 2026-11-25 20:52 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/25/us-education-department-probes-virginia-schools-after-sexual-abuse-scandal?traffic_source=rss

item.title: 10-year Treasury yield slides despite sticky inflation data as investors buy bonds for protection
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

U.S. Treasury yields fell on Wednesday, with investors fleeing to bonds for protection after October's personal consumption expenditures price index showed that inflation continued to accelerate.

The 10-year Treasury note yield — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — was more than 3 basis points lower at 4.866%.

The yield on the 2-year Treasury note, which typically moves in line with short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, was down more than 2 basis points at 4.65%.

The longer-dated 30-year Treasury yield, which tends to track geopolitical events, was more than 3 basis points lower at 5.254%.

One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.

The personal consumption expenditures price index — the Federal Reserve's preferred gauge of underlying inflation — rose 3.8% year over year for October, in line with the Dow Jones consensus estimate. Separately, economic growth came in much stronger for the third quarter. Gross domestic product rose at a 4.3% annualized rate, according to a revised Commerce Department estimate.

The data reinforced expectations for another Fed rate hike in December.

"[I]t is more urgent than ever that Fed officials step up the pace of interest rate hikes to cool off economic demand," said Chris Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS. "Rate hikes are coming. Lots of them. Bet on it. The economy and inflation are literally on fire."

Wednesday's drop comes after yields steadied on Tuesday, with traders digesting softer demand for a 5-year Treasury auction.

Trading is shortened this week due to the Thanksgiving holiday. Bond markets will be closed all day Thursday for Thanksgiving, and will close at 2 p.m. E.T. on Friday.

— CNBC's Jeff Cox contributed reporting.

Source: CNBC Top | Published: 2026-11-25 21:02 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/25/treasury-yields-bonds-inflation.html

item.title: Vance says he was assured Jensen Huang was not under DOJ investigation
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Vice President JD Vance said Wednesday that Attorney General Todd Blanche told him Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was not under investigation.

"I was told by the Department of Justice and multiple officials in our national security apparatus that he was under no investigation," Vance told reporters in Ohio on Wednesday after being asked what assurances he had gotten that Huang was not under investigation. "Not even that he was about to be prosecuted; that he's under no investigation."

Vance spoke two days after President Donald Trump told CNBC in an interview that an investigation had been done.

Trump was asked what Blanche had told him about potential criminal liability for Huang and the question of whether Nvidia chips had ended up in China in violation of U.S. export laws.

"They did a pretty good investigation, and they felt that he, himself, was exonerated," Trump said Monday.

Reuters reported Wednesday that the Department of Justice did not conduct a formal investigation into Huang before Trump pushed for his reinstatement as CEO.

Blanche had concluded there was no evidence Huang had broken any laws based on investigations into Nvidia clients Super Micro Computer and Megaspeed, according to the report.

The DOJ did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Reuters report. And the White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on Vance saying Huang was under no investigation when Trump had said there was one. Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment about Vance's remarks.

Blanche on Tuesday dodged questions about whether there had been an investigation.

"What the president said is that he talked to a lot of people going into the decision that he made to encourage the board to reinstate him," Blanche said after being asked whether the DOJ had investigated Huang and, if so, what were the results of the probe.

Huang was reinstated as CEO of Nvidia on Monday, after the chipmaker's board of directors said it had received "input from senior levels of the United States government" that Huang was not a national security risk. Trump took credit for Huang's reinstatement in the interview with CNBC shortly after Nvidia's announcement.

Huang resigned following The New York Times reporting multiple affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who is alleged to be a spy for Beijing and who was an executive for the Singapore-based cloud provider Megaspeed.

The reporting added fuel to allegations that Nvidia should have known its artificial intelligence chips were being diverted to China and being used by Chinese companies, violating U.S. export laws.

"The product they create is a very important part of us staying ahead of the SI arms race with China. We really do care about ensuring those chips do not fall into the wrong hands," Vance said, using the Trump administration's preferred acronym for AI, which the president calls "super intelligence."

"We actually see this is an opportunity for Nvidia to focus on complying with American export controls, and we think Jensen Huang is going to take that very seriously," Vance continued.

"We received the assurances that he was not under any significant — he was under no investigation — and the accusations against him were based on anonymous reporting, not on actual evidence," Vance said.

On Tuesday, Trump left the door open to pardon Huang in an interview with the New York Post, but Vance said on Wednesday that the CEO doesn't need one.

"I don't think he needs a pardon at all," Vance said. "I haven't seen any evidence again that he committed a crime. And if there is evidence that he committed a crime, then that's up to relevant authorities to actually bring a prosecution against him."

Huang is scheduled to appear for a closed-door interview with House committees about his dealings with Megaspeed on Tuesday. At the same time, Nvidia will hold its annual conference where it showcases new technology in Washington.

— Kevin Breuninger contributed to this report.

Source: CNBC Top | Published: 2026-11-25 21:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/25/vance-jensen-huang-nvidia-doj-investigation.html

item.title: Did GTA 6 really recreate Charlie Kirk's assassination?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Did GTA 6 really recreate Charlie Kirk's assassination?

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

Issued on:

Just days after its release, Grand Theft Auto 6 has become a vehicle for political misinformation. Viral footage falsely claims the game features a mission recreating Charlie Kirk’s assassination, while pro-Russian accounts are sharing fake screenshots containing anti-Ukrainian messages. Meanwhile, Russia’s own Defence Ministry has exploited the game's popularity to promote military recruitment. Vedika Bahl explains how GTA 6 is being used to push real political agendas in Truth or Fake.

After years of anticipation, Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6) finally hit the shelves on November 19. Almost immediately, social media users began sharing footage of supposedly controversial scenes and missions incorporated into the new video game.

Known for its violent gameplay, satire of American society and deliberately provocative content, the franchise has become fertile ground for political misinformation.

Fake Charlie Kirk assassination mission goes viral

On the day of the game's release, a video began circulating on X claiming that developer Rockstar Games had included a mission recreating the assassination of American conservative activist Charlie Kirk, who was killed in September 2025.

One post amassed nearly a million views, with several social media users expressing outrage over the developers' alleged decision to incorporate Kirk's killing into the storyline.

However, the footage has nothing to do with GTA 6. Fact-checkers at NewsGuard traced the video back to GTA Online, the multiplayer component of the franchise's previous instalment, GTA 5, where players can design and publish their own missions.

Rockstar Games did not create the mission. In fact, according to reporting by entertainment magazine Variety earlier this year, the company removed user-created missions recreating Kirk's assassination and added his name to a list of prohibited terms.

While the user-made footage is genuine gameplay, it has been shared out of context to capitalise on the popularity of the new release.

Fabricated screenshots push anti-Ukrainian narratives

Beyond American politics, GTA 6's release is also being exploited by pro-Russian accounts to spread anti-Ukrainian misinformation.

Several Telegram channels have circulated an image supposedly showing graffiti depicting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky alongside the word "WANTED". Users claimed the graffiti appeared specifically in the Polish-language version of GTA 6.

While the game supports Polish, changing the language settings does not alter its virtual environment. Verified gameplay footage of the same location shows the "WANTED" graffiti without Zelensky's face, indicating that the image was digitally manipulated.

Another fabricated screenshot supposedly shows an in-game television news broadcast featuring a map depicting Ukraine as part of Russian territory.

As reported by Ukrainian news agency Ukrinform, the image contains SynthID, an invisible digital watermark embedded in content generated or edited using Google's artificial intelligence tools.

These types of fabrications appear aimed at exploiting the game's global popularity to imply that anti-Ukrainian narratives are culturally accepted in the mainstream.

Russia uses GTA 6 imagery to recruit soldiers

Meanwhile, Russia's own Defence Ministry has capitalised on the excitement surrounding the game's release to promote military recruitment.

On November 19, the day of the game's release, the ministry published a recruitment poster on Telegram imitating GTA 6's distinctive visual style, encouraging Russians to sign up for military service to fight in Ukraine.

Accompanied by the slogan "Choose your own mission", the advertisement borrows from the language and aesthetics of the video game.

Unlike the fabricated gameplay screenshots circulating online, the recruitment poster was genuinely published by the Russian Defence Ministry, although the artwork itself appears to have been AI-generated.

Source: France24 English | Published: 2026-11-25 20:38 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/truth-or-fake/20261125-did-gta-6-really-recreate-charlie-kirk-s-assassination

item.title: Certain fungi turn specialized plant cells into water-carrying cells using one protein
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence, and concrete detail

Certain fungi turn specialized plant cells into water-carrying cells using one protein

Can a pathogen that causes damage to a plant also make that plant more resilient to drought? An international research team led by the University of Göttingen has investigated this apparent paradox. The researchers discovered how certain fungi promote the formation of new water-conducting cells in plants. At the same time, infected plants showed increased tolerance to drought stress. The results were published in the journal Cell Host & Microbe.

The team analyzed fungi of the genus Verticillium, which can infect many crops and cause significant damage to plants such as oilseed rape. By comparing the genomes of various Verticillium strains that cause different disease symptoms, the researchers discovered a crucial genetic difference. They were then able to demonstrate, through targeted genetic modifications of the fungi and by studying infected plants, which fungal protein is responsible for the unusual alteration in the plant's "xylem"—the system that moves water to the plant's stems and leaves.

This protein, known as TRADE ("Transdifferentiation Effector"), is released by the fungus and enters the plant cells. There, it interferes with the regulation of genetic messenger molecules (mRNAs), which serve as blueprints for proteins. Through a cascade of different plant proteins, TRADE prolongs the lifespan of certain mRNAs. This activates developmental programming that causes certain specialized plant cells to abandon their original identity and transform into new water-conducting xylem cells.

"Surprisingly, plants infected by the Verticillium fungi investigated in our study retain higher water contents under drought stress than uninfected plants. Whether the additional water-conducting cells are directly responsible for this increased tolerance to drought remains to be investigated," said professor Volker Lipka at Göttingen University's Department of Plant Cell Biology, who led the research.

"The fact that a pathogen can, on one hand, damage plants but, on the other hand, increase their resilience to drought highlights the astonishing complexity of these interactions," adds lead author Dr. Konrad Subieta from the same department.

The study was carried out in close collaboration between the Department of Plant Cell Biology and other plant science and microbiology departments within the Faculty of Biology and Psychology and the Faculty of Forest Sciences and Forest Ecology at Göttingen University, as well as the University of Tokyo and the RIKEN Centre for Sustainable Resource Science (CSRS) in Japan.

In the future, this knowledge could help make crops more resilient to drought. An understanding of the molecular mechanisms involved could be used independently of the fungus to improve plant resilience.

Publication details

Konrad Subieta et al., Drought tolerance-enhancing fungal pathogens reprogram plant cell identity through mRNA turnover, Cell Host & Microbe (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.chom.2026.11.002

Journal information: Cell Host & Microbe

Provided by University of Göttingen

Source: Phys.org | Published: 2026-11-25 21:20 UTC | Difficulty: 80/100

Original link: https://phys.org/news/2026-11-fungi-specialized-cells-protein.html

item.title: Carbon nanotube measurements reveal quantum model better explains collective electron behavior
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original research, technical detail

Carbon nanotube measurements reveal quantum model better explains collective electron behavior

An international team of scientists from Lithuania, Finland and Israel has conducted both theoretical and experimental research into carbon nanotubes, becoming the first to demonstrate which physical model governs the motion and interactions of electrons within them.

Researchers from the Center for Physical Sciences and Technology (FTMC) in Lithuania, who participated in the study, emphasize that these results will provide fresh momentum for the development of highly sensitive devices. The paper, published in ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces, was featured on one of the journal's covers.

Highly sensitive sensors as the goal

Let us first take a closer look at the cover illustration itself, which was largely created by one of the study's authors, Dr. Justinas Jorudas, a physicist at the FTMC Department of Optoelectronics. The image depicts intertwined graphene nanotubes, microscopic hollow "straws" approximately 20,000 to 30,000 times thinner than a human hair, with walls consisting of a layer only one carbon atom thick.

"It is important to understand that such a nanotube is not simply a graphene sheet rolled up several times. It is a continuous cylindrical structure. The electrical and mechanical properties of a nanotube depend on the orientation of the graphene lattice, that is, the arrangement of the atoms. As a result, different nanotubes can 'behave' differently," explains another co-author of the study, Dr. Irmantas Kašalynas, head of the Terahertz Photonics Laboratory within the FTMC Department of Optoelectronics.

According to the scientist, these structures could in the future be used as electrodes in a variety of devices. Compared with conventional metallic electrodes, carbon nanotube electrodes can be not only electrically conductive but also flexible and transparent. This makes them particularly promising for next-generation displays, sensors and wearable electronics.

FTMC receives these microscopic "straws" from its research partners at Aalto University in Finland. Individual nanotubes cannot be seen with the naked eye, but when vast numbers of them form a network, the material resembles a very lightweight sponge. Depending on the thickness of the network, its color can range from grayish to almost black.

Kašalynas's laboratory is particularly interested in the potential of nanotubes in technologies that utilize terahertz waves, electromagnetic waves located in the frequency range between microwaves and infrared radiation. One area of research currently being pursued involves highly sensitive sensors based on terahertz plasmonics.

Put simply, plasmonics studies collective oscillations of electrons known as plasmons. Certain materials absorb terahertz waves in distinctive ways, making it possible to identify them using specialized devices, much like recognizing a unique fingerprint. Plasmonics strengthens the interaction between electron oscillations and a material, making it easier to detect and distinguish even very small amounts of a substance from others.

"Such sensors could be useful whenever only a very small quantity of a sample is available, for instance when detecting specific biological molecules, nucleic acids or other substances. We are currently conducting experiments with lactose and sucrose. Our goal is to determine whether such compounds can be detected using extremely small samples, even smaller than a single drop of liquid.

"Various standard methods already exist for measuring large quantities of material. However, when only minute amounts are available, more sensitive solutions are required. It is precisely in such situations that plasmonic sensors may offer a significant advantage," says the FTMC researcher.

A similar principle is used in certain biological tests. During the COVID-19 pandemic, for example, plasmonic sensors were developed that could detect specific molecules through the changes they produced on a sensor's surface. Such technologies can operate at room temperature and do not require complex laboratory conditions. Moreover, much of plasmonics research is conducted in the infrared or visible-light range, whereas the FTMC team investigates these phenomena in the terahertz frequency domain.

Practical applications are expected in the near future. However, the study was featured on the journal cover because of the theoretical and fundamental calculations that successfully described the experimental results.

Theoretical knowledge that provides the foundation for future technologies

Why is this significant? Carbon nanotubes are excellent electrical conductors, but it has not been fully understood whether their properties remain the same under different conditions. To address this question, Lithuanian researchers and their international colleagues investigated how electrons move within nanotubes and how their behavior changes when exposed to electromagnetic waves of different frequencies.

In classical physics, electrons in metals are typically described as particles that interact only weakly with one another. This model successfully explains the electrical properties of many conventional materials. However, according to Kašalynas, the situation in nanotubes is different. Unlike in most other materials, electrons here can move only through extremely narrow channels. In addition, nanotubes form interconnected networks, meaning that electrons continuously transfer from one tube to another.

By examining the material across a broad frequency range, using ultraviolet, visible, terahertz and infrared radiation, the researchers found that electrons in carbon nanotubes do not behave as independent particles. Instead, they interact with one another, and the nature of these interactions depends on the frequency.…

Source: Phys.org | Published: 2026-11-25 21:00 UTC | Difficulty: 80/100

Original link: https://phys.org/news/2026-11-carbon-nanotube-reveal-quantum-electron.html

item.title: Your risk of heart attack and stroke could be forecasted 30 years in advance, study suggests
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original research, significant health implications

Your risk of heart attack and stroke could be forecasted 30 years in advance, study suggests

Researchers knew that cholesterol and blood pressure are important for estimating stroke risk, but a new study suggests these should be measured far earlier in life.

Cardiovascular disease has long been linked to risk factors like high blood pressure and cholesterol — but a new study suggests that these factors, combined with proteins in the blood, could help forecast people's risk of heart attack and stroke decades in advance.

The new study, published Monday (Nov. 23) in the journal JAMA Network Open, took a broad view of the factors that spike the risk of stroke or heart attack. The researchers found that warning signs for these conditions can be seen in patients' health data up to 30 years before they happen.

The researchers say their work shows that some understudied biomarkers — measurable signals in the blood — could be useful tools in anticipating later conditions.

"We did know that there are some well-established risk factors that are related to heart disease, for example, blood pressure, cholesterol," said study co-author Dorien Kimenai, an epidemiologist at the University of Edinburgh. But "nobody really has looked at the patterns of these risk factors prior to when these people are getting cardiovascular events — not systematically."

For the new study, the scientists tracked data patterns from a diverse group of nearly 114,000 healthy people over 34 years. Their data spanned four long-term health studies conducted in the U.S., U.K., and Norway. At the end of the study period, the researchers divided data from participants who were still healthy at that juncture from those who had experienced heart attacks or strokes and either died or survived the events.

But even at the study's outset, these two groups' blood pressure and cholesterol data showed a clear divergence.

"We did see that, even three decades before, already, that these patterns were different," said Kimenai. That suggests, she added, that the difference between the two groups likely began even earlier than that.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The team also divided their participants by sex and age, finding that men and women experienced different trajectories in their cardiovascular disease risk over time. Women, on average, started with lower blood pressure than men in middle age, but that switched later in life.

"It shows that the age effect is as important as the sex differences," Kimenai said. In short, both factors need to be taken into account.

Dr. Sintip Pattanakuhar, a clinician scientist at the University of Strathclyde in Scotland who was not involved in the study, said that while these risk factors can't be modified in the way blood pressure or cholesterol can, age and sex could be incorporated into personalized screening programs for cardiovascular risk.

The team also looked at the trajectories of biomarker proteins that circulate in the bloodstream and are linked to cardiovascular disease. These include cardiac troponin and N-terminal pro B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), which are released by damaged heart muscle tissue and used to diagnose a heart attack. They also included C-reactive protein, a liver-borne molecule that signals rising inflammation in the body.

Differences in cardiac troponin and C-reactive protein were visible in people who would go on to have a heart attack or stroke up to 30 years before they happened. For NT-proBNP, the differences emerged about 10 years before.

That said, Kimenai cautioned that the biomarker data came from fewer participants than the full study cohort, so these results bear further confirmation.

Dr. Deepak Bhatt, director of the Mount Sinai Fuster Heart Hospital in New York, said the study's blood pressure and cholesterol data confirmed what cardiologists had long suspected about these risk factors: that these modifiable factors predict cardiovascular disease. Bhatt, who was not involved in the study, added that the biomarker data in this study built on other studies that have also shown that cardiovascular events can be predicted years before they happen.

"What this adds is that it's actually predicting events decades before," he said.

The study's clearest message was that people should get their cardiovascular risk factors checked early, Kimenai said.

"When you're 40 years old, get your risk assessments and your blood pressure measured," she said. "Because these are the things you can change. If you've then been identified as having hypertension, then you can get those drugs that are very effective and safe and efficient to alter the pattern."

However, while the value of checking blood pressure and cholesterol is well established, Kimenai and Bhatt agreed that the clinical value of the biomarker data was less clear at this stage. Bhatt said that he might advise a patient with high blood pressure to start medication and cut out salt, for example, but the way forward for someone with an elevated biomarker reading is less clear for now.

"Ideally, more work will be done" to see whether panels of biomarkers, perhaps combined with tools that measure genetic risk, could flag patients at very high risk of having heart attacks and strokes and should be treated differently than a patient with lower risk, Bhatt suggested. "That's sort of the missing piece of the Holy Grail of prevention."

item.title: James Webb and Euclid telescopes discover record-breaking black hole at the edge of the universe
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original discovery, significant astronomical implications

James Webb and Euclid telescopes discover record-breaking quasar at the edge of the universe

Scientists have discovered the earliest-known quasar lurking in the ancient universe — and it's growing at a slower rate than scientists believed possible.

Astronomers have just discovered the earliest-known quasar — and it's 40 million years older than the previous record holder. The finding, which observed the object at just 630 million years after the Big Bang, could help researchers to better understand how black holes developed in the early universe.

"Finding quasars at ever-increasing distances, at the edge of the observable universe, teaches us something about how the black holes in their centres grew," study co-author Julien Wolf, a researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy, said in a statement. "The closer to the Big Bang we find them, the faster their black holes must have grown or the more massive they must have been at birth — or both."

The object — estimated to have the mass of 360 million suns — was described in a new study published Tuesday (Nov. 24) in the journal Astronomy and Astrophysics.

A quasar, short for "quasi-stellar radio source," is an incredibly bright core at the center of some galaxies —a region known as the active galactic nucleus (AGN). They form when supermassive black holes, which lurk at the hearts of most galaxies, start to binge on nearby matter. Once enough swirling material accumulates around these black holes, it heats up and glows intensely before falling into the object. What sets quasars apart from other AGNs is their sheer luminosity; they can be brighter than all the stars in a galaxy combined.

Quasars were much more common early in the universe than they are today. They are thought to have peaked in number about 10 billion years ago. Observing them can give scientists important clues as to how galaxies evolve — and how their supermassive black holes develop.

Because it takes time for light to travel, observing celestial objects that are very far away is tantamount to peering back in time. We see galaxies very near to Earth as they were only a few thousand years ago; conversely, we see galaxies very far away from us as they were billions of years ago, because their light is only now reaching our telescopes. The older the galaxy, the more red its light becomes as it stretches across the universe — a phenomenon called "redshift."

Using data from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the European Space Agency's Euclid Wide Survey, the researchers behind the new study identified a quasar with a redshift of 8.13 — the first such object ever found with a redshift beyond 8. This makes it the oldest quasar yet observed, at approximately 13.1 billion years old. For reference, the universe itself is thought to be 13.8 billion years old.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

- 'Baby quasars' spotted by James Webb telescope could transform our understanding of monster black holes

- The oldest, brightest black holes in the universe were born from violent gas attacks, new study suggests

- James Webb Space Telescope sees lonely supermassive black hole-powered quasars in the early universe

The scientists named the object Dún Aonghasa, after a prehistoric cliff fort on the Atlantic-facing edge of Inis Mór, an island off the coast of Ireland. The name is meant to reflect the quasar's position at the very edge of our current observational frontier for the cosmos.

According to the researchers, Dún Aonghasa also appears to be growing more slowly than astronomers previously thought possible, given its size. This suggests that its supermassive black hole may have gone through a massive growth spurt, followed by a period of much slower growth in the distant past. The discovery could put new constraints on black hole growth models, which are already being challenged by previous JWST detections of supermassive monsters that seem to have grown too big for their early place in cosmic history.

Future observations from Euclid and JWST could help researchers test this hypothesis and see if it holds for other ancient quasars, the researchers said.

See how much you know about black holes with our black hole quiz!

Joanna Thompson is a science journalist and runner based in New York. She holds a B.S. in Zoology and a B.A. in Creative Writing from North Carolina State University, as well as a Master's in Science Journalism from NYU's Science, Health and Environmental Reporting Program. Find more of her work in Scientific American, The Daily Beast, Atlas Obscura or Audubon Magazine.

item.title: The Scientist Who Wants to Save Cranberries
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, environmental impact

A Thanksgiving staple faces an uncertain future if the weather disruptions wrought by climate change continue to disrupt the harvest.

But in Wisconsin, the region that leads the nation in producing this native North American fruit, some growers are seeing harvests decline as the state’s cranberry bogs have been hit by heat waves, drought, cold snaps, and hailstorms in the past couple of years. Last month, Sondra Brancel, an appraiser specializing in cranberry marshes, or bogs, and a member of the American Society of Farm Managers and Rural Appraisers, told RFDTV that Wisconsin cranberry growers were expecting reduced yields, as they had last year, attributing the downtick to climatic disruptions.

“For the second year in a row, we’re experiencing a lower harvest,” she said. “Most of that almost always has to do with Mother Nature, of course, like in all aspects of agriculture.”

Read more: “What Exactly Is a Superfood Anyway?”

More recent numbers from the Department of Agriculture indicate that the Wisconsin harvest, which accounts for about 60 percent of the national crop, was somewhat rescued by a late-season harvesting push, with a four percent increase over last year. But the warning signs of a shifting climate worry cranberry farmers and enthusiastic consumers of the fruit alike.

One self-described “cranberry fanatic” is Todd Michael, a plant genomicist at California-based Salk Institute for Biological Studies. Michael and his collaborators published research earlier this year in the journal Plants People Planet that offers a ray of hope to the continued production of cranberries in a changing climate. The scientists experimented with crossing Vaccinium oxycoccos, a wild cranberry relative that grows in northern latitudes, with the cultivated cranberry (Vaccinium macrocarpon) that makes its way onto Thanksgiving tables and, more importantly, into leftover turkey sandwiches.

I spoke with Michael about his findings, the wonders of bog-front living, the future of the iconic Thanksgiving fruit, and what about cranberries mesmerizes him.

Why cranberries?

I’m a cranberry fanatic. We think of cranberries this time of year, because it’s Thanksgiving, and it’s iconic for Thanksgiving because it’s also from the harvest in the fall. I grew up in New Jersey, right on the edge of the bogs, so I’m very familiar with it. I’ve always eaten cranberries. I drink cranberry juice every single day. So it’s just a part of my life.

My first faculty position was at Rutgers University, and as soon as I got there, I reached out to the USDA researchers at the cranberry station wanting to do some of these genomics. Basically, I want to go back to my roots, so to speak.

You say there’s a decrease in cranberry production. Is Vaccinium macrocarpon imperiled in some way? And if so, how is that playing out?

I don’t know if I’d say “imperiled.” Cranberry has been cultivated for 200 years, and there really hasn’t been much breeding done on cranberry. A lot of the varieties that are grown in Massachusetts, which is the second highest producer of cranberries, New Jersey, which is the third, and then Wisconsin, which is the number one producer of cranberries, all have different varieties that are really one step removed from “land races,” or wild selections of cranberry.

There’s a real opportunity to do some breeding in cranberries and for those specific locations. It’s predominantly a bog-grown plant. So both in New Jersey and Massachusetts, it’s like right on the coast in the bog areas.

So imperiled is the wrong word. But as I understand it there are some areas of its traditional range where—I don’t know if endangered is the right word—I think there are places where they’re losing wetland habitat. Is that right?

Oh, yeah. I mean the loss of wetlands is definitely a huge factor in terms of the decrease of the species in general. In Massachusetts, it’s a combination of water and stress from changing climate but also houses—so loss of wetlands or bogs. They do have a pretty aggressive program in Massachusetts at least where they don’t really want bogs to go out of production. So they’re incentivized to either do restoration of bogs or bring them back into a native state instead of building houses.

In other words, discouraging bog-front living?

Which isn’t as fun as it might sound, because they harvest the cranberries very early in the morning, and they go work on them very early in the morning. People build these big houses on the edge of bogs, and then they’re like, “What are all these people doing in our backyard?”

Getting to your research, the idea was to breed in traits from wild relatives of cranberries that might help them weather some of the things that you just talked about—the drying out and the cold snaps. I don’t think you went about it as someone who was breeding plants might have a hundred years ago in terms of just taking one plant, breeding it with the next, and seeing what happens. You did a little more of a targeted approach. How did that work?

We’d classify this as pre-breeding. In our previous paper, we actually sequenced the small cranberry genome, Vaccinium oxycoccos, which is native to the northern latitudes. The plant that we talk about and that we work on is actually native to Alaska.

We started off by sequencing the genome and getting some ideas that there could be alleles or genes that are important that we’d want to move over to the cultivated variety. And that gave us an idea of what we could be looking for in terms of traits if we made crosses with the cultivated cranberry.

Then, in the actual experiment that we describe in our most recent work, we wanted to know if we make a hybrid between the wild cranberry and the cultivated cranberry, what type of immediate responses do they have to changes in temperature?…

item.title: While Exploring a 500-Year-Old Shipwreck Off the Coast of Sweden, Underwater Archaeologists Discovered Medieval Chain Mail That May Have Belonged to German Mercenaries
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original discovery, historical significance

While Exploring a 500-Year-Old Shipwreck Off the Coast of Sweden, Underwater Archaeologists Discovered Medieval Chain Mail That May Have Belonged to German Mercenaries

“Gribshunden” was the “floating castle” of King Hans of Denmark and Norway. It exploded and sank in 1495, but the Baltic Sea’s low salinity has kept contents remarkably well preserved

More than five centuries after a royal Danish warship exploded and sank off the coast of Sweden, underwater archaeologists have uncovered finely crafted chain mail armor resting on the Baltic seafloor.

The copper-alloy mail fragments were recovered in October from the wreck of Gribshunden, or Griffin, the 15th-century flagship of King Hans of Denmark and Norway. Researchers discovered the armor alongside a rare munitions chest while surveying the area beneath the vessel’s forecastle, an elevated combat platform at the ship’s bow.

“It was in the process of documenting the chest that I unexpectedly discovered exposed mail-armor fragments in the vicinity of the chest, along other items that could indicate more chests,” Rolf Warming, an archaeologist at Stockholm University who leads the project with Södertörn University’s Johan Rönnby, tells Live Science’s Kristina Killgrove in an email. “It was only by chance that we came across it, and it shows just how much is still on the wreck site.”

To map the newly explored section of the ship, the researchers paired diver-led excavation with high-resolution 3D photogrammetry and an uncrewed robotic survey boat operating on the surface, according to a statement. Together, the armor, the munitions chest and earlier finds of lead objects possibly linked to ammunition molds could point to a dedicated military storage zone.

“Historical sources indicate that German mercenaries, or Landsknechts, were aboard Griffin when it sank in 1495,” Rodrigo Pacheco-Ruiz, a maritime archaeologist at the University of Southampton and co-investigator on the project, says in the statement. “This part of the ship may therefore have been used to stow equipment associated with these soldiers, including their armor, although we’ve yet to establish a precise function for the space.”

When Gribshunden set sail from Copenhagen in the summer of 1495, it led an 18-ship royal fleet bound for a political summit in Kalmar, Sweden, as Smithsonian magazine’s Jo Marchant reported in 2021. Hans, who ruled Denmark and Norway from 1481 to 1513, hoped to quell Swedish rebels and revive the Kalmar Union, which united the three kingdoms. Acting as both a diplomatic showcase and a “floating castle,” Marchant wrote, the flagship carried Danish noblemen, courtiers, a royal astronomer and roughly 150 German mercenary soldiers.

“It was important to demonstrate military prowess, and the German and Swiss mercenaries were the finest you could get at that time,” Warming tells Live Science.

The voyage ended in catastrophe while the ship lay anchored north of the small island of Stora Ekon, near Ronneby in southern Sweden. Gribshunden erupted in flames and sank rapidly. A 16th-century account of Hans’ life suggests its gunpowder stores accidentally ignited, while other hypotheses point to a possible lightning strike. Many aboard perished in the fire or drowned, though Hans survived because he was ashore at the time.

Rediscovered by local divers in 1971 and formally identified in 2013, the Gribshunden has survived in remarkable condition, thanks to the Baltic Sea’s low salinity, which keeps wood-eating shipworms at bay.

In fact, they may have weakened the hulls of the ships of the Spanish Armada when it failed in attacking England in 1588, leaving the ships vulnerable to cannonballs and storms.

item.title: Ancient 'supermountains' under Antarctica supercharged complex life on Earth, study claims ‪—‬ but not everyone agrees
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original research, geological implications

Ancient 'supermountains' under Antarctica supercharged complex life on Earth, study claims — but not everyone agrees

A study claims that ancient 'supervolcanoes' hidden under Antarctica may have provided the nutrients that led to an explosion of complex life millions of years later. But not everyone agrees.

Scientists have found the remnants of supermountains in the seabed around Antarctica. They say these ancient peaks may have provided the nutrients that led to an explosion of complex life millions of years later. However, others are more skeptical about these conclusions.

About 600 million years ago, landmasses in the Southern Hemisphere collided to form the supercontinent Gondwana, which included what is now South America, Africa, Arabia, Madagascar, India, Australia and Antarctica. At that time, there was multicellular life, but it was very primitive.

Previous research suggested that the continental collision created massive Himalaya-like mountains in what is now Antarctica. Now, in a new study, published online Sept. 12 in the journal Earth and Planetary Science Letters, scientists say they've found the sediment that accumulated in the oceans when the Gondwanan mountains eroded over millennia.

"The results suggest that the assembly of Gondwana involved multiple major continental collisions, producing an extensive network of mountain belts comparable in scale to the modern Himalayas and Tibetan Plateau," Nathan Daczko, a petrologist at Macquarie University in Australia who was not involved in the research, told Live Science in an email.

"The study highlights just how much geological history remains hidden beneath Antarctica."

Ancient minerals

Most of Antarctica is trapped beneath an ice sheet, so it is difficult to understand its evolutionary history.

To address this, the team drilled into the seabed at 12 locations around Antarctica, extracting soil samples. They were looking for ancient crystals called detrital zircon. Zircon is a mineral that grows in rocks and is strong enough to remain chemically intact when the rock erodes.

"We can date it very, very precisely, and from the geochemistry, and especially the trace elements, we can determine where the zircon came from," Ian Campbell, a geochemist at the Australian National University and a co-author of the study, told Live Science.

They dated 1,712 zircon grains extracted from marine sediments and compared the abundance of zircons in Antarctica with a global zircon database, across different time scales.

"We have used the zircon record to show that the mountains that formed during the amalgamation of Gondwana were the largest and most extensive in the history of the Earth, and they included some very high mountains like the Himalayas today," Campbell said.

Alan Collins, an earth scientist at the University of Adelaide in Australia, said that he was surprised by the scale of the erosion from these rocks. "It beautifully supports ideas that the mountains that formed as the supercontinent Gondwana amalgamated were amongst the largest on Earth through deep time," he told Live Science in an email.

The formation of Gondwama produced one-fifth of the world's zircons, and the creation of the supercontinent Pangaea around 320 million years ago produced 14%, the study found.

Elias Rugen, a geochemist at the University of Southampton in the U.K. who wasn't involved in the research, was surprised by the "abundance of zircons associated with Gondwana's assembly in the Antarctica samples." "It is remarkable how much information about Antarctica's geological past can be recovered from these tiny minerals, particularly when so much of the continent remains hidden beneath ice," he said.

However, he cautioned against estimating the range's height from the zircon data. "It is really difficult to infer a mountain's height from data like this," he said.

Sedimentary life source

The formation and erosion of the Gondwana supermountains had consequences for the rest of the planet and the life on it, the authors said.

"In order to get life, you need nutrients," Campbell said. "At that time, most of the life was in the oceans, so you need to get nutrients into the ocean."

Today, the world's biggest ongoing erosion event is the Himalayas. This massive mountain range is eroding, and sending sediment down rivers and into the ocean. This deep-sea sediment deposit is called the Bengal Fan and is Earth's largest such deposit.

In a similar way, Gondwana's massive mountains also "sent lots of nutrients into the ocean," Campbell said, which "significantly advanced the evolution of life" on Earth.

Soon after the formation of Gondwana, the planet entered the Cambrian period. This era, which lasted from about 541 million to 485 million years ago, saw a dramatic diversification of life on Earth, known as the Cambrian explosion. The period saw the rise of creatures such as chordates (animals with a dorsal nerve, including humans) and arthropods (the ancestors of insects and crustaceans).

The study's authors drew a link between Gondwana's supermountains and this rapid evolution of complex life. While the supermountains don't explain the Cambrian Explosion directly, they "provide the opportunity for it to happen," Campbell said. The paper suggests that these nutrients fed organisms that formed the base of the animal food web.

However, Daczko and Rugen are skeptical. "The methods used in this study cannot directly demonstrate that this particular mountain belt was directly responsible for the rise in oxygen or the Cambrian Explosion," Rugen said. "However, the evidence for a Gondwanan supermountain belt that would inevitably have had a substantial impact on Earth's biogeochemical cycles is growing."

Daczko said he would frame the link between the Gondwana's supermountains and the Cambrian explosion as "an exciting hypothesis rather than an established causal relationship."…

Source: Live Science | Published: 2026-11-25 20:06 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100

item.title: Five reasons why we should still make things with our hands
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original perspective, cultural significance

Five reasons why we should still make things with our hands

"Alex, time to wake up! You have a busy day ahead, with an important meeting at 8:30," announces the alarm in a soft but firm voice. Alex wakes up immediately, already thinking about the presentation that still needs a few finishing touches. In the kitchen, the coffee machine, set up for 7 a.m. sharp, has just finished brewing. "Alexa, set the temperature to 20 degrees," says Alex, reaching for the coffee.

But then, something catches Alex's attention: a little bonsai tree on the windowsill. For the next few minutes, Alex forgets about the coffee, the presentation and the meeting. Carefully trimming new shoots, removing dead leaves and checking the soil, Alex becomes completely absorbed in the task. The technology fades into the background. So does the stress.

For a few precious minutes, Alex is simply enjoying doing something with his own hands.

Whether it's gardening, knitting, cooking or repairing an old chair, making things with our hands can do much more than produce a finished object. AI will therefore never take away this pleasure, since our fascination with making things by hand has survived centuries of technological progress.

With your own hands

After months of reading research from psychology, medicine, arts and marketing, I brought together the findings of 181 studies in a review published in the journal Psychology & Marketing. What did I discover? In a world where AI and machines can do almost everything for you, there are at least five good reasons why you should still bother making things with your own hands:

1) Making things can make you happier.

Just like Alex, have you ever become so absorbed by making something with your hands that you completely forgot about your worries? You are not alone! In my review, out of the 181 studies, 38 explored the psychological benefits of handmade activities, while another 35 focused on the feelings of control and independence that these activities can provide. The repetitive and immersive nature of working with our hands gives us a break from the hectic pace of daily life, and some researchers even suggest it can transform us.

A study of 3,545 knitters worldwide found that those who knitted more frequently reported feeling calmer and happier. But the benefits go beyond relaxation. Creating something with your own hands, whether a simple Christmas decoration or a cake, can give you a sense of accomplishment that makes you feel more capable, in control and, overall, more empowered.

2) It changes your relationship with the things you own.

Not only will you feel better, but there is also this famous Ikea effect: People tend to value things more simply because they've made them themselves. A slightly crooked bookshelf might become your favorite piece of furniture if you made it yourself! Why is this good? Because, as explored in 42 of the studies I reviewed, making things can change the way you relate to them.

Students who were encouraged to make their own equipment for physical education classes increased their enthusiasm for exercising. But it doesn't stop at enthusiasm!

Studies show that people performed better when using equipment they've assembled themselves, partly because they felt more capable. The lesson? Next time you want your children to eat more vegetables, get them involved in preparing dinner! Or, next time you want to perform better at something, why not try assembling the equipment yourself?

3) It keeps your mind and body active.

Medical research has explored how handmade activities can improve physical endurance, motor skills, concentration and memory. In fact, 26 studies in my review explored the link between handmade activities and physical health. The health benefits of art therapy are widely talked about. But why wait until you have a health problem to take care of yourself? You can start today with something as simple as cooking, knitting or making a small artistic composition with your own hands!

4) It can connect you with others.

Making things doesn't have to be a solitary activity. From knitting circles to community workshops and online crafting groups, handmade activities can bring people together, creating friendships and a sense of belonging. Interestingly, 47 studies I reviewed explored the social connections that develop around handmade activities, while 41 examined how making things allows us to learn, teach and pass on traditions from one generation to the next.

Although I didn't always appreciate my father's DIY adventures as a child, I often helped him renovate the house or assisted him in repairing his car. The moments spent together in those shared activities were priceless. His passion for making things stayed with me. And perhaps that's another wonderful thing about making things with our hands: Sometimes, what we pass on isn't just a skill or an object, but a way of interacting with the world.

5) It can help you live more sustainably.

Why buy something new when you can repair, reuse or transform what you already own?

Among the studies I reviewed, 22 papers explore how upcycling old clothes or restoring furniture can help reduce waste and encourage more sustainable consumption habits. The growing maker movement, bringing together people who enjoy creating and repairing things themselves, is often associated with anti-consumption and a more environmentally conscious lifestyle.

In my recent ongoing research, I explored this topic through three experiments involving more than 1,700 participants in the United States. I found that people who considered restoring old furniture themselves anticipated stronger feelings of satisfaction from doing something good and greater feelings of well-being. They also perceived their choices as more sustainable and reported stronger intentions to engage in repairing activities.

Offer the gift of making…

item.title: These deer walk 300 miles a year. The race is on to save their migration
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: clear reporting, concrete detail, learning value

These deer walk 300 miles a year.

On a spring morning, a mule deer and her fawn follow a well-worn trail through the Wyoming sagebrush. They're on a 150-mile journey, one of the longest land migrations in the lower 48 states.

Like many other migrations in the U.S., the mule deer's epic journey is hidden in plain sight. Mule deer move in small groups instead of large herds, following pathways likely used for millennia. They're part of the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem in western Wyoming, a place where elk, deer and pronghorn antelope still have the space to move across vast landscapes.

They migrate with careful seasonal choreography, timed to reach the best feeding grounds in summer and avoid the harshest winter weather. Still, as the climate gets hotter, that timing is being tested.

Loading...

Droughts are getting more intense in the Western U.S., limiting the food supplies for deer. Their migrations are also being constricted by development, forcing them to navigate a complex maze of fences, roads and subdivisions. Research shows mule deer may be able to adapt to increasingly unpredictable seasons, but development is limiting that ability.

Wyoming is working to keep migration routes from being severed. It's one of the few states that has protected migratory corridors for wildlife, restricting development in the most crucial paths. Landowners and conservation groups are also permanently preserving open lands and working ranches.

The question is whether that work can keep pace with growth. Wyoming's migratory wildlife are on the decline. The state's mule deer population was more than 500,000 in 1990. It's now half of that number.

"The history of wildlife migration is one of loss – we've lost migrations around the world," says Matt Kauffman, wildlife biologist with the U.S. Geological Survey and the University of Wyoming. "We are in this little race to map the migrations and figure out what tools we need to keep those landscapes open, as the American West continues to change."

Loading...

On the path of mule deer

In the foothills outside Pinedale, Wyoming, Kauffman and research associate Ashley Townsend make their way through the sagebrush, scanning for a radio signal. They pick one up – a beep, beep, beep – from a mule deer with a tracking collar, which the team put on months earlier.

"This was a fawn, a nine-month-old fawn that we caught on winter range," Kauffman says, scanning the horizon.

This year, Kauffman and his colleagues tracked the spring migrations of about 100 mule deer with GPS collars. It's part of the Wyoming Migration Initiative, a multi-year project run by the University of Wyoming, that has revealed migration routes in unprecedented detail. The deer make far more arduous journeys than once thought, crossing highways, rushing streams and ice-covered lakes. One mule deer set a record, migrating more than 240 miles one way.

Kauffman says for mule deer, the need to migrate is hard-wired. This herd these deer are part of spends summers in the mountains south of Grand Teton National Park, where the food supply is ample. But deep snow in the winter makes it impossible to stay, so the deer migrate south to Wyoming's Red Desert. There, the deer have very little to eat.

"These animals are basically coming out of, if not starving, losing fat all winter," he says. "They come into it with a lot of fat and they're burning those fat stores all through winter. At the end, animals are always in their worst shape."

In the spring, the deer set off to find food, but long-distance migration comes with risks, like for the fawn Kauffman has been tracking. The signal from the tracking collar shows it hasn't been moving, a sign that the fawn may have died.

After homing in on the tracking signal for about 10 minutes, the team finds the collar on the ground, next to a few bones left by scavengers.

"She probably started migrating a few weeks ago from the desert, but yeah, she didn't make it," Kauffman says.

Loading...

In years with harsh conditions, thousands of deer can die in Wyoming, which was seen in 2022-23, when a severe winter brought cold temperatures and heavy snowfall. Drought can also take a heavy toll on the population. The best insurance deer have against tough years is to build up fat reserves by eating as much as possible.

"The fatter animals survive the harsh winters better," Kauffman says. "The fatter animals survive the dry summers better. Fat is really the currency of life and of reproduction."

Surfing the green wave

In their quest to bulk up, migration can give deer an edge, because underfoot is the best possible food – the young plants and grasses that emerge after the snow melts.

These tender shoots are protein-rich and have little fiber, so they're easy for deer to digest.

"It's like this sort of spring salad mix," Kauffman says. "We like the spring salad mix because it's nutritious. It's sort of sweet, easy. And that's the same thing that mule deer like."

Loading...

The land begins to green up at lower elevations and, over weeks, spreads to higher elevations where the snow melts later. The deer follow this progression of green closely to eat the best food, what Kauffman says is known as "surfing the green wave."

"I like to say they're choreographing their movements," he says. "If you're ahead of the wave, you move less quickly and let the wave catch you. And if they're behind the wave, they move more quickly to catch it."

Some years, following this spring green-up is trickier for deer. Kauffman says in drought years, the green wave doesn't last as long, or it can be spotty, making it hard to find. Droughts in the Western U.S. are getting more intense as the climate gets hotter.

Kauffman says mule deer have the flexibility to adapt to shifting green waves, even as climate change makes them less predictable. But another challenge may be holding them back.

An obstacle course of development…

item.title: Study suggests BMI alone may miss obesity-related dementia risk
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, learning value

Study suggests BMI alone may miss obesity-related dementia risk

A newer way of defining obesity that looks beyond body mass index (BMI) may identify more older adults with an increased risk of dementia than BMI alone, according to a study published Nov. 25, 2026, in Neurology.

BMI looks only at weight and height. Use of BMI to assess obesity has been criticized for failing to distinguish between fat and muscle and not capturing the impact of other conditions related to obesity, such as high blood pressure.

The newer definition, called the European Association for the Study of Obesity framework, considers BMI, body fat distribution through the waist-to-height ratio and obesity-related conditions such as high blood pressure and diabetes.

"These findings underscore the inadequacy of using BMI alone to define obesity," said study author Rui Zhou, Ph.D., of Guangdong Pharmaceutical University in Guangzhou, China. "The results support the integration of body fat distribution and other health conditions into classifying obesity."

Researchers used data from British and Chinese studies to classify participants according to the traditional BMI method and the new framework. Then they examined the associations between obesity and the risk of dementia or death from any cause.

Using the new definition, more than 80% of those who had been classified as overweight were now classified as having obesity. Comparing people with obesity to people with normal weight and no other health conditions, people with obesity were more likely to develop dementia in both study groups and more likely to die during the study in one group. People who were overweight were less likely to develop dementia or die during the study.

The study does not prove that obesity causes the increased risk of dementia and death or that being overweight protects against dementia and death. It only shows an association.

The British study had 6,542 participants with an average age of 65 who were followed for an average of 12 years. The Chinese study had 12,402 participants with an average age of 58 who were followed for an average of eight years.

Under the traditional BMI criteria, the British participants were 27% normal weight, 44% overweight and 29% obese. Under the new framework, 5% were normal weight with no conditions, 22% were normal weight with other health conditions, 6% were overweight and 67% were obese.

For the Chinese participants under the traditional BMI criteria, 57% were normal weight, 31% were overweight and 12% were obese. Under the new framework, 12% were normal weight with no conditions, 45% were normal weight with other health conditions, 6% were overweight and 37% were obese.

Researchers compared dementia rates using person-years, which represent both the number of people in a study and the amount of time each person spent in the study. Dementia rates were:

- Obesity: about eight cases per 1,000 person-years for British participants under both frameworks and about 12 cases for Chinese participants

- Overweight: about three cases per 1,000 person-years for British participants and about seven cases for Chinese participants

- Normal weight with health conditions: nine cases per 1,000 person-years for British participants and 14 cases for Chinese participants

Researchers then adjusted for other factors that could affect risk of dementia and death, such as age, sex and physical activity. Combining both groups under the new framework, people with obesity were 93% more likely to develop dementia than people with normal weight and no other health conditions. Among the Chinese participants, people with obesity were 30% more likely to die during the study than people with normal weight and no conditions.

Compared with people with normal weight, people who were classified as overweight were 39% less likely to develop dementia and 68% less likely to die during the study.

"These results indicate that relying solely on BMI may overlook people who could benefit from earlier risk assessment and intervention," Zhou said.

A limitation of the study was that obesity was measured only at the beginning of the study, so any changes over time were not captured.
