item.title: Same oncogenic mutation, different outcomes: Why some blood vessels develop malformations while others remain resistant
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, learning value

Same oncogenic mutation, different outcomes: Why some blood vessels develop malformations while others remain resistant

Why do certain cancer-associated mutations cause malformations in some blood vessels while leaving others largely unaffected? The answer lies in the identity and developmental stage of endothelial cells, the cells lining the inside of blood vessels.

Published in Nature, the study led by Dr. Mariona Graupera and Dr. Ana Angulo-Urarte, from the Josep Carreras Leukaemia Research Institute, helps explain a striking clinical observation: vascular malformations associated with a gene called PIK3CA predominantly affect veins and capillaries while arteries are largely spared.

The same mutation, different cellular responses

PIK3CA is a gene involved in regulating cell proliferation and growth. When this gene is mutated at birth or during development, its mutations can also cause rare disorders characterized by excessive tissue growth and vascular malformations, in which blood vessels develop abnormally. Alterations in PIK3CA have also been implicated in certain blood cancers, including mantle cell lymphoma.

To understand why different blood vessels respond differently to the same mutation, the researchers used experimental models that track mutated endothelial cells, the cells lining the inside of blood vessels, during vascular development, as they develop and acquire their distinct identities.

They found that mutant cells in veins and capillaries proliferate excessively, whereas mature arterial cells remain remarkably resistant to these effects, maintaining their normal growth and identity. However, when the mutation affects immature cells destined to become arterial cells, the outcome is strikingly different. The mutation prevents these cells from developing normally into arterial cells, instead pushing them toward the characteristics of cells found in veins and capillaries. Therefore, like the mutant cells in veins and capillaries, they can also multiply excessively. Together, these effects contribute to the formation of vascular malformations.

Two complementary mechanisms driving vascular malformations

The researchers identified a molecular mechanism underlying this change in cell maturation. A PIK3CA-related mutation in a regulatory axis of the cell increases levels of COUP-TFII, a protein that promotes venous identity, preventing immature endothelial cells from developing into arterial endothelial cells.

The team demonstrated that excessive cell proliferation and altered cell identity are distinct but complementary effects of the same mutation. In the lab, they saw that reducing excessive cell multiplication in PIK3CA-mutated cells did not restore the cells' arterial identity. Conversely, interfering with COUP-TFII allowed these cells to develop their arterial identity but did not prevent endothelial cells in veins and capillaries from multiplying excessively.

"These findings demonstrate that reducing abnormal cell growth does not necessarily correct the changes in cell identity caused by the mutation," says Graupera, corresponding author of the study and group leader at the Josep Carreras Institute.

Beyond vascular malformations

The study highlights a broader principle: the consequences of a cancer-associated mutation depend not only on the mutation itself, but also on the identity and developmental stage of the cell in which it occurs.

Although the research focuses on blood vessels, the findings may help explain other rare childhood disorders in which mutations in PIK3CA cause excessive growth of tissues and organs. They also raise questions for future research into blood cancers and other hematological disorders. In the bone marrow, endothelial cells form part of the supportive environment, or niche, that sustains normal blood formation and can also support leukemia cell survival and resistance to treatment.

Previous studies in mice have shown that genetic changes in other cells within this niche can contribute to the development of blood cancers. While the current study does not directly investigate these processes, its findings suggest that understanding how mutations alter endothelial cell identity could inform future research into the vascular niche in blood cancers.

More broadly, the findings raise the possibility that the effects of other cancer-associated mutations may also depend on the identity and developmental stage of the cells in which they arise. Exploring this possibility could deepen our understanding of disease mechanisms and, in the longer term, help identify new therapeutic approaches.

Publication details

Helena Sabata et al., Context-dependent response of endothelial cells to PIK3CA mutation, Nature (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11318-5

Journal information: Nature

item.title: Creatine is popular with bodybuilders—could it help older adults stay independent?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, learning value

Creatine is popular with bodybuilders—could it help older adults stay independent?

Climbing stairs or getting out of a chair can become harder with age, partly because muscle mass and strength tend to decline.

Resistance training, such as lifting weights or exercising with resistance bands, can help maintain muscle strength in later life. Research suggests that creatine, a supplement more commonly associated with bodybuilders and athletes, may help older adults gain a little more strength from this type of exercise. Whether that makes everyday tasks easier or helps people stay independent for longer is less clear.

Creatine is a naturally occurring compound that the body makes from amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. It's also found in foods such as meat and fish. Most of the body's creatine is stored in muscle, where it helps replenish the energy needed for short bursts of intense activity, such as lifting weights.

Taking creatine increases the amount available in muscles. That may let people complete a few more repetitions before their muscles tire. Over time, that extra work could help explain some of the gains in strength.

Muscle strength in later life

A 2026 review of 11 randomized trials found that adults aged 60 and over who added creatine to a resistance training program gained slightly more strength than those who did the training without creatine. The review found no clear improvement in muscle mass or in how well people performed physical tasks.

Participants were generally healthy and were 67 on average, so the findings tell us less about people in their 80s and beyond. It's also unclear whether the same benefits apply to people with sarcopenia, a condition in which low muscle strength is accompanied by reduced muscle mass or quality.

An earlier review found that people who took creatine gained about 1.3 kg (2.9 pounds) more lean tissue, on average, than those who took a placebo while following the same training program. Measures of lean tissue include water. Creatine can make muscles hold more water, especially in the first few days, so it's difficult to tell how much of that increase was new muscle.

When people take creatine without doing resistance training, some small studies suggest their muscles take longer to tire. The evidence for gains in strength is clearer for people who also train.

Everyday movement and falls

One way researchers test whether strength gains carry over into daily life is with the sit-to-stand test, also known as the chair-rise test. Researchers count how many times someone can stand up in 30 seconds or time how long it takes them to stand up five times, usually without using their arms for support.

A 2026 review pooled results from five trials of the chair-rise test. Middle-aged and older adults who added creatine to their training performed better than those who trained and took a placebo. The evidence for walking and balance was limited and inconsistent.

In a two-year trial involving 237 postmenopausal women, whose average age was 59, both groups were asked to do resistance training and walk regularly. On average, the women taking creatine walked 80 meters (262 feet) about 1.5 seconds faster than they had at the start of the trial, while the placebo group's time barely changed.

There was no clear difference in reported falls through the end of the third year. The trial was designed to study bone health, so it gives limited information about whether creatine affects the risk of falling.

Research involving frailer older adults is also limited. In two trials involving people who were frail or at risk of frailty, participants got stronger with resistance training. Adding creatine produced no clear extra benefit. There is still too little evidence to say whether creatine helps older people avoid falls or remain independent for longer.

The brain also uses creatine to help maintain its energy supply. This has led researchers to investigate whether taking creatine might help preserve memory in later life.

A review focused on older adults found just two studies that tested supplements. They reached different conclusions. The other studies estimated how much creatine people got from food, so they could only identify links between intake and performance on cognitive tests. There is too little evidence to say whether taking creatine can slow cognitive decline or prevent dementia.

What to know about taking creatine

Creatine monohydrate is the most widely studied form. Some trials have used 3 to 5 g a day, while others have used higher doses. The amount that might improve everyday physical function is still uncertain.

Creatine is generally well tolerated at the doses studied. Some people report stomach discomfort, and the extra water in muscle can lead to weight gain. Studies in people with healthy kidneys have generally found no evidence of reduced kidney function. There is less evidence on safety for people with kidney disease.

Creatine can raise blood levels of creatinine, a natural waste product, which is produced when the body breaks down creatine. Because blood tests use creatinine to estimate how well the kidneys are working, taking the supplement can make those results harder to interpret. Research on interactions with prescription medicines is limited. If you have kidney disease or take several prescription medicines, check with a primary care doctor or pharmacist before starting.

For older adults who want to stay strong, regular strength exercises are the place to start. NHS guidance for adults aged 65 and over recommends exercise to build strength and improve balance and flexibility on at least two days a week. For people who already do resistance training, creatine may offer a small extra gain in muscle strength.

item.title: Date-rape drug GHB disappears within hours, but molecular trace could reveal use two days later
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, learning value

Date-rape drug GHB disappears within hours, but molecular trace could reveal use two days later

GHB has long posed a major challenge for the criminal justice system. The substance is eliminated from the body so quickly that proving cases of drugging and drug-facilitated rape can be extremely difficult. Now, researchers at Aarhus University have made a crucial discovery.

It has been the perfect date-rape drug. A clear, tasteless liquid that makes you drowsy, causes memory loss and disappears from the body extremely quickly.

GHB, also known as "G" and "fantasy," has been virtually impossible to detect. Until now.

Researchers from the Department of Forensic Medicine at Aarhus University have identified a marker that can reveal GHB intake for up to 48 hours after ingestion. Until now, the detection window has been no more than 12 hours.

The study has just been published in the journal Science Advances, and the findings could mark a paradigm shift for victims worldwide.

A 30-year-old mystery

"We set out to solve a forensic challenge that has been known for 30 years—and remains highly relevant today," says Charlotte Uggerhøj Andersen, consultant physician and clinical associate professor at the Department of Forensic Medicine.

GHB emerged as a recreational party drug in the 1990s, and it has probably been used for at least as long in drugging offenses, including rape.

Unlike most other illicit drugs, which can be detected in blood or urine for several days after ingestion, GHB has only been detectable in blood for a few hours and in urine for a maximum of 12 hours.

This creates major challenges for the criminal justice system because blood and urine samples are rarely secured immediately after an offense. At the same time, victims are often left with uncertainty: Were they drugged, or had they simply consumed more alcohol than they could tolerate?

That may now change, because the researchers have succeeded in identifying a molecule that can be detected in urine for up to 36 hours and in blood for up to 48 hours after GHB intake.

Fishing for clues in bodily fluids

The study began in 2023, and the breakthrough is the result of collaboration across several disciplines at Aarhus University, involving physicians, forensic chemists and researchers in synthetic chemistry and metabolomics from the Department of Forensic Medicine and colleagues from the Department of Chemistry.

In a clinical trial, 30 participants received either GHB or a placebo, after which the researchers began searching for relevant markers in both blood and urine.

"You could say that we went fishing for differences between the two groups of participants," explains associate professor Kirstine Lykke Nielsen.

The experiments confirmed that a previously unidentified molecule was present in higher concentrations in people who had taken GHB. Even more importantly, the molecule remained in the body significantly longer than GHB itself.

Through extensive scientific detective work, the research team developed a proposed chemical structure for the molecule. A central assumption was that GHB formed part of the new molecule. If so, the molecule could be directly linked to GHB intake.

The decisive confirmation came when chemists from the Department of Chemistry synthesized the molecule and demonstrated that it was identical to the unknown substance identified in the clinical study.

The molecule was also found in authentic samples collected by the police from drivers who were under the influence of GHB. This supports the biomarker's potential value in forensic practice.

The researchers have named the molecule GHB Beta Ribose, and work is now beginning to make the discovery applicable in the criminal justice system.

Three years in the making

The publication of the study represents both a professional and personal culmination for many of the researchers involved, because the findings have the potential to strengthen legal safeguards in serious cases—both in Denmark and internationally.

"The substance has been like a ghost that we have been unable to catch. We know it exists in society, we see it in blood samples from drivers, and hospitals encounter it in poisoning cases. We simply do not know very much about where and how it is being used," says senior researcher Jørgen Bo Hasselstrøm, one of the initiators of the study.

"But now that we know the structure of the molecule and can distribute the reference standard, colleagues around the world may eventually be able to implement the method in their laboratories and offer victims testing even when a day or more has passed.

"This could provide victims with answers, assist the police in investigations and strengthen legal safeguards more broadly. At the same time, it could give us better knowledge about the prevalence and use of the drug," he says.

Before the method can be used in the criminal justice system, further validation is required. Among other things, the researchers are now investigating whether certain diseases or alcohol consumption affect the levels of the biomarker in biological samples.

Publication details

Kathrine Bohn Faldborg et al., Identification of gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB)–β-ribose as a promising biomarker enabling prolonged detection of GHB intake, Science Advances (2026). DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeh1261

Journal information: Science Advances

item.title: Early-life stress may leave lasting traces in the brain that increase risk of chronic pain
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, learning value

Early-life stress may leave lasting traces in the brain that increase risk of chronic pain

Researchers from the Heidelberg Faculty of Medicine of Heidelberg University and the Central Institute of Mental Health (ZI) in Mannheim have identified a neural mechanism in female mice through which early-life stress may increase vulnerability to chronic pain and anxiety disorders. The findings have been published in the journal Science.

Early-life stress, such as neglect or other adverse experiences, has long been recognized as a risk factor for both mental and physical illness. However, why its effects often emerge only many years later, and why women appear to be more strongly affected than men, remains poorly understood. Researchers from the Heidelberg Faculty of Medicine of Heidelberg University and the Central Institute of Mental Health (ZI) Mannheim investigated, in an experimental mouse study, the brain mechanisms that may underlie the link between early stress and later chronic pain.

Their findings show that early-life stress can create a hidden vulnerability to chronic pain in female mice that becomes apparent only after a subsequent nerve injury.

Childhood adversity may increase the risk of chronic pain and anxiety

The research team led by Dr. Sebastian Wieland from the Institute of Anatomy and Cell Biology at Heidelberg University and the Department of General Internal Medicine, Psychosomatics and Psychotherapy at Heidelberg University Hospital (UKHD) investigated how early social stress, modeled by isolation after weaning, influences the response to a later nerve injury.

The results revealed that female mice exposed to early-life stress developed significantly greater and more persistent hypersensitivity to mild mechanical stimuli after nerve injury, as well as more pronounced anxiety-related avoidance behavior compared with animals that had not experienced early stress. This stress-induced amplification was not observed in male mice. Early-life stress alone also did not produce the observed combination of behavioral changes.

A hidden pain amplifier in the brain

The team also identified a potential biological mechanism. They discovered a lasting alteration in the neural connections between the paraventricular thalamus and the central amygdala, two brain regions involved in processing stress, threat and pain.

In female mice, early-life stress changed the function of this brain circuit in a way that caused it to transmit certain neural signals more strongly following a later nerve injury. No such alteration was observed in male animals. In addition, the circuit showed increased activity even in anticipation of a potential threat, promoting anxiety-related avoidance behavior.

By selectively inhibiting this neural network, the researchers were able to reduce both the additional pain hypersensitivity and the heightened avoidance behavior without affecting the acute pain response caused by the injury itself. This finding suggests that the identified circuit contributes specifically to the stress-related, long-term amplification of pain sensitivity and avoidance behavior.

"Our study shows that early-life stress can leave lasting traces in the brains of female mice by persistently altering a threat-processing network. These changes do not immediately result in chronic symptoms. Instead, they create a hidden vulnerability that only becomes apparent after a later injury and may selectively increase susceptibility to chronic pain. The findings help us better understand how experiences during early stages of life can influence the risk of chronic diseases in adulthood," explains study leader Wieland.

A neurobiological explanation for a clinical observation

The findings were obtained in an animal model and cannot be directly transferred to humans. Nevertheless, they are of particular importance from a psychosomatic perspective because they provide a neurobiological explanation for the long-standing clinical observation that early psychosocial adversity can influence later vulnerability to chronic pain.

"This study strikingly illustrates how closely psychological experiences and physical processes can be linked at the biological level. The findings therefore underscore the importance of a biopsychosocial understanding of chronic pain disorders," says Hans-Christoph Friederich, medical director of the Department of General Internal Medicine, Psychosomatics and Psychotherapy at Heidelberg University Hospital.

The study is the result of a long-standing collaboration between the Department of General Internal Medicine, Psychosomatics and Psychotherapy at Heidelberg University Hospital, the Division of Functional Neuroanatomy at Heidelberg University's Institute of Anatomy and Cell Biology, and the Department of Psychopharmacology at the Central Institute of Mental Health Mannheim within the framework of Collaborative Research Center (SFB) 1158. The experimental work was conducted primarily in the Division of Functional Neuroanatomy in close cooperation with the ZI Mannheim.

"The combination of psychosomatic medicine and experimental neuroscience enables us to investigate clinical observations on the long-term consequences of psychosocial adversity at the level of neural circuits. This interdisciplinary collaboration helps us better understand the biological foundations of the interaction between psychosocial experiences, pain processing and behavior," explains Thomas Kuner, head of the Division of Functional Neuroanatomy.

Wieland's research group will now investigate the spatial and molecular signature of the pain vulnerability induced by early-life stress. In the long term, this work may contribute to the identification of new biomarkers and the development of more targeted, sex-specific therapies for chronic pain. Whether comparable mechanisms also play a role in humans will need to be examined in future studies.

item.title: AI could identify psoriasis and assess its severity from a single photo
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, learning value

AI could identify psoriasis and assess its severity from a single photo

Widely available artificial intelligence models could not only recognize psoriasis from a single photo but also assess its severity, according to an international study by researchers at Semmelweis University. The study, published in Frontiers in Medicine, found that ChatGPT-5 identified the skin condition and correctly assessed its severity with nearly 100% accuracy. However, the researchers caution that, despite the promising results, artificial intelligence cannot replace dermatologists, and anyone experiencing symptoms should seek professional medical advice.

Psoriasis is a lifelong skin condition that may worsen without proper treatment. However, patients do not always seek medical advice promptly, as they may mistake their symptoms for those of other skin conditions, such as eczema. In some countries, long waiting times for dermatologists can also delay diagnosis. As a result, some people may turn to artificial intelligence (AI)-based models to get initial information about their symptoms.

To assess how reliably these models could identify psoriasis, researchers at Semmelweis University analyzed 303 standardized clinical photographs from 160 patients. Taken with a professional camera under controlled conditions, the photographs included 163 photographs showing psoriasis and 140 showing other skin conditions with similar symptoms.

Rather than using software developed specifically for dermatology, the researchers tested four widely available AI models: ChatGPT-5, ChatGPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Gemini 2.5 Flash. The researchers compared the models' ability to identify psoriasis, assess its severity and recommend treatments. Dermatologists evaluated the results.

ChatGPT-5 was the most accurate model, identifying psoriasis in 93.1% of cases. ChatGPT-4o followed, with over 90%. Among the cases it correctly identified, ChatGPT-5 also accurately assessed disease severity in 93.3% of cases.

What is psoriasis?

Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin condition that affects an estimated 200,000 people in Hungary and around 2% of the global population. Although genetic factors play a major role in its development, stress, obesity and a diet high in sugar and saturated fat may also contribute to the onset or worsening of symptoms. The characteristic patches usually appear on the elbows, knees and scalp, but in more severe cases, they can affect larger areas of the body.

"The results show that these AI models could perform certain medical analyses with a high degree of accuracy. However, relying solely on their answers can be risky, as AI can sound confident and convincing even when providing false information. Treatment decisions based on incorrect information could even put patients' health at risk," said Dr. Mehdi Boostani, former Ph.D. student at Semmelweis University, researcher at the Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center in Buffalo and first author of the study.

The researcher also emphasized that the models were less reliable at recommending treatments: even the best-performing model, ChatGPT-5, suggested an appropriate treatment in 83.7% of cases in which it correctly identified psoriasis. According to the expert, this is partly because choosing the proper treatment is more complex than recognizing a skin condition.

"Making safe medical decisions requires more than just a photograph. Doctors also need to know patients' medical histories, comorbidities and whether certain treatments might be unsuitable for them. AI models do not have access to this information when they analyze photographs alone," explained Dr. Norbert Kiss, assistant professor at the Department of Dermatology, Venereology and Dermatooncology at Semmelweis University and the last author of the study.

Despite these limitations, the researchers believe that AI could become a useful tool to help patients better understand their condition. The findings support this view: although the models did not always provide accurate diagnoses, they often gave reliable information. The researchers therefore hope that further advances in AI could help people recognize the signs of skin conditions and seek appropriate medical care sooner.

More information

Mehdi Boostani et al., Evaluation of multimodal large language models for psoriasis diagnosis, severity grading, and treatment recommendations from clinical photographs: ChatGPT shows superior performance compared to other large language models, Frontiers in Medicine (2026). DOI: 10.3389/fmed.2026.1791488

item.title: Alzheimer's drug targets tau protein in promising clinical trial
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, learning value

Alzheimer's drug targets tau protein in promising clinical trial

An experimental Alzheimer's drug that reduces the production of a protein called tau has slowed the decline in memory and thinking skills by up to 54% in a clinical trial.

The drug, called diranersen, works differently from approved Alzheimer's treatments. These focus on clearing amyloid, one of two proteins that build up abnormally in the brain. Diranersen targets the other protein—tau.

Amyloid forms sticky plaques between brain cells, while tau clumps together inside them, forming tangled structures. Both proteins damage brain cells, disrupting the signals they use to communicate and the processes that keep them alive.

Tau has an important job in a healthy brain. It helps stabilize tiny structures called microtubules, which act like railroad tracks, transporting nutrients and other materials around brain cells.

In Alzheimer's, tau changes structure, detaches from these tracks and clumps together inside brain cells, forming tangles. These tangles interfere with the cell's internal transport system, contributing to its eventual death. The amount of tau accumulating in the brain is closely linked to how quickly people's thinking skills decline.

Two drugs, lecanemab and donanemab, have been approved by most regulators (including in the U.S., Europe and the U.K.) for treating people with early-stage Alzheimer's, although they are not available on the NHS.

Both help to remove amyloid plaques from the brain and modestly slow the decline in memory and thinking skills. Neither targets tau, and both can cause significant side effects, including brain bleeds.

Researchers have found it harder to develop drugs that target tau. Several experimental treatments have used antibodies designed to recognize and destroy abnormal tau. However, these drugs have struggled to improve patients' symptoms. The problem is that tau builds up inside brain cells, where antibodies find it difficult to reach.

Diranersen takes a different approach. Instead of trying to remove tangles that have already formed, it reduces how much tau brain cells produce in the first place.

The trial

The drug was tested in a Phase 2 clinical trial, involving 416 people with early Alzheimer's disease. Phase 2 is the stage when researchers investigate whether a drug appears to work and which dose is most effective.

The most promising results—which are yet to be peer-reviewed—came from the group given the lowest dose (60 mg twice a year as an injection in the spine). After 96 weeks, 60 people taking this lower dose had 38% less decline compared with 115 participants originally assigned to placebo on a scale measuring memory, thinking skills and ability to carry out everyday activities.

On a separate test of cognitive performance, their decline was 54% slower. A third measure, assessing everyday activities, showed 30% less decline.

Most side effects were mild. The most common were pain and headaches linked to the spinal injections, and short spells of confusion that typically cleared up within a week. The researchers found no new safety problems over the two years of follow-up.

Diranersen is a gene-silencing drug. It belongs to a class of medicines called antisense oligonucleotides, which are designed to switch off specific genetic instructions.

The drug attaches to messenger RNA—the molecule that carries the instructions for making tau—and causes it to break down. Without these instructions, brain cells make less of the protein.

Reducing tau raises an important question: could lowering a protein that brain cells need to function also cause harm? Studies in mice have suggested that substantially reducing tau does not significantly disrupt these processes, and the trial found no serious short-term side effects. But nobody knows whether lowering tau in people is safe over many years.

How strong is the evidence?

There are important reasons to be cautious about the two-year results. They come from an extension of the original trial in which participants and researchers knew who was receiving the drug. After a year and a half, participants who had initially received a placebo were switched to diranersen. This meant researchers could no longer compare the drug with a placebo group over the full two years.

The original 18-month trial also failed to meet its main objective, which was to show that different doses produced a clear difference in clinical decline. Although some other measures showed improvements, missing this main target makes it harder to know how much confidence to place in the longer-term findings.

What is needed next is a much larger Phase 3 trial, comparing the drug with a placebo in many more people. Regulators would want to see the results of such a trial before considering it for approval.

For years, Alzheimer's research has concentrated on amyloid. Targeting tau offers another possible way to tackle the disease. Combining drugs that act on both proteins might eventually prove more effective than either approach alone. But both possibilities still need to be tested in larger trials.

item.title: Five local tools and what to check before you commit
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

This is edition 1 of my weekly picks for The Repo Dude, a side project where I sort open-source GitHub repos by the job you need done.

A star count will not tell you whether a tool works on your machine. This edition is five local-workflow tools: a first thing to try, and a catch taken from each project's own docs.

These picks are documentation research, not hands-on test results.

The original edition is here:

https://www.therepodude.com/updates.html?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=launch_2026_11#edition-2026-11-19

Check that a heading actually appears on a page you control

That's microsoft/playwright.

- First trial: Use a page you control and check that an expected heading appears.

-

Check first: Each Playwright version needs matching browser binaries. After you install or update Playwright, re-run npx playwright install before you test.

- Source: Playwright — Browsers

Transcribe a recording you own, on your machine

ggml-org/whisper.cpp has a documented CPU-only path.

- First trial: Transcribe a short recording you own and compare proper names against the audio.

-

Check first: Model size changes memory needs. The project's README lists about 273 MB for the tiny model and about 3.9 GB for large — pick a model your machine can actually hold.

- Source: whisper.cpp README — Memory usage

Get structured output from a messy PDF

Start with one difficult table and the reading order. That's docling-project/docling.

- First trial: Inspect one difficult table and reading order in a representative document.

-

Check first: A finished conversion can still need a manual check. Docling's docs say complex layouts or poor scans can produce results that require review, and they ship confidence grades (mean_grade / low_grade) for that. The table-quality score is listed as not yet implemented.

- Source: Docling — Confidence scores

Trim a clip without building a whole editor

That's mifi/lossless-cut.

- First trial: Cut a copy of a clip, then inspect its start and end in a player.

- Check first: Lossless cuts can start earlier than your chosen timestamp because of keyframes. Inspect the exported clip.

- Source: LosslessCut troubleshooting — Export starts a few seconds before my cut point

Convert a short video inside a browser tab

That's ffmpegwasm/ffmpeg.wasm.

- First trial: Convert a short sample you own and inspect the output and browser memory use.

-

Check first: The project's FAQ says WebAssembly is still a lot slower than native FFmpeg. The optional multithread build is around 2× faster but uses a lot more memory and CPU. The wrapper (@ffmpeg/ffmpeg) is MIT; @ffmpeg/core follows FFmpeg and its external-library licenses.

- Source: ffmpeg.wasm FAQ — speed and license

It's early, and I'd love your honest thoughts. Want the next edition? Join the weekly email list:

item.title: attackscout-agent: a read-only website security check you run on your own server
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Most website security scanners look at your site from the outside. Those are visible from the server.

attackscout-agent is a small command line tool that checks those things from the inside. It is free, MIT-licensed, written in Go, and it only reads.

What it does

Run attackscout-agent scan on a Linux, macOS or Windows server. It detects the web root and your nginx or Apache configuration, then runs seven checks:

- End of life: PHP, Node.js, .NET, WordPress (core, plugins, themes), Drupal, Joomla, PrestaShop, React and Next.js, compared with an end-of-life table embedded in the binary.

- Known vulnerabilities: npm, Composer, PyPI, NuGet and Go lockfiles, plus Terraform and OpenTofu provider versions, matched against the OSV database with Google's osv-scalibr library.

-

Sensitive files: .env, .git/, SQL dumps, archives, phpinfo.php, logs, private keys, .htpasswd, terraform.tfstate. Names only, contents are never opened.

-

File permissions: world-writable files and directories, 777, world-readable wp-config.php and .env (Unix only).

- Web server configuration: HSTS, CSP, X-Content-Type-Options, frame protection, Referrer-Policy, version disclosure and directory listing in nginx, Apache and IIS configuration.

-

wp-config.php: default or missing salts, WP_DEBUG, WP_DEBUG_DISPLAY, DISALLOW_FILE_EDIT. Secret values are never printed.

- Certificates: PEM files, for expiry, a certificate expiring in under 30 days, weak keys and SHA-1 or MD5 signatures.

Every finding has a stable identifier, a severity from info to critical, and a fix. A check that cannot run says not_checked, and one that makes no sense on the system says not_applicable. Neither is ever shown as a pass.

Example

I ran it on the fake WordPress site and nginx configuration that ship in the repository's testdata/ folder (on a Windows machine, so the permissions check is not_applicable):

Checks

[fail ] End of life - End-of-life table embedded in the binary, dated 2026-11-25

[not checked ] CVE (OSV) - CVEs not checked for 5 components that OSV does not track (WordPress, Joomla extensions, ...)

[fail ] Sensitive files

[not applicable] File permissions - Not applicable on Windows: Unix permission bits do not exist there and ACLs are not read

[fail ] wp-config.php

[fail ] Web server configuration

Findings

[CRITICAL] sensitive-env: Sensitive environment file in the web root: .env (content not read)

[CRITICAL] wpconfig-salt-default: wp-config.php keys or salts empty or left at the default value: AUTH_KEY, SECURE_AUTH_KEY (values not shown)

[HIGH] php-eol: PHP 7.4 is end of life (branch 7.4, since 2022-11-28)

[MEDIUM] header-hsts-missing: nginx configuration does not set Strict-Transport-Security

...

Summary: 4 critical, 4 high, 5 medium, 10 low, 0 info

Note the second line: WordPress and Joomla extensions are not in OSV, so the tool says "CVEs not checked" instead of pretending there is none.

Does it send anything?

Not by default. There is no telemetry and no update check. Two commands use the network, and only them:

- attackscout-agent db update downloads the public OSV archives. Nothing about your server is sent.

- attackscout-agent scan --online sends package names, versions and ecosystems to api.osv.dev, and nothing else (no path, file name or domain).

This is enforced by tests: one parses every source file and only allows the vulnerability package to import a networking package, another runs a full default scan with a guard on the HTTP transport and fails on any request.

Use it in CI

attackscout-agent db update

attackscout-agent scan --root . --project . --fail-on high

The command exits with 1 when a finding is high or critical, 0 otherwise, and 2 for a usage error. --json gives a report you can keep as an artifact. In CI it is most useful for lockfiles and Terraform files; the file and configuration checks need the real server.

Install

go install github.com/attackscout/attackscout-agent@latest

Prebuilt binaries for Linux, macOS and Windows (amd64 and arm64) are attached to each GitHub release, with a checksums.txt file.

What it does not do

- It reads certificate files. It does not connect to your site, so it does not test TLS versions or cipher suites.

- It reads configuration files. A header added by a proxy or CDN in front of the server is not seen.

- It does not analyse Terraform configuration; tfsec and Checkov do that well.

- Its end-of-life table is as fresh as the release you run.

See the other side too

This tool sees the inside of the server. What a visitor or a scanner sees, such as the headers actually served and what is reachable from the Internet, needs an outside look. For that I run AttackScout, an external audit of a domain. The CLI is separate and free; it is not part of that service.

Repository and docs: https://github.com/AttackScout/attackscout-agent

Feedback and issues are welcome, especially false positives and server layouts the auto-detection misses.

Source: Dev.to | Published: 2026-11-25 21:21 UTC

Original link: https://dev.to/attackscout/attackscout-agent-a-read-only-website-security-check-you-run-on-your-own-server-2b1j

item.title: A Practical Color-Reference Workflow for Photographing Translucent Materials
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Photographing translucent materials is a calibration problem before it is a photography problem. Two shots of the same stone, taken ten minutes apart under the same lamp, can look like two different materials once the camera decides on a white balance. I ran into this while helping document jadeite pieces for a small trading archive, and the fix turned out to be mostly code, not gear.

The problem

A camera's auto white balance optimises for a pleasant average, not for consistency. With a strongly coloured subject filling the frame, the camera compensates for the colour it sees and neutralises exactly the signal you want to measure. Dark green material on a light background pulls the exposure one way; the same material on dark velvet pulls it the other.

Step 1: fix the light, then stop trusting the camera

I settled on a single diffused source at a fixed distance, a matte grey card in the corner of every frame, and manual exposure. The grey card is not decoration: it is the anchor the script uses to normalise every image to the same reference point.

Step 2: sample the card, not the subject

from PIL import Image

import numpy as np

def grey_reference(path, box):

img = Image.open(path).convert("RGB")

patch = np.asarray(img.crop(box)).reshape(-1, 3).astype(float)

# median is robust against dust and specular highlights

return np.median(patch, axis=0)

The crop box is fixed once and reused for the whole series, so every frame gets the same treatment. Median instead of mean matters: a stray highlight on the card will drag a mean badly and leave a colour cast that no later step can undo.

Step 3: apply a per-channel gain

def balance(img, ref, target=(200, 200, 200)):

arr = np.asarray(img).astype(float)

gain = np.array(target, dtype=float) / np.maximum(ref, 1.0)

out = np.clip(arr * gain, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)

return Image.fromarray(out)

Two lines and the whole series lands on a common neutral. I keep the gain values in a CSV next to the images; when a new lamp or a new diffuser shows up, the drift is visible as a step change in that column instead of being buried in the pictures.

Step 4: describe the material in numbers, not adjectives

Once the frames are comparable, a short feature extractor makes the archive searchable. For translucent material the useful features are narrow: mean hue in the subject mask, saturation spread, and a crude translucency proxy built from the ratio of edge brightness to centre brightness.

def translucency_proxy(img, mask):

arr = np.asarray(img.convert("L")).astype(float)

edge = arr[mask & ~erode(mask)]

core = arr[erode(erode(mask))]

return float(np.mean(edge) / max(np.mean(core), 1.0))

This is not a grading system and it does not pretend to be one. It is a way to sort two hundred photographs into groups that a human can then look at side by side, which is the only part of the job that actually needs eyes.

What I would do differently

- Put the grey card in the frame before the first shot, not after the fortieth.

- Store the raw gain values in the filename. EXIF rewriting is a rabbit hole.

- Resist the urge to make the numbers look nice. A feature that separates your groups but has no physical meaning will not survive a change of lighting.

If you only take one thing from this: the difference between two photos of the same piece is usually a measurement error, and measurement errors are cheaper to fix in code than in a studio. The reference archive this workflow was built for lives at https://www.jjjadeite.com, and a shorter buyer-facing write-up of the same ideas is at https://sites.google.com/view/jadeite-buyer-guide — both were useful to me as examples of how the same material is described for two very different audiences.

Source: Dev.to | Published: 2026-11-25 21:20 UTC

item.title: Google search alternative Kagi launches Gmail rival
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Kagi, a small, Palo Alto, California-based software company that provides a subscription-based search engine as an alternative to Google, has launched a Gmail-like e-mail service. Dubbed Kagi Mail, it makes many of the same claims as the search engine product: privacy, personal data sovereignty, customization, and control.

Additionally, Kagi is rolling out a calendar as part of the mail service. Right now, both the email and calendar interfaces are web-only, but native Android and iOS apps are planned for the fourth quarter of next year.

The email interface, currently in public beta, is minimalist. It emphasizes keyboard commands, as well as a private and ad-free experience. (You can see more details in Kagi’s blog post about what they mean by private.) Other feature offerings include unlimited aliases and domains, an anti-lock-in policy for user data, 50GB of storage, rule-based filtering with Sieve, an MCP server, and several optional, off-by-default AI features, like chatting with an agent to search email history, do large-scale re-labeling, or define additional filtering rules.

Some major features are still missing, though. As noted, there are no native apps yet. Critically, there is no contacts address book, but that is also coming in 2027 (Q1 in this case) according to the roadmap.

Like the search engine, Kagi Mail is a paid service. It’s not included in the $5 per month basic Kagi plan, nor is it in the $10 per month unlimited search plan. It is, however, included in the $25 per month Kagi Ultimate subscription, which also offers frontier AI models.

If you want to get Kagi Mail without the $25 per month subscription, you can subscribe for $9 per month or $99 per year, and there’s a 60-day trial right now.

Opinion: An alternative more of us should maybe consider

That’s a lot to pay for email when Gmail has historically been such a strong product. To most people, it seems ridiculous to imagine paying for a subscription, and that’s understandable.

item.title: FCC approves SpaceX plan to put AI data centers in space
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

SpaceX was given conditional approval by the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday to deploy and operate a constellation of up to 1 million satellites for its orbital data center business, a regulatory victory for Elon Musk and his bid to move AI data centers into space.

The FCC authorization was granted despite objections from Amazon, Viasat, and the American Astronomical Society, which flagged concerns over orbital debris and congestion, radiofrequency interference, and environmental consequences. Amazon, which is building a competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink service, argued in its petition that the application lacked basic details and described it as a “lofty ambition rather than a real plan.” Despite that lack of detail, Amazon also said the proposal “risks real harm.”

The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority.

FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement that the action “opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.”

Musk thanked Carr in a post on X, writing “Much appreciate. This will be a great asset to America and the world.”

This initial regulatory approval doesn’t mean orbital data centers are imminent.

SpaceX faces a number of technical and economic challenges, including how to dramatically reduce the cost of manufacturing and launching satellites, cool processors in space, and even how to secure financing for chips that are destined for orbit.

The company must also clear other regulatory hurdles. The FCC has not yet approved SpaceX’s plans to handle orbital debris for satellites that would operate above 600 kilometers, for instance. SpaceX requested a waiver of existing FCC rules, which requires satellites ending missions below 2,000 kilometers reenter Earth’s atmosphere within five years of completing those missions. The company is interested in moving some of these retired satellites into other orbits around Earth or even around the sun, according to the FCC authorization document.

SpaceX has said it plans to deploy the satellites, known as Starmind, at altitudes ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers. The FCC’s approval gives SpaceX the authority to use radiofrequency communications to maintain contact with and control its orbital data centers from Earth if their primary communications systems fail. The Starmind satellites would primarily communicate using lasers to connect with other satellites, including SpaceX’s Starlink.

The FCC has given SpaceX time to sort out these issues. Under the approval, SpaceX has seven years to get its first operational satellite into orbit and 14 years to deploy the entire constellation.

Source: TechCrunch | Published: 2026-11-25 20:56 UTC

Original link: https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/25/fcc-approves-spacex-plan-to-put-ai-data-centers-in-space/

WhatsApp’s 3 billion users are getting an option that Meta says is one of the most requested features, with the ability to schedule messages in advance for both private conversations and group chats. Most messaging platforms have had this for a very long time, but now it’s on WhatsApp too.

WhatsApp’s new scheduled messages let you choose the right time to send

You can schedule WhatsApp texts you might forget to send up to two weeks ahead of time.

If you think of a text at an inconvenient time or don’t want to forget to fire off a birthday message at 4AM, you can draft it and set it to send anywhere from 10 minutes to two weeks later. The feature works with photos and videos, too.

Meta:

To schedule a message, press and hold the send button and pick the date and time you want it to arrive. It will look like any other message to the person receiving it. You can see all future messages you have lined up, and delete them beforehand if you change your mind.

Even if your phone is off or out of battery, your scheduled message will still show up at the time you chose, and it remains end-to-end encrypted like all your personal messages, so no one else can read it, not even us.

Scheduled messages work with text, photos and videos, and are rolling out globally over the coming weeks. It’s one more way to show up for the people who matter to you, now at exactly the right time.

item.title: State AGs are trying to stop Character.AI from auctioning off users' chat histories
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

State AGs are trying to stop Character.AI from auctioning off users' chat histories

The proposed sale would include explicit conversations with children, officials say.

Character.AI is still drawing controversy and legal scrutiny even during its bankruptcy proceedings. A group of 42 attorneys general are trying to block the chatbot company from auctioning off users' chat histories and other sensitive information.

The company, which had faced numerous investigations and lawsuits over its safety record, filed for bankruptcy last month. The company said at the time that it would begin a "a court-supervised sale of all or substantially all of our assets" but that users data would continue to be "protected" by its privacy policy.

But the auction for Character.AI won't actually safeguard users' data at all, according to the state AGs. "Character.AI's plan to auction off its platform, including the IP addresses and private chats histories of its users — many of them children — with zero protection for those users is appalling," California Attorney General Rob Bonta said in a statement. "If this sale goes through, users' sensitive data would go into the hands of a buyer even though Character.AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold."

According to Bonta's office, the proposed sale includes chat histories, including conversations "in which AI characters drew children and adults into explicit sexual conversations." The buyer would also get access to chats in which users interacted with AI characters posing as physicians and therapists and discussed self harm, eating disorders, suicidal thoughts and other sensitive topics.

The AGs have also raised concerns about the fact that only one anonymous bidder has been disclosed so far. That entity, called Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC, was formed "one day before Character.AI picked it as the base bid for the auction," and its source of funding hasn't been disclosed. "Nothing in the agreement restricts what the buyer may do with the data after closing, including selling it," the AGs say in a court filing.

The auction is currently scheduled for December 1. The AGs are asking the bankruptcy court to block the sale to Smirks and deny a "break-up fee" that would allow the company to collect $350,000 if Character.AI sells to another buyer. They're also asking for children's chatbot conversations and "sensitive" data to be barred from any potential sale.

"Children and families who shared their most personal thoughts with Character.AI never imagined those conversations could be auctioned off to the highest bidder," Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser said in a statement. "A company's financial troubles do not give it the right to disregard its responsibility to protect consumers, especially children.

Source: Engadget | Published: 2026-11-25 20:04 UTC

item.title: OpenAI says heavy ChatGPT users may hit limits sooner as it merges Chat and Work
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

OpenAI has started rolling out a unified Chat and Work experience in ChatGPT to a few of its users, amid criticism from some subscribers that the merger could restrict their usage.

The rollout follows OpenAI’s earlier announcement of the merger in an email to users. An OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that while most users are not expected to face more frequent usage resets, a small fraction of its heaviest users may hit their limits sooner.

That’s among the concerns raised by some ChatGPT subscribers on social media and OpenAI’s community forum recently. The users fear that merging the usage limits for Chat and Work could leave them with less access to advanced reasoning models than they currently have, even as they continue paying the same subscription fees.

Under the new system, Chat and Work will share a single usage meter across ChatGPT, the OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch. Conversations using the Instant model will, however, remain unlimited and will not count toward the shared allowance. Users can also continue using Instant after exhausting their usage limits. The spokesperson added that OpenAI would continue working to improve efficiency so subscribers could get more out of their plans.

While the rollout has started for a small group of users, OpenAI plans to bring shared usage limits more broadly in December, per its support page.

Similar to OpenAI, rival Anthropic also moved to bring its conversational chat service Claude and work-focused Cowork under one interface in September.

The changes come as AI companies face mounting infrastructure costs and growing demand for increasingly capable models, putting pressure on their computing resources. Bringing conversational and work-related tools into a single interface could also make AI chatbots simpler to use, allowing users to move between chats and more complex tasks without switching tabs.

item.title: The FCC gave SpaceX approval for up to 1 million AI data centers in space
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: In-depth reporting on a significant technological development with clear prose and useful vocabulary.

The Federal Communications Commission authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million satellites that would operate as data centers in space, according to an order the agency released on Wednesday.

The FCC's Space Bureau granted SpaceX's application in part and deferred part of it, with conditions. The authority covers radio communications for the constellation, called Starmind, that serve as a fallback and in emergencies to carry telemetry and to track and command the satellites, in the 18.8-19.3 GHz and 28.6-29.1 GHz bands. SpaceX must operate in those bands on an unprotected, non-interference basis. The satellites will rely on optical links for their primary communications, the order said.

The constellation would sit in orbital shells at altitudes from 500 to 1,002 kilometers (311 to 623 miles). The FCC deferred SpaceX's request for a waiver of the rule requiring satellites that end their missions below 2,000 kilometers (1,243 miles) to be disposed of through atmospheric re-entry. Before deploying any satellites that operate above 600 kilometers (373 miles), SpaceX must file an application to modify the authorization with a final orbital debris mitigation plan.

The grant sets deployment milestones. SpaceX must deploy one satellite by Nov. 25, 2033, 10% of the authorized satellites by Nov. 25, 2035, and 50% by Nov. 25, 2038. It must launch the remainder by Nov. 25, 2040, or the authorization becomes null and void. The license term is 15 years and begins when SpaceX certifies that the first Starmind satellite is in orbit and operating under the authorization's terms.

Three parties filed petitions to deny the application: Kuiper Systems, which operates as Amazon $AMZN Leo; Viasat; and the American Astronomical Society. The bureau said it dismissed environmental and optical astronomy concerns as matters outside the Commission's authority.

The proposal prompted a comment tally from the public north of 1,500, according to Bloomberg. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said the commission was, for the first time, approving orbital data centers.

SpaceX had revealed the design of its first orbital data center satellite, called AI1, in a video posted to X $TWTR in June, ahead of its IPO. The orbital compute initiative was central to the company's pitch to investors.

The FCC is weighing other proposals for data centers in orbit and plans to rule on every one, according to The Wall Street Journal. Blue Origin has also applied to the FCC to put its own data centers into orbit and is still waiting for a decision, according to Bloomberg.

item.description:

Poundland collapses putting 11,000 jobs at risk

Poundland has collapsed into administration, putting 11,000 jobs at risk, after its owners failed to find a buyer to keep it in business.

The retailer's shops and distribution centres will remain open and continue to trade during the administration process with the business likely to be broken up and some of its stores sold off to rival retailers.

Poundland's US owners held talks with several bidders over a last-minute rescue deal, but no agreement was reached.

Poundland boss Barry Williams said in a note to staff that the board had "no alternative but to take this decision", but was making it with "sincere sadness and intense regret".

He said the US owners Gordon Brothers had removed "all borrowing facilities and access to our bank accounts" on 27 October, and adequate funds had not been released since then to keep the business solvent.

"Under these circumstances, it is impossible for the board of directors to see how Poundland can continue to operate as a going concern," he added.

'My income is gone'

Kelvin Blake, 62, who has worked for the firm for 25 years, and whose partner has been there 29 years, said he was feeling "down, depressed", and because of his age, feared he would not find a job elsewhere.

"We didn't want it, but it's come so now we've just got to face it and see what the future holds.

"My income's gone," he added. "Obviously, we'll be working until we're told to leave."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Poundland was "part of the fabric of high streets and communities up and down the country".

He said the news of it going into administration just weeks before Christmas would be "deeply concerning for workers and their families".

He added: "While it is worrying, going into administration does give other potential buyers the opportunity to engage and we will work hard with all the relevant parties to ensure the best possible outcome."

Alix Partners, which has been appointed as administrator, said they would look at all options for the business, "including sales of the business and its assets, either in whole or part".

"We appreciate this is a deeply concerning time for all involved - customers, suppliers and, in particular, Poundland colleagues," they said.

Gordon Brothers has been criticised over how it handled a potential sale of Poundland, with accusations the investment firm hoped to profit from selling off the chain's 600 shops and stock piecemeal after running it into the ground.

Gordon Brothers, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied such claims.

On the funding question, Gordon Brothers said it had loaned the firm Â£85m over a year to help save it from insolvency.

But insiders critical of the US firm have said it stands to make its loans back and more from the insolvency process.

Previously, Gordon Brothers netted millions from liquidating the stock of fashion retailer LK Bennett, and in insolvency fees.

Labour MP Liam Byrne told the BBC the House of Commons' Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee will recall Gordon Brothers before Parliament.

He said: "I am really worried that a 'greed is good' approach to business by its owners has forced [Poundland] into an administration."

He added the committee wants to know "how much money they're ripping out and crucially, how do we make sure, as a country, that we don't have this kind of scenario unfold again".

- What's gone wrong at Poundland?

Gordon Brothers said on Wednesday that despite the Poundland management bringing about a turnaround over the past year, the firm was "still vulnerable" to inflation and any downturn in sales or profit margin, and it had faced "several years of instability".

A spokesperson added the firm's "thoughts are with Poundland colleagues".

It said it had stepped in to take over the retailer in 2025 when it was struggling, and when "no-one else was willing to finance the business".

One of the central stumbling blocks in negotiations to keep the business afloat was a shareholder loan Gordon Brothers inherited when it bought the business for less than Â£1 last year.

Gordon Brothers was owed Â£22.5m of that loan, while the previous owner Pepco was owed Â£7.5m.

Gordon Brothers rejected various offers to buy the business as a going concern with deals to pay off that loan.

Irish firm Martin Property Group offered to pay off Â£5m of the loan up front, and defer the rest of the payments to 2030.

London-based Xyra group offered Â£12.5m up front but ran out of time to get a deal over the line.

German investment firm Zachert Private Equity is also understood to have made a late offer.

All of these were rejected.

The crisis at Poundland really came to a head over the past few weeks after Gordon Brothers restricted access to funds for day-to-day operations.

This meant that stock at the retailer was not being replenished at the necessary pace in the vital run-up to the festive period.

item.title: GTA VI was built by hand. The man who ran Take-Two during GTA IV says AI could let a filmmaker make the next breakout game
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Engaging article with insights into the gaming industry and AI, though not as technical as the top pick.

Grand Theft Auto VI, on track to be the biggest entertainment launch of any kind, was made the old-fashioned way: Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick said in February that Rockstar Games built the game without generative AI.

“With regards to GTA 6, generative AI has zero part in what Rockstar Games is building. Their worlds are handcrafted. That’s what differentiates them,” Zelnick told GamesIndustry.biz. “They’re built from the ground up, building by building, street by street, neighborhood by neighborhood.”

That’s not to say it didn’t take time and money. Analysts estimate Take-Two spent more than a billion dollars on the game, which came out more than 13 years after its predecessor (Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick never confirmed the amount but admitted the game was “expensive”). But the next blockbuster video game might come sooner, cheaper—and with an even more cinematic lens, according to Ben Feder, who ran Take-Two Interactive when Grand Theft Auto IV came out in 2008.

“Some great creative mind who would have otherwise gone to make a film will make a video game because it’s as simple as point and click,” Feder said to Fortune in a long-winding conversation that quickly became more philosophical than experiential about the state of the entertainment industry.

Feder, now managing partner of TIRTA Ventures, said in a Fortune commentary this month that AI will change how big games get made. His firm invests in AI-native game projects. “We put our money where our mouth is,” he said of TIRTA’s investments.

The next great video game maker might be someone who would otherwise have gone into movies, and that’s because AI would make it easier for a filmmaker without a technical background to get into video games. And Feder doesn’t expect that shift to hurt the franchise he once oversaw.

“I don’t think GTA is going anywhere. In fact, it probably goes from strength to strength,” Feder said. “But that’s not to say it’s going to get created in the exact same way that it got created here.”

Video games have long sat at the intersection of the software and entertainment businesses. Feder said AI will shrink the software side as writing code gets cheaper and easier.

“The argument would be that because AI is making software development commoditized, and software points to zero, it becomes much more about entertainment than it does about both entertainment and computer science,” he said.

Feder described the result as “somewhere between democratizing creativity, the cynic would say commoditizing creativity, but I don’t believe that creativity, true creativity, really gets commoditized unless you’re such a believer in AI that you think AI can also be creative.”

A 13-year ROI

More games won’t mean more hits. Feder expects a flood of new titles, with only a small share breaking through, and pointed to YouTube.

“I don’t know how many billions of minutes of video have been on YouTube, but how many of them actually are good? How many of them actually get traction?” he said. “But the ones that do get traction and are good reach billions of people, literally, and can create enormous outcomes, both creatively and commercially.”

Grand Theft Auto VI shows how large those outcomes can be. Take-Two has not disclosed the game’s cost, though estimates put its development budget at $1 billion to $1.5 billion. Brokerage Oppenheimer projected about $1.85 billion in gross revenue in the game’s first three days, Reuters reported.

“Thirteen years of investment you make back in a day. Unbelievable,” Feder said. “But it only happens if you create the most awesome game ever.”

AI tools could change that math across the industry, he said. “It’s going to get harder to justify a $2 billion game in a world where the next best alternative is two orders of magnitude less.”

GTA VI, ironically, did make back all the money it poured into it, and then some. Feder said that counterargument is a pretty good devil’s advocate. “What’s the argument for not spending another $2 billion on the next one and making it back in a day?” he said. “That’s a valid argument.”

At this point, the conversation became a lived experience of the entertainment industry at large. While most people think of film and cinema as making up the lion’s share of what people consider entertainment, video games have always been there, and they’ve been blockbusters of their own. But recently, as with movies, it seems big publishers have long concentrated their money on a handful of games, or, as the Marvel Cinematic Universe has shown, on the franchise model.

“Even when I was at Take-Two for GTA IV, we were the first, and others followed, to develop a strategy of fewer, bigger titles,” Feder said. And just like movies, the non-Indie games have a tough time breaking through the noise. Feder said the pressure falls on games in the middle, those with big budgets and smaller audiences.

“It’s hard to make the numbers work.”

Feder said that when he ran Take-Two, he saw the industry’s next frontier as characters that look like movie actors rather than figures in a game. Of GTA VI, he said, “This gets as close to it as I’ve ever seen.”

Source: Fortune | Published: 2026-11-25 20:13 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Former Pentagon officials say Hegseth blocking senators from visiting Gulf bases amid Iran war ‘smells like a lack of transparency’
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Important news with clear reporting, though the subject matter is complex and may be less relevant to a broader audience.

The Pentagon is banning U.S. lawmakers from visiting Gulf military bases, and former Pentagon officials warn the move is creating tension between the executive and legislative branches and raising questions about why the Department of Defense is limiting access to information about the Iran war.

“It smells like a lack of transparency in order to thwart Congressional oversight, in order to either hide that the Iran war is costing more, or to use the Iran war as an excuse to get more money,” Evelyn Farkas, executive director of the McCain Institute at Arizona State University and former deputy assistant secretary of defense for Russia, Ukraine, and Eurasia, told Fortune.

Last month, Connecticut Democrat Sen. Chris Murphy detailed his experience of the Department of Defense barring him from visiting the Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar and meeting with military leadership, accusing the Pentagon of obscuring details about the impacts of the Iran war.

“I have been to the Middle East probably a dozen times at least,” Murphy said in a video uploaded to Facebook. “While I have been a member of Congress, I have never, ever been denied access to military facilities. This is part of a coordinated, deliberate campaign by the Department of Defense to try to hide the consequences and the true cost of this war.”

Iowa Republican Sen. Joni Ernst was similarly turned away from a base visit around the same time, The Atlantic reported this week. Ernst did not respond to Fortune’s request for comment.

U.S. Congress members have a long-standing practice of conducting visits of military sites as part of their constitutional oversight. In March, following the U.S.-Israel attacks on Iran, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth published a memo to “further discourage visits to the [U.S. Central Command Area of Responsibility] requiring DoW support by members of Congress and their staffs…and no DoW support shall be made available for congressional travel to the USCENTCOM AOR without my approval.”

Congress has expressed increased misgivings around Hegseth, introducing articles of impeachment this month, which did not pass, in part on the grounds that the secretary began military conflict in Iran without Congressional authorization. Hegseth has sharply reduced the number of routine press briefings and limited press access to briefings, as well as refused to provide information to the Congressional Budget Office ahead of its update to the cost of the Iran war in September. Meanwhile, the Pentagon is seeking $1.5 trillion in allocations—the largest defense budget in U.S. history—to modernize military infrastructure and restock munitions drained in the conflict in the Gulf.

What is the history of U.S. lawmakers visiting military bases?

Legislators have been visiting U.S. military bases in times of conflict since at least 1943, when five U.S. senators embarked on a 65-day inspection tour of global military sites during World War II. Visits increased during and after the Vietnam war, when American lawmakers and journalists returned home with stories that vastly differed from former President Richard Nixon’s narrative that the U.S. was winning the war.

Farkas, who served for eight years as a staff member of the Senate Armed Services Committee and took several trips to the Gulf as part of a congressional delegation (CODEL), said congressional visits to these military bases are a way to not only increase public knowledge of the status of a war overseas, but in many cases justify granting the military additional and targeted resources for specific operations.

During the Iraq war, for example, the U.S. sent a CODEL to the Gulf following improvised explosive devices targeted U.S. personnel in armored vehicles, Farkas recalled. The vehicles were not capable of deflecting the explosives, and following a tour of U.S. military sites, Congress conducted a bipartisan effort to ramp up production of the vehicles.

“It’s legitimate, and also necessary and desirable, for members of Congress to go even during a hot war,” Farkas said.

Why would the Pentagon turn away U.S. lawmakers from military bases?

The Pentagon also has some legitimate reasons for turning lawmakers away from military bases, Elizabeth Dent, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy and former director for the Gulf and Arabian Peninsula in the Office of the Secretary of Defense, told Fortune.

Hosting a CODEL requires resources like military aircraft and personnel to protect and move lawmakers. In a military theater, armed forces may be unable to spare resources, and when specific threats are made against the military, both troops and elected representatives can be put in harm’s way. In 2016 under then-President Barack Obama, the military asked Congress to limit visits to Afghanistan during a fighting season, though it was not an express ban. Across both Republican and Democrat administrations, U.S. Central Command has ordered limited visits to military sites.

However, Hegseth’s prohibition of military visits has continued, even after the end of “Operation Epic Fury” in May, and when, prior to this month, the last known U.S. attack on Iran was in September. Typically, restrictions are lifted after “hot phases” of conflict end, and the Pentagon’s decision to turn away legislators even during lulls in attacks is what raised suspicions of ulterior motives beyond protecting troops and lawmakers.

“The big concern I would have is, the administration has said that Operation Epic Fury is over. Is this more of a lack of transparency and an attempt to hide some of the things that are going on, like the destruction of some of the bases?” Dent said.

What is Hegseth’s strategy in withholding access to information about the Iran war?…
