item.title: The midterms showed boomers losing their grip on politics. Their grip on the money is another story
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Analysis of generational shifts in politics and wealth with useful vocabulary, though the subject matter is complex.

A wave of Democrat support in the midterms swept across the U.S. in the beginning of November marking a change of power in politics—not just from the flipping of red to blue, but also from old to young: non-boomer politicians in Congress are at their highest point since the turn of the century. But even as the Baby Boomers are losing their hold on political power, their economic influence remains considerably more difficult to dislodge.

Americans born between 1946 and 1964 still control more than half of the nation’s wealth, despite representing a continuously shrinking share of the population. And their financial advantage has implications for younger generations struggling with housing costs, student debt and the rising cost of living—especially as the transfer of wealth from older generations to their children remains sluggish.

Reshaping the political landscape

The shift away from Baby Boomer leadership in government has been building for years, but the 2026 midterms accelerated the transition. For the first time in decades, the generation that dominated congressional leadership and policymaking is losing its grip.

The House already moved past the point of Boomer dominance. According to Pew Research Center, Boomers accounted for 39% of House members at the beginning of the 119th Congress, down from a majority just two Congresses earlier. Gen X became the largest generation in the chamber, representing 41% of lawmakers while Millennials accounted for another 15%. The Senate has been slower to change. Boomers still represent 60 of 99 senators at the beginning of the 119th Congress, or roughly 61%.

But that imbalance is beginning to change. According to Quorum’s analysis of newly elected lawmakers, Gen X and Millennials account for 87% of the incoming 120th Congressional class. Of the 120 new members, just 13 are Boomers—while 56 Gen Xers and 48 Millennials will occupy the new seats.

The change is also visible in the pipeline of candidates seeking office. Future Caucus found that Millennials and Gen Z accounted for roughly one-third of congressional candidates in 2026, up from one-quarter in 2024 and one-sixth in 2022. According to the report, Millennials also became the largest generational group running for Senate for the first time in the report’s history.

Still, the political transition is not complete as the Senate continues to be a stubborn stronghold for older Americans. The incoming chamber’s median age will fall to 63 from 64, but will still remain among the oldest Senates in American history, according to Reuters.

The wealth divide

According to the Federal Reserve’s Distributional Financial Accounts, Baby Boomers held approximately $97.4 trillion in household net worth in Q2 2026. That represents 52.5% of all U.S. household wealth, despite Boomers accounting for just 27% of the country’s adult population.

In contrast, Millennials and Gen Z together represented 22.4% of real estate but only held 11.2% of household wealth—about $20.8 trillion. Generation X held another 25.7%.

And while the great wealth transfer is coming, younger Americans are waiting. Visa’s Business and Economic Insights report in July estimated approximately $36 trillion of Baby Boomers’ $93 trillion in assets could transfer to younger generations over the next 20 years—after accounting for liabilities, taxes, fees, retirement spending and other exclusions.

“Imagine you are sitting on a winning lottery ticket. You hit the jackpot, but you immediately lose half by— smartly—taking the lump sum,” the report read. “Next, you lose another 30–40 percent through taxes and fees. The advertised jackpot is enormous, but after the lump-sum haircut, taxes and fees, the take-home number is much lower. A similar dynamic applies to the great wealth transfer.”

But that doesn’t mean the younger Americans will now get access to that same financial security. The transfer is likely to be uneven, with most of the wealth being concentrated among families that already have substantial assets.

According to Visa’s research, nearly 75% of inheritance recipients already have higher net worths than the average household. That means much of the inherited wealth from the transfer will be saved or invested, not immediately spent. Visa also estimated that one in four millennial homeowners received financial assistance from their parents for a down payment.

But perspective matters. A 2025 analysis by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis found that Millennials and Gen Z households actually had more inflation-adjusted wealth at approximately age 34 than Boomers did at that same age.

According to the analysis, Millennials and Gen Zers owned $1.23 for every $1 of wealth owned by Gen Xers at the same age—and $1.35 for every $1 of wealth owned by baby boomers.

The next generational fight

The generational war has a six-year deadline, set by Social Security and the national debt.

According to the 2026 Social Security trustees report, the combined retirement and disability trust funds are projected to be depleted by 2032. At that point, incoming revenue would only cover 83% of scheduled benefits unless Congress changes the program.

Boomers have held the presidency since 2001, spanning George W. Bush to Donald Trump, with the exception of Joe Biden—who is part of the Silent Generation. In that time span, the national debt climbed from $5.81 trillion to over $40.17 trillion through September 2026, according to the Treasury’s fiscal data, during which time, they have passed a series of tax cuts leaving their own generation’s retirements endangered.

Democrats have argued for increasing revenue by raising the cap on earnings subject to Social Security payroll taxes, while Republicans mostly emphasized economic growth. But Sen. Ron Johnson—the Wisconsin Republican who chairs the Senate Budget Committee and is a Boomer himself—has a typically Boomerian fix: make other generations pay for it.…

item.title: Nvidia's board under fire for handling of CEO's alleged affairs
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: News article with clear reporting, though the subject matter is specific to a company and may be less relevant to a broader audience.

Nvidia's board under fire for handling of CEO's alleged affairs

Even as Jensen Huang has returned to work, Nvidia's board is facing criticism over how it handled the crisis brought on by the CEO's alleged affairs.

MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:

How did a board that unanimously decided that its CEO must go decide a few days later to bring him right back? We're talking about Nvidia and its founder, former and now current CEO Jensen Huang. NPR's Andrea Hsu has been gathering reaction to the board's handling of the crisis, and she's with us now to tell us more.

Good morning, Andrea.

ANDREA HSU, BYLINE: Good morning.

MARTIN: OK, so let me just point out here that at an all-hands meeting on Tuesday, Huang apologized for hurting his family and violating the company's code of conduct. That's according to a livestream of the meeting which was viewed by The New York Times. He also reportedly said that President Trump didn't pressure the board into bringing him back. NPR has reached out to Nvidia for confirmation of this, but hasn't heard back. You've been hearing from people who know how boards are meant to operate. What are you hearing from them?

HSU: Yeah. Well, there's been criticism from both those who think Jensen Huang shouldn't have been brought back and also those who think it was the right thing to do. And, Michel, let's remember the role of boards - they exist to make informed and deliberate decisions that are in the best interests of the company and its shareholders. In many instances, they are the only mechanism of accountability for companies and CEOs. And in the case of Nvidia, you know, a lot of people say the board fell short on these duties, and we've asked Nvidia for a response to that, but we haven't heard back on that, either.

MARTIN: Now, recognizing that you're getting a range of opinions there, do these experts have thoughts on what should have happened?

HSU: Yeah. Well, many are saying that the board should have made different choices. Our colleague Shannon Bond spoke with Rob Lalka. He's a professor at Tulane's Freeman School of Business (ph), and he points out that in the last decade, there have been a number of high-profile cases similar to what allegedly happened at Nvidia - you know, a CEO having an affair with an employee. It happened at Intel, McDonald's, Nestle. And Lalka says those boards followed their policies, and those CEOs were out. They decided it had to happen to preserve company values and credibility. But then, as for Nvidia, here's what Lalka says.

ROB LALKA: The board basically went around its entire process that it had set in place for that investigation to put him back into power.

MARTIN: But you also mentioned that there are people who think bringing Huang back was the right thing to do. Say more about that.

HSU: Yeah. I spoke with Betsy Atkins. She is a three-time CEO, a tech entrepreneur and someone who served on several dozen boards. And she is in the camp of people who say, look, Jensen Huang is not just any CEO. He is a genius founder, someone who built this multi-trillion dollar company from nothing.

BETSY ATKINS: I'm not saying that you get to break the law and break all the rules, but it requires nuanced business judgment to weigh many other factors.

HSU: And her complaint is that Nvidia's board acted too quickly in forcing Huang out. She says the real litmus test for board members is do they have courage and conviction and character to do the right thing and to withstand pressure when times are difficult? And she thinks Nvidia's board failed this test, essentially. But now that Huang is back, her hope is that the board can go back to focusing on what she calls the business of the business.

MARTIN: OK. But given that Nvidia, as she pointed out, is such a powerful, high-profile company, such a big footprint in the economy, what signal is this board's flip-flop sending more broadly?

HSU: Yeah. Well, people I've talked to this week says it just drives home the idea that in Silicon Valley, all that matters really is money. Rob Lalka, the business professor, takes it a step further. He describes the board's decision to bring Jensen Huang back as rash and aimed at boosting short-term profits. He says that doesn't make for a robust economy. And he points out that AI leaders have repeatedly said they want to do what's in the best long-term interests of humanity. And he says what's unfolded at Nvidia speaks to quite the opposite.

MARTIN: That is NPR's Andrea Hsu.

Andrea, thank you.

HSU: Thank you, Michel.

item.title: Michigan just hit pause on a plan to update the controversial Line 5 oil pipeline
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Clear reporting on a significant environmental issue with useful vocabulary and context.

This coverage is made possible through a partnership between Grist and Interlochen Public Radio in northern Michigan.

Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer said Tuesday that she’s pausing both pending and issued state permits for the plan to replace a segment of the Line 5 oil pipeline beneath the Straits of Mackinac.

Whitmer said regulators at the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy, or EGLE, need to answer questions about the full scope of the plan’s threats to the environment.

Those questions, according to Whitmer, were raised by a Michigan Supreme Court ruling this summer on a related Line 5 tunnel permit. Justices tossed out a permit issued by a separate state agency, saying their review of environmental harms was too narrow.

Line 5 has been transporting oil and natural gas liquids 645 miles between Ontario and Wisconsin since 1954. A 4-mile segment passes through the Straits of Mackinac, the narrow waterways that connect Lake Michigan to Lake Huron, separating Michigan’s Lower and Upper peninsulas. Sensitive coastal and wetlands habitats are found in the straits, and the area is sacred to Anishinaabe peoples, featuring prominently in their creation story and serving as burial grounds for their ancestors.

“I have always said my ultimate goal is to get Line 5 out of the water,” Whitmer, whose second and final term will end January 1, said in the announcement. “Just one spill threatens irreparable damage to our water, our economy, and our way of life.” The permit pause comes weeks after regulators in Wisconsin had been dealing with a spill on the portion of Line 5 that crosses that state.

It’s the latest setback for pipeline owner Enbridge Energy, which first proposed the plan to replace an aging portion of the pipeline with a new one, buried in a tunnel beneath the straits, almost a decade ago.

Enbridge maintains that the pipeline is safe. In a statement, spokesperson Ryan Duffy pointed to the company’s record of permit approvals — including the pending EGLE permit, which would have been a renewal of one it received in 2021.

Line 5 delivers the energy people depend on every day, Duffy said. “At Enbridge, we remain committed to that purpose and equally committed to safeguarding the Great Lakes,” he said.

The permit freeze is a win for Line 5 opponents who have protested for years against the tunnel project and have fought to shut down the entire pipeline.

“I think this is a really, really excellent step in the right direction,” said Ashley Rudzinski, climate and environment program director for the nonprofit Groundwork Center for Resilient Communities. “We’re seeing the Whitmer administration, finally, putting some real strength behind the words that she had already spoken.”

The Line 5 tunnel project has received federal approval, but with the remaining state permits in question, it’s unclear what its future looks like. Separately, Line 5 faces legal challenges from groups that have fought to shut down the entire pipeline for years, including the Whitmer administration.

Lawyers representing Michigan tribes in their fight to shut down Line 5 said they hope this momentum continues into the administration of Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson, who, like Whitmer, is a Democrat. All 12 federally recognized tribes in Michigan oppose the pipeline.

“No matter who the governor is, it’s in all of our interests to keep the Great Lakes free of oil and to transition away from Line 5,” said Laura Berglan, senior attorney with the legal nonprofit Earthjustice, which represents the Bay Mills Indian Community, the Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians, and the Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians. “We need to protect our shared resources and our tribal resources for the future.”

Source: Grist | Published: 2026-11-25 17:52 UTC

item.title: As food prices rise, do shoppers still care about sustainability?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Explains the impact of rising food prices on sustainability with relevant context and vocabulary.

The headlines say what people already know: Food is getting more expensive. Consumers have been feeling an uptick in the overall price of both dining out and preparing meals at home this year, according to numbers from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.

And just in time for the holidays, things seem to be getting worse. The American Farm Bureau Federation found that the price of goods usually found in a Thanksgiving dinner increased this year for the first time since 2022. One economist told Bloomberg that Americans should expect food prices to keep creeping up into next year.

The high price of fuel, driven by the war in Iran, has contributed to the sticker shock Americans are feeling at the grocery store. Farmers need diesel to harvest, process, store, and transport produce and other crops from the field to retailers. Climate change, as well as El Niño spurring extreme weather globally, is also at play.

And yet, however flummoxed U.S. consumers may be about the high costs of living — a major driver of the midterms’ “blue wave” — consumer spending has only gone up. In fact, consumer spending, which makes up about two-thirds of the U.S. gross domestic product, or GDP, and has driven the economy for some time, increased by 3.8 percent in the third quarter of this year.

At the same time, food systems are still responsible for somewhere between a quarter and a third of global greenhouse gas emissions. With food prices creeping up, it’s worth asking whatever happened to the idea of consumers as climate or environmental activists. The concept of “voting with your dollars” is often described as a meaningful tool for combating carbon-intensive practices in the food supply chain, such as deforestation. But do today’s shoppers still care about where their food comes from and how it’s grown when they’re worried about their supermarket bill (and all the other ones)?

The research is mixed. Some studies suggest that shoppers are comfortable springing for the more eco-friendly option, such as climate-proof wine, even if it costs a premium. But buyer motivations are complex: When it comes to food, even when consumers are paying for more sustainable options, some research shows that they’re more likely to have made that choice for other reasons, such as its taste or health claims.

If the question is whether consumers are motivated by sustainability or by price, the answer may be both, said Sandra Goldmark, a professor at the Columbia Climate School focused on circular economies. “People want a sustainable option. They want it to be healthy for their body and the planet,” said Goldmark. “And they have a price factor,” she added.

The practice of voting with your dollar “has limits,” said David Ortega, an agricultural economist and professor at Michigan State University. Such a practice works when “the sustainable option costs about the same [as the standard option] — less so when there’s a real premium and budgets are tight.”

Eggs, Ortega said, are a good example. When the price of eggs ballooned last year, higher-income households were more likely to be able to afford the more expensive, more sustainable options like cage-free eggs. “Most shoppers can’t, so they reach for the cheapest eggs or conventional products at the supermarket,” he said.

Additionally, the share of GDP that comes from consumer spending may overstate shoppers’ leverage in the food sector, said Ortega, as the bulk of that spending currently goes toward housing costs. What’s more, Ortega noted that the way cage-free eggs have become the industry standard had more to do with shifting state laws and retailer commitments than just “shoppers choosing to pay more.”

Still, history shows that public pressure campaigns can still push companies to flip their supply chains. This works best when the campaigns are targeted and sustained — like when the Coalition of Immokalee Workers, a worker-led human rights group, led boycotts of Taco Bell across the U.S. over its supply chain agreements with tomato farms that mistreated workers. After four years, Taco Bell’s parent company agreed to only work with suppliers that are compliant with a code of conduct developed by farmworkers.

Companies gain something when they respond to consumer demands for change — they avoid reputational harm. In the early 2000s, outrage over a Greenpeace report on deforestation in the Amazon led to soy traders agreeing not to purchase soy from newly deforested lands. Although it fell apart earlier this year, that agreement lasted for nearly two decades — and it was considered widely successful.

The end of the Amazon soy moratorium presented a major blow to conservation efforts in Brazil — but that doesn’t mean consumers today have no say in where their food comes from. The growing influence of the Make America Healthy Again, or MAHA, movement shows that these concerns matter more than ever to many households.

Real change may come when policy changes and public investment in sustainable food systems matches consumer desires, said Jody Kirchner, director of market insights at Good Food Institute, a think tank focused on the alternative protein economy. When the option that’s better for the environment and the planet costs more than the status quo, “shoppers can’t break that loop on their own,” Kirchner added. But maybe they can do it together.

Source: Grist | Published: 2026-11-25 09:45 UTC

Original link: https://grist.org/economics/as-food-prices-rise-do-shoppers-still-care-about-sustainability/

item.title: The ‘drill, baby, drill’ Democrat who will soon help oversee Texas’ oil industry
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Interesting political shift in Texas with potential environmental implications.

This coverage is made possible through a partnership between Grist and KERA, a public media organization serving the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex.

This month’s midterm elections featured a previously unthinkable result in Texas: Democrats won every single statewide race in the Lone Star State. Some of those newly elected Democrats have become household names, like Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa and Senator-elect James Talarico. But the list of Democratic victors also includes a centrist set to occupy a little-known office with outsize influence over the country’s oil and gas industry.

Jon Rosenthal won a contentious race for a seat on the Texas Railroad Commission against Republican Bo French, whose racist social media posts drew national bipartisan backlash. Rosenthal, the first Democrat elected to the commission since 1990, isn’t trying to usher in radical change, and his influence will be limited by the two Republicans already sitting on the commission. But he’s aiming to bring transparency, accountability, and a bigger budget to the regulatory board.

“Voters have delivered a mandate for a change,” said Rosenthal at a post-election press conference. “My top priority … is doubling the Railroad Commission’s budget. I believe the commission needs more resources to do the work they are [tasked] to do.”

The Railroad Commission was established in 1891 to regulate the rail industry. Over the years, the agency’s focus shifted to overseeing the state’s booming oil and gas industry. In 2024, Texas accounted for almost half of the country’s crude oil production. This fact makes the Railroad Commission one of the most powerful state-level regulatory agencies in the country. The commission generally takes a deregulatory approach and is widely considered friendly to the industry it regulates, especially with oil companies donating generously to the campaigns of commissioners they support.

Rosenthal describes himself as a “drill, baby, drill” Democrat, arguing a clean environment and good jobs can coexist. He worked in the oil and gas industry for over 25 years as a mechanical engineer. In 2018, he was elected to the Texas House of Representatives, representing parts of Houston, and was reelected three times before running for the Railroad Commission.

His victory likely has much to do with the unpopularity of his opponent. French, a former local Republican Party chair, prompted widespread criticism when he made a racist social media post in September about South Asian students celebrating at a University of Texas football game. The race also drew attention to French’s previous offensive remarks, like posting a since-deleted online poll in 2025 asking whether “Jews” or “Muslims” pose a bigger threat to the United States. Several prominent Republican politicians denounced French’s bigoted comments, which led to a fundraising boost for Rosenthal.

Rosenthal will join Republicans Wayne Christian and Christi Craddick on a commission that has recently attempted to shield itself from public scrutiny. In August, the agency adopted a new public participation policy that does not guarantee public comments at its monthly meetings. A public comment period is now included only if a commissioner requests it on the agenda.

Christian, a far-right conservative, championed the new policy, while the more moderate Craddick voted against it. Christian faced criticism from Democratic state lawmakers for not showing up to a legislative hearing that would have included discussion of that decision, and he used profanity when defending the vote from Commission Shift, a nonprofit watchdog group.

In a social media post, Rosenthal called the new policy “shameful.” He campaigned on making hearings more accessible. Virginia Palacios, the executive director of Commission Shift, expressed optimism that the new commissioner can help increase transparency.

“It’s a possibility that if we have someone like Jon Rosenthal who ran his campaign on the idea that open meetings should be open, you could potentially have two commissioners that would vote for open public meeting policy,” she said.

Rosenthal could occasionally team up with Craddick to neutralize Christian on other policy questions as well. “There are times when [Craddick and Christian] vote differently on some of these permit … or policy approvals, even though the vast majority of their votes tend to be the same,” Palacios explained.

Palacios does not expect “drastic changes” with Rosenthal’s election, but she does believe there will be greater opportunity for public engagement. According to his campaign website, Rosenthal wants the commission to hire regional community liaisons to make it easier for Texans to offer input.

“We’ve recently heard of communities that requested the Railroad Commission to go out and visit them in person … and the Railroad Commission denied those requests,” said Palacios. “We would hope to see that this new sitting commissioner would be more responsive to the public and try to show up in person where others haven’t.”

Apart from improving transparency and community relations, Rosenthal’s biggest ambition is to double the agency’s biennial budget from approximately $500 million to $1 billion. He argues this will help “turbo-charge” the plugging of orphaned oil wells, those that have been inactive for at least 12 months, and zombie wells, those whose plugs are failing.

Thousands of these wells across Texas are leaking methane, a potent greenhouse gas that contributes to trapping heat in the atmosphere. The Railroad Commission plugged over 2,000 orphaned wells during its last fiscal year — a record number — but still ended up with more of them at the end of the year than they started off with. That’s because a large number of low-producing and inactive wells become orphaned.…

Source: Grist | Published: 2026-11-25 09:30 UTC

Original link: https://grist.org/elections/jon-rosenthal-texas-railroad-commission-orphaned-wells/

item.title: A Disappointing UN Climate Summit Concludes With Little Action on Food Systems
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Detailed coverage of the UN Climate Summit with clear reporting and useful context.

The first day of the United Nations’ COP31 climate talks in Turkey focused on the nexus of food, agriculture and health, setting a hopeful tone for negotiators and advocacy groups that have been pushing to make food systems a bigger priority at the annual gatherings.

Even before the talks wrapped up Sunday, those hopes had faded. Despite the increasing evidence that cutting emissions from agriculture and the land it occupies represents the most expedient path to lowering climate pollution in the short term—an emergency break on global warming—negotiators left the event with little action on the farming front.

Farmers in the world’s most vulnerable countries will pay the price, advocates and researchers warn, pointing to this year’s “super” El Niño as a case in point.

As the event got underway, a new report from the International Fund for Agricultural Development and Turkey’s Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry said the weather phenomenon could cost the global economy $11 trillion.

“The weather shock is becoming an economic shock, and it is arriving at the worst possible time,” said Jahan-Zeb Chowdhury, the fund’s lead technical specialist for the environment and climate. “Farmers are already vulnerable because of the two other shocks they have experienced—fertilizer and energy.”

The report noted fertilizer prices skyrocketed in 2026 as its main ingredients were stalled in the Strait of Hormuz due to the war in Iran. Fuel prices also soared because of the blockage of the strait. These financial pressures, along with expected volatile weather over the next several months, could push tens of millions more people into acute food insecurity by the end of next year, the report said.

In its latest analysis, the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organization projected that the El Niño could cause major droughts across much of Africa, Central America and parts of South and Southeast Asia.

A separate FAO analysis submitted to the conference found that 86 percent of countries include food systems and agriculture in Nationally Determined Contributions, their roadmaps for meeting the goals of the 2015 Paris climate agreement. If those countries executed those contributions, emissions from agriculture could shrink more than 40 percent within four years and 76 percent by 2035, compared to 2019 levels.

Yet negotiators at the conference failed to produce any meaningful measures to address the climate crisis through agricultural practices. Governments did not reach any agreement on a cover decision, the concluding statement of the conference, which not only omitted any reference to fossil fuels, but also lacked any mention of food systems or agriculture.

“At a time when urgent and ambitious action is needed, commitments fall far short of what is required to protect our planet and support the hundreds of millions of smallholder farmers who are already bearing the brunt of unpredictable weather, declining harvests and increasing hardship,” said Surita Sandosham, president and CEO of Heifer International, in a written statement.

Countries first developed an agriculture-specific negotiating track at the conference held in Egypt in 2022. The intention was to bring a greater focus on agriculture and, ultimately, more financing for farmers to adapt to changing weather conditions.

But the FAO points out that financing for food and agriculture has fallen by 10 percent since 2024, and receives about 5 percent of climate-related development finance, despite needing nearly 20 percent.

“In their new climate plans countries clearly recognize the opportunities for actions that can build resilience while also reducing emissions significantly from the agricultural sector,” said Kaveh Zahedi, who directs the FAO’s Office of Climate Change, Biodiversity and Environment, in a statement. “But the urgency for action is not being matched by climate finance, nor reflected in the negotiated outcomes.”

Those negotiations likely will resume at COP32, which will be held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

Already, the leadership seems poised to tackle agriculture issues.

During the first week of this year’s conference, Ethiopia announced it would join the Alliance of Champions for Food Systems Transformation, a coalition of governments that are urging more robust negotiations around agriculture. Another group, the True Animal Protein Price Coalition, issued a declaration on low-emitting food systems, saying its members would explore “protein diversification”—a diplomatic term for the sensitive topic of reducing emissions from livestock through dietary shifts.

The U.N. has noted a lack of progress on reducing emissions from the livestock sector, which currently accounts for at least 15 percent of total greenhouse gas emissions and one-third of methane, the super-polluting greenhouse gas. Livestock industry lobbyists continue to show up in full force at each year’s conference, contributing to the collapsed efforts on food systems, critics said.

Source: Inside Climate News | Published: 2026-11-25 14:12 UTC

Original link: https://insideclimatenews.org/news/25112026/a-disappointing-un-climate-summit-concludes-with-little-action-on-food-systems/

item.title: Storm Costs Are Sending Maine’s Power Bills Soaring
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Explains the impact of storms on energy costs with clear reporting and useful context.

Squeezing blood from a stone.

That’s how Seth Berry describes rising electricity prices in Maine. As executive director of Our Power, a coalition focused on clean energy and utility regulation, Berry talks with people all over the state who are no longer able to afford their power bills.

Combined with recent price increases for heating fuel and gasoline, he said electricity bills could create “a world of hurt” for many Maine households this winter. “People are really at their wits’ end, and I expect to see a whole lot of folks cold this winter, desperately cold in their homes,” Berry said.

Maine has one of the highest energy burdens in the country, due in part to the cost of downed power lines and other repairs after severe storms. The state’s biggest power company is currently requesting another rate increase, and Maine is now reckoning with the balance between needed grid repairs and affordable power bills.

Maine’s Energy Burden

Electricity prices in Maine increased 64 percent between 2019 and 2025, compared to an average 38 percent increase nationwide, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Only Washington, D.C., and California had larger increases.

The state also has one of the highest average household energy burdens in the nation. A 2024 report to Maine’s Electric Ratepayer Advisory Council found that low-income households spend about 8 percent of their income on electricity and an additional 6 percent on other sources like propane and heating oil. Anything above 6 percent is considered a high energy burden by the U.S. Department of Energy.

Maine’s rural, heavily forested character means utility companies require more miles of power lines to reach their most remote customers, and these lines are more likely to be hit by tree branches, the most common cause of outages.

Climate change has fueled more intense storm seasons in recent years. Maine had the highest number of power outages per customer in the U.S. in 2023 and 2024, federal data shows. The state also had the highest average minutes of power outage in 2023 and the second-highest in 2024.

Central Maine Power, the largest electricity provider in the state, reported more than $600 million in storm recovery costs between 2021 and 2025, a span that included the three most expensive storm years in the company’s history.

“Storm costs have become one of the largest and fastest-growing items on customers’ bills,” said Rebecca Schultz, the senior advocate for climate and clean energy at the Natural Resources Council of Maine.

Advocates like Berry and Schultz say that the way CMP is reimbursed for its storm recovery costs incentivizes the company to overspend, leaving customers to shoulder an even greater burden.

“It’s broken, people understand that it’s broken,” Berry said.

CMP did not respond to interview requests. The company noted in comments to the state Public Utilities Commission in September that the commission’s review of its storm costs from 2023 to 2025 showed “no findings of imprudence.”

The Maine Legislature in March directed the PUC, which regulates utilities in the state, to conduct a review of energy pricing and metrics for affordability. Managing storm costs will be essential to the affordability discussion.

Accounting for Storms

Power companies don’t treat storm costs like regular expenses because severe weather can be so unpredictable and costly.

CMP customers currently pay $14.1 million per year in storm recovery as part of their base rates, which goes toward a reserve account. Each storm event is classified into tiers based on how much CMP spends on the recovery.

Depending on the tier, CMP is responsible for paying up to a certain threshold of each storm’s recovery costs out of its reserves. Beyond that threshold, costs are split equally between the company and its customers—up to a point.

CMP’s share when costs exceed its storm reserve is capped at $3 million per year. The rest is charged directly to customers. The largest events, like an April 2024 storm where CMP spent more than $100 million, are billed to customers over two years, plus additional carrying costs.

CMP customers have paid for $57.8 million just in carrying costs over the last five years, according to testimony by Maine’s Office of the Public Advocate to the PUC.

Since CMP’s financial liability is capped, “it deprives the company of an incentive to control costs,” Schultz said.

Schultz said the company can contract more out-of-state line crews, which require higher hourly rates and additional housing and travel expenses, than it may actually need for storm response because there’s no reward for efficient planning.

In the past five years, CMP has hired external crews for 18 storms per year, averaging about 93 crews each time. While contractor crews are essential when major storms surpass the company’s regular capacity, Schultz said CMP’s approach creates “a huge amount of overpreparedness.”

Heather Sanborn, the state’s public advocate, said CMP’s storm response is “carefully calibrated” to be profitable, not cost-efficient or faster at restoring power.

Even in 2025, a year with less severe weather, CMP racked up $43 million in recovery costs, more than three times the base recovery costs that customers pay, according to its filings with the PUC.

“All of these costs get rolled up into customers’ bills whether the storm turns out to be a big one and whether there’s work to do or not,” Berry said.

An Alternate Method

The other major electricity provider in Maine, Versant Power, has a different storm cost structure, in which customers’ base rates include the five-year average of recovery costs.…

item.title: Maryland Regulators, Air Force Squabble Over Fuel Spill and Golf Course at Joint Base Andrews
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Detailed account of a local environmental issue with clear reporting.

Recent testing at Joint Base Andrews found a thick layer of jet fuel beneath the airfield, eight months after a spill was detected near Piscataway Creek. But the Air Force and Maryland environmental regulators remain at odds over basic facts of the spill, such as how much fuel was leaked and whether the base skipped its reporting obligations, while the leak’s source has yet to be found.

At the same time, they are locked in a separate dispute over a golf course renovation, which the base says is beyond the reach of the state’s regulatory authority due to an exemption from President Donald Trump.

Between Nov. 9 and 13, the Air Force conducted pressure testing and drilled several soil borings along the section of pipeline where the leak was suspected. Maryland inspectors were also on site watching. One boring, along a pipe known as Lateral Row 7, found a layer of fuel 3.32-feet-thick, the Air Force said .

In separate statements, both sides said the finding significantly narrowed the search. But neither can yet determine where exactly the pipe broke. The Air Force said that will require digging the line up or inspecting it directly.

Its next step is to pump the fuel out of the ground and do more drilling to map how far it has spread. That work will begin once contracts are in place, the base said, without giving a start date.

According to the Maryland Department of the Environment’s Nov. 18 report, the agency representatives visited the base to oversee the leak testing of the west-side hydrant loop between Nov. 9 and 13. No leaks were found during the testing, which excluded Lateral Row 7—already isolated from the system—and the above-ground piping inside the pump house. The testing was supposed to be completed by Nov. 12 per the deadlines conveyed by the MDE. The base said both sides agreed to adjust the original date to Nov. 13 due to contracting delays and a federal holiday.

The latest testing came after MDE Secretary Serena McIlwain pressed the base in an Oct. 28 letter to identify the source of the fuel leaks and pinpoint the point of failure, warning that “the pace of that progress has not matched the urgency of the situation.”

McIlwain’s letter also set deadlines for the base to finish its investigations and complete actions between Nov. 12 and Dec. 27. It included correcting JBA’s fuel inventory records and reporting any losses to the state, completing overdue corrosion testing and repairs, and submitting a schedule for repairing or abandoning Lateral Row 7. It also required the base to evaluate whether the storm drain systems were carrying fuel to Piscataway Creek.

“If these deadlines are not met, I will consult with our Office of the Attorney General to determine appropriate next steps to ensure compliance,” McIlwain warned.

In a Nov. 9 response, JBA Commander Col. Karl Seekamp only acknowledged the March fuel spill, contradicting McIlwain’s letter describing “major jet fuel releases” that occurred in December and in March.

“JBA’s operational and environmental records do not indicate or support an environmental release in December 2025,” a JBA spokesperson said in emailed comments. The base said its routine testing on Dec. 11, 2025, found a mechanical leak inside a valve at the pump station for its west-side fueling system, and that all of the fuel stayed within “closed, impermeable piping infrastructure,” with no discharge to the environment.

According to MDE’s timeline, the base’s fuel system failed a precision tightness test on Dec. 11, 2025, and records showed inventory losses in January and February. The department was not notified until fuel odors and a sheen were seen near the Piscataway Creek’s headwaters on March 23. On April 8, the base told MDE that 22,000 gallons of fuel had been released into the environment, out of a total system loss of about 32,000 gallons.

Nine members of Maryland’s Congressional delegation, including Sen. Chris Van Hollen, wrote to Air Force Secretary Troy Meink in May, requesting an accounting of how much fuel had entered the creek and how much remained underground.

After the Air Force arranged a staff-level briefing for Van Hollen in late September, his office requested more information, but has yet to receive a response, a spokesperson said in a statement last week.

In its emailed comments, JBA said it has provided two full years of raw fuel inventory records directly to MDE, and the Defense Logistics Agency is conducting an independent audit of contractor inventory to reconcile accounting figures.

Meanwhile, water testing from Piscataway Creek just outside the base still shows petroleum compounds washing into the waterways. In the most recent results by MDE, an Oct. 21 sample detected diesel-range hydrocarbons, which include jet fuel, at 84 parts per billion, well above MDE’s surface-water action level of 47ppb. Every off-base sample listed since testing began in April has exceeded the agency’s action level.

Late-September samples detected a spike across several fuel compounds.

“We can not verify whether release from the fueling infrastructure have stopped. The most recent sampling results, available on our website, continue to show fuel constituents at the Piscataway Creek off-base location,” MDE spokesman Jay Apperson said in a written response.

As the state and federal agencies clash over fuel spill contamination, another regulatory fight between them has surfaced over renovation of the golf course on Joint Base Andrews.

An MDE report dated Aug. 28 and reviewed by Inside Climate News shows an agency inspector visited the base to investigate a complaint that the golf course renovation might be impacting a nearby stormwater basin built for a separate project.

“Access to the site was not permitted during the complaint investigation; however, I was able to observe the potential impacts,” wrote the inspector, who recorded his observations from the roadside.…

Source: Inside Climate News | Published: 2026-11-25 09:55 UTC

Original link: https://insideclimatenews.org/news/25112026/joint-base-andrews-jet-fuel-spill-cleanup-golf-course-renovation/

item.title: New Paper Challenges Cruelty Exemptions for Food-Producing Animals
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Important topic with clear reporting but may require some background knowledge.

Clipping off chickens’ sensitive beaks without anesthesia. Cramming sows in crates so small they can’t turn around. Castrating or dehorning livestock without painkillers. Slamming piglets on the ground to kill them—a practice known in the industry as “thumping.”

These are all considered standard, common or accepted practice in U.S. animal agriculture and are exempt from state animal cruelty laws. Even in a country that overwhelmingly says it wants animals treated well—not just the 150 million or so kept as pets, but the 10 billion raised for food—this is the status quo.

The vast majority of the animals that are consumed or generate animal products in the United States are raised in intensive confinement, out of public view. Animal cruelty laws largely don’t apply to them mostly because of the immense power of the American farm lobby, which has convinced lawmakers that the industry itself can decide what is standard practice and therefore legal.

But a new paper argues that these exemptions for food-producing animals—which have been widely accepted as the norm for decades, even by animal advocacy groups—aren’t legally ironclad after all.

“The narrative has gone that these exemptions put farmed animals beyond the law—even if we wanted to, we could not prosecute for cruelty that’s happening on the farms,” said Delcianna Winders, a law professor and director of the Animal Law and Policy Institute at the Vermont Law and Graduate School. “What I’ve done is challenged that and said: What does the law actually say?”

In Winders’ new paper, which she discussed on a Harvard University panel Thursday and will be published next April in Ecology Law Quarterly, she found that, in fact, the state laws covering animal cruelty on farms aren’t as pervasive or sweeping as commonly believed. Winders examines the laws, state by state, interpreting the specifics of the exemptions.

“Not one of them—not a single one—says farm animals are not covered by the law,” Winders said.

This argument, in theory, could open up legal avenues for animal advocacy or other groups to pursue factory farm operators for industry-standard practices that are arguably or obviously cruel. Winders points out that these practices have allowed American factory farms to proliferate on a massive scale—causing water pollution, air pollution and more emissions of methane, the especially potent greenhouse gas, than major developed economies, including Spain.

“If we were not engaging in these practices that Americans deem unacceptable—we were not crowding animals so tightly, mutilating them—we would not be able to produce animals on the scale that we are,” Winders said. “If you were going to have animals in conditions that are considered acceptable, it would be a different system, and it would have to be smaller.”

That’s because humane care undercuts profits. Many of the common practices in factory farm settings, such as de-horning or de-beaking, are performed to address the aggression that animals show when tightly confined and stressed. But giving animals space makes feeding and medicating inefficient and costly, while also limiting the economies of scale that has enabled the industry to get so big.

Most people would be surprised, Winders says, to learn that no federal regulation or law covers the treatment of food-producing animals on the industrial farms where they spend the majority of their lives. States have enacted animal laws that criminalize unjustified or unnecessary cruelty to animals, but they were crafted more than a century ago before factory-scale farming became the norm. Starting in the late 1980s and 1990s, states began crafting laws that exempted on-farm practices from criminal prosecution. Today, 38 states have some form of these exemptions.

This story is funded by readers like you.

Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.

Donate Now

But even in the 12 that don’t, criminal prosecutions for on-farm cruelty happen rarely. That, Winders said, is because there are no regulations that require oversight under federal animal cruelty laws in factory farms, which means the only way to know what’s actually happening is with a search warrant based on probable cause, and to do that the law requires evidence. Even after clearing those obstacles, prosecutions are difficult, largely because of vagueness in the law that tends to get interpreted in a defendant’s favor.

There is, she says, a more fundamental problem. “The fact that we’re just using criminal law to regulate a massive industry—that’s not generally how you regulate industries. Normally, you have a regulatory regime with licenses or permits and inspections. None of that is happening, and so the result is cruelty only ever comes to light if there’s an undercover investigation.”

These are exceptionally rare.

In 1996, legal scholar and lawyer David Wolfson published a seminal law review article and later a book based on that article, explaining how states had carved out exemptions for livestock in state animal cruelty laws.

Wolfson, who was Winder’s co-panelist at Harvard Thursday, wrote that the agriculture industry lobbied state legislatures to craft animal cruelty laws so it couldn’t be prosecuted for any farming practice that the industry deems acceptable, regardless of how painful or cruel it may be.

In a subsequent book that Wolfson co-authored with animal law expert Mariann Sullivan, they wrote: “As a result, in most of the United States, prosecutors, judges, and juries no longer have the power to determine whether or not farmed animals are treated in an acceptable manner. The industry alone defines the criminality of its own conduct.”

At least one animal welfare legal group has challenged these exemptions, arguing that they’re unconstitutional because only legislatures can make laws.…

item.title: Pollution Driven by U.S. Data Centers Causing Hundreds of Early Deaths
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Technical topic with clear reporting but may require some technical understanding.

U.S. data centers are driving greater power demand, and with it, more pollution from coal and gas power plants. Researchers estimate that worsening pollution is leading to hundreds of early deaths.

The new modeling study finds that, in 2023, the added power demand from data centers led to an estimated 650 early deaths across the U.S. Given the rapid buildout of data centers, their impact would likely be even greater today, authors say.

The study further suggests that pollution is often intensifying far from where data centers are located. For instance, data centers in Virginia — which are connected to a large regional power grid — might spur power plants in the Midwest to ramp up. As their power output grows, so does particulate pollution, a contaminant linked to heart attacks, strokes, and lung disease.

“Even if you don’t think you are affected because there is not a data center near you, think again,” said coauthor Noelle Selin, head of the Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy at MIT. The findings were published in Environmental Research Letters.

A separate study, published this month in Nature Sustainability, looks at the impact of more than 400 hyperscale data centers across the U.S. It found the facilities are using as much electricity as 8 million homes. In Oregon and Virginia, two data center hotspots, they are consuming more than 15 percent of the electricity sold in each state.

item.title: 2026 Was the Year Restaurants Went Full Midwest
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, detailed analysis

This is an excerpt from Pre Shift, our newsletter for bartenders, restaurant workers and the hospitality industry.

2026 Was the Year Restaurants Went Full Midwest

It’s a giardinera- and tavern-style-stuffed, totally welcoming time in hospitality

At Kyle Knall’s Milwaukee restaurant Cassis, the showstopper dish is ravioli Dauphiné, a sheet of 24 tiny squares stuffed with the Wisconsin cheese Pleasant Ridge Reserve. Topped with glazed seasonal veggies, kernels of sweet corn in summer and sliced honeynut squash in late fall, it speaks to Knall’s Midwestern-meets-French approach—one of the reasons why his restaurant earned a slot on Eater’s 2026 list of the Best New Restaurants in America.

The Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, feature serious Midwest representation. The Best New Restaurants list includes Chicago’s Creepies, which also digs into that Midwest-French mashup, and Kansas City’s Akoya Omakase, which brings a distinct viewpoint to the omakase experience. Meanwhile, the pickled walleye cheeks at Rosy in Cleveland and the puffed grain toast at All Well in Chicago are among the Restaurant Dishes of the Year, and Chicago’s Bad Butter, a place best-known for its croissant take on a Chicago-style hot dog, is one of the Best New Bakeries. It even includes drinks—Culebra, a Puerto Rican spot that draws on the Latinx influences of its Chicago neighborhood, is on Punch’s Best New Bars list. Between these accolades and other national recognition, all eyes are on the Midwest right now. And that’s even before we get into the impact of the Chicago-set show The Bear, which put Italian beef on everyone’s radar, and the rise of tavern-style pizza around the country.

The Midwest has always had great restaurants, of course, but it’s undeniable that something has shifted. “People are flying into these cities rather than flying over them,” says Vinnie Cimino, the Cleveland chef who co-owns Rosy and Cordelia. “I think that word is getting out about these smaller pockets of culture and cuisine.” Some of this is attributable to diners being more willing to explore outside big coastal cities, but it’s also due to chefs returning home to the region. “Post-pandemic, a lot of folks moved out of larger cities and back home,” says Cimino. “Now they’re setting up shop and creating great things in the spaces that they grew up in.” David Posey, chef and co-owner of Creepies and Elske in Chicago, agrees, adding: “For a long time, it felt like we were playing catch-up with trends on the coasts. Now I think we’re less quick to follow trends and are more confident in having our own voice of what the Midwest is.”

One of those chefs who left New York is Knall, a Birmingham, Alabama, native who cooked at Gramercy Tavern in New York before moving to his wife’s hometown of Milwaukee in 2020. Another is Peter Hoang, who worked at his father’s Kansas City, Missouri, sushi restaurant before gaining experience in Chicago and New York restaurants. When he returned to open Akoya Omakase, he crafted menus with the audience in mind, with two omakases, priced more affordably than many at $85 and $165, as well as an à la carte menu. “My sushi is honed by Japanese techniques and sourcing,” he says. “But I interpret what I think is best for the fish, whether that’s highlighting the textures and flavors through different garnishes or using aging or salting techniques.”

It’s not simply that these are good restaurants located in the Midwest—these restaurants are deeply Midwestern in ethos. In Chicago, David and Anna Posey, who run the Michelin-starred Elske, wanted to open a French bistro for their second venture. But as they developed Creepies with chef de cuisine Tayler Ploshehanski, David Posey says they began expanding its focus: “We started taking flavors and adapting them to things that we’re a little more familiar with.” This means dishes that draw on the traditions of Michigan, Wisconsin, and Illinois—think tarte flambée on a tavern-style pizza crust and mussels with giardiniera. And it’s not just the food at Creepies that reflects the Midwest: “We told our designer that our inspiration board was a Midwest basement with wood paneling and low ceilings meets a bistro in the French countryside.”

At Cordelia, Cimino leans into the traditional cuisine of Northeast Ohio, with offerings like raw-beef cannibal sandwiches and kielbasa with cabbage salad. “It’s the familiar flavors that we grew up eating, rethought into this more modern light,” he says. Meanwhile, Rosy “is a deeper dive into the culture of our region” and features dishes like Balkan cevapi and Italian cotechino cooked over live fire. The approach is drawing a wide range of Cleveland diners, from 20-somethings there for the cool, candlelit vibe to grandparents there to taste the food they grew up with. “I think that’s what the Midwest is,” Cimino says. “Being able to be that transgenerational space everybody feels welcome in.”

That welcoming community sensibility is a key component of Midwestern restaurants. Knall counts several farmers and shoppers at the West Allis Farmers Market, where he sources for Cassis, as some of his regulars. “To me, it shows that’s really what Midwest food is: supporting those communities,” he says.

Perhaps more than anything, it’s hospitality that sets these spots apart. “Hospitality is our biggest focus between both restaurants and maybe even more of a focus than the food,” Knall says. “To me, the way that our team makes you feel in the restaurants is such a Midwest thing.” And at Cordelia, where the slogan is “Midwest Nice,” Cimino says: “It’s welcoming you into our proverbial home.”

Source: Eater | Published: 2026-11-25 15:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Why it is here: original recipe, fusion cuisine

I’ve always loved Italian American food. Maybe because Italian and Korean cooking have traits in common: Both are homey and resourceful, and grandmothers are revered for their signature dishes made without formal recipes. This recipe was one of the first Korean Italian fusion recipes I developed, and it makes use of my two favorite secret weapons: kimchi and fish sauce. The result is the Bolognese you know and love, but with a deep, tangy twist. Fish sauce in Italian cooking is not a new idea, actually—Romans have been using salted anchovies and garum, an ancient kind of fish sauce, for centuries. For an extra-special finish, I love garnishing this with baek (white) kimchi for acidity. But it’s optional, and regular kimchi (or no kimchi) works just fine, too.

Need to make a substitution?

Preparation

- Step 1 Start the Bolognese sauce: Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large Dutch oven or pot over medium-high heat. Stir in 1 medium-yellow onion, finely diced (about 1½ cups), 2 carrots, peeled and finely diced, and 3 stalks celery, finely diced, and cook, stirring occasionally, until the onions have softened and the edges start to brown, about 4 minutes. Stir in 4 cloves garlic, minced, and a pinch of kosher salt and cook for 30 seconds, then stir in 1 cup chopped kimchi and 1 Tbsp. tomato paste and cook until the kimchi pieces start to soften, about 3 minutes. Pour in ½ cup red wine, increase the heat, and simmer, stirring with a wooden spoon to dislodge any bits that have stuck to the bottom, until the wine has nearly disappeared, about 2 minutes. Step 2 Add the meat: Stir in 1 lb. ground beef, season with generous pinches of salt (at least ½ tsp.), and cook, breaking up the beef into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until cooked through, 6 to 8 minutes. Step 3 Add the tomatoes: Pour one 28-oz. can whole San Marzano tomatoes in a bowl. Using clean hands, squish the tomatoes into small pieces. Pour the tomatoes into the pot and add 1 cup beef broth or water, ½ tsp. dried Italian seasoning or dried oregano, a pinch of salt, and a few grinds of freshly ground black pepper. Bring to a simmer and lower the heat to medium-low. Gently cook, stirring occasionally, until the sauce is just thick enough to stand up on a spoon, about 20 minutes. Stir in 2 Tbsp. fish sauce and taste, then add more salt or fish sauce if needed. Step 4 Cook the noodles and serve: In a pot of boiling salted water, cook 1 lb. spaghetti according to package instructions, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking, until al dente. Drain the noodles in a colander, then give the colander a shake to get rid of extra water. Divide the noodles among serving plates and spoon the Bolognese on top. Garnish with 1 cup chopped kimchi (white or regular; if using) and 2 Tbsp. chopped flat-leaf parsley and serve. Do Ahead: Leftover Bolognese sauce (without the noodles) keeps in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days, or in the freezer for up to 2 months.

One pot, four hits of lemon: Juice (limone #1) and zest (limone #2) in the cooking water, then more juice (limone #3) and zest (limone #4) to ﬁnish. The contrast of cooked and fresh citrus yields a lemon experience as wild as it gets—at least as far as pasta goes. Crème fraîche and Parmigiano-Reggiano mellow the acid into submission, delivering a creamy yet punchy ﬁnal product just begging for forks… and maybe one more squeeze of lemon.

Want some protein here? Add one pound of peeled and deveined medium shrimp to the pot as soon as the pasta turns uncomfortably al dente.

- Total Time 30 minutes

- Yield 4–6 servings

Ingredients

2 or 3

3¾

2

Need to make a substitution?

Preparation

- Step 1 Remove the zest from 2 lemons with a vegetable peeler in long, lengthwise strips. Chop the strips very fine. (You should have a heaping 2 Tbsp.) Transfer half the chopped zest to a large pot or Dutch oven. Reserve the remaining half. Step 2 Squeeze enough juice from the lemons to measure ½ cup (120 ml); reserve the remaining lemon for squeezing at the finish. Transfer ¼ cup (60 ml) of the juice to the pot with the zest and reserve the remaining juice for serving. Add 3½ cups (840 ml) water, 1 large shallot, peeled and thinly sliced, 2 Tbsp. (30 g) unsalted butter, 4 thyme sprigs, leaves stripped and stems discarded, and 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal kosher salt. Step 3 Place the pot over high heat and bring to a boil. Add 1 lb. (454 g) egg noodles. (Don’t worry if they’re not fully submerged.) Cook, stirring, until the pasta is uncomfortably al dente, 5–7 minutes. Reduce the heat to medium to maintain a lively but gentle simmer and add 1 cup (2 oz./60 g) finely grated Parmigiano-Reggiano and ¼ cup (60 ml) water, stirring to incorporate and create a pan sauce. Continue cooking and adding water, ¼ cup (60 ml) at a time, until there is a generous amount of sauce pooling in the pot and the noodles are al dente, 3–5 minutes more. Add ⅓ cup (80 g) crème fraîche, the remaining finely chopped lemon zest, and the reserved ¼ cup (60 ml) lemon juice. Season with kosher salt and taste. If the only flavor you’re getting is lemon, continue salting to bring out the creaminess. Step 4 Serve topped with a big dollop of crème fraîche and a squeeze of lemon juice. Shower with the remaining 1 cup (2 oz./60 g) finely grated Parmigiano-Reggiano and pinches of flaky sea salt. (Yes, this is a lot of Parm! But stay with me here… it’s a vital balance to the punches of lemon.) Top with more thyme leaves, and if desired, cracked black pepper and chopped roasted hazelnuts.

item.title: This Is the Number One Cheese You Need on Your Holiday Cheese Board (No, It’s Not Cheddar)
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: unique dish, cultural significance

This Is the Number One Cheese You Need on Your Holiday Cheese Board (No, It’s Not Cheddar)

I chatted with two cheesemongers to find out exactly what I should be putting on my cheese spreads this holiday season. Surprisingly, a classic cheddar isn't at the top!

After playing Tetris in my oven an hour before a holiday party, I’m always relieved I decided to serve a cheese board as the appetizer. Cheese boards don’t require much time to put together (and take up zero oven space), but I seem to linger on the cheese selection, always asking myself the same question: Which cheeses would everyone like to eat?

So, I sat down with the experts: Molly Browne, dean of mongers at Cheese State University and education director at Dairy Farmers of Wisconsin, and Emilia D’Albero, the first American ever crowned World’s Best Cheesemonger. They gave me the scoop on putting together the perfect holiday cheese board. Molly and Emilia recommend three to five cheeses per board, representing a variety of milk types, styles and flavors.

But which cheese should I buy that everyone would like? More specifically, what feels indulgent but won’t alienate picky eaters? I expected Molly and Emilia to recommend some extremely specific, hard-to-find cheeses, but both suggested varieties I could pick up at the grocery store.

What is the best cheese for a holiday cheese board?

According to Molly, the best cheese for a holiday cheese board that appeals to all ages is butterkase. This semi-firm cow’s milk cheese is creamy, smooth, relatively mild and exceptionally buttery—hence its German name, which translates to “butter cheese.” (If you’re as chronically online as I am, you may have heard of butterkase from @courtneycookinsta, who famously stuffs butterkase in a warm sweet potato and eats it for lunch.)

Butterkase is typically aged for only about a month, so it doesn’t have much funk, making it approachable for the under-10 and over-60 crowd. “I’ve seen my own child pick up a piece of it and eat it like an apple on multiple occasions,” says Molly. But because of butterkase’s slight complexity, Molly explained that it won’t leave those in the middle feeling devoid of flavor or a good eating experience, so it’s a safe bet for a charcuterie board.

Butterkase is made in Wisconsin and sold nationwide, but if you’re having trouble finding it, Gouda is a good alternative, especially Emilia’s recommendation: aged Gouda.

Aged Gouda is a Dutch-style hard cheese that matures anywhere from nine months to five years. As Gouda matures, the soft paste turns firm and speckles with those irresistible crunchy crystals. It takes on an indulgent butterscotch flavor, with subtle tropical notes, so it’s on the sweeter side. The longer the Gouda ages, the more intense those characteristics become. “In my experience, nobody’s ever turned down an aged Gouda,” says Emilia.

What pairs well with butterkase?

Because it’s especially buttery and mild, butterkase pairs well with tangy, acidic foods, like olives, the foods on a relish tray and all kinds of pickles: classic pickles, pickled vegetables and pickled fruit. Their acidity cuts through the richness of the cheese. Butterkase would also be a fantastic addition to a supper club board. Its soft texture is great on crisp crackers studded with nuts and fruits, with a German mustard nearby.

For wine and cheese pairings, opt for something light and refreshing, like Prosecco or an unoaked chardonnay, to balance the richness of the cheese. Even a bottle of inexpensive champagne makes the cheese board feel a little fancier.

Slice butterkase while it’s still cold from the fridge. If it sits for a while, butterkase can become soft enough to spread, making it difficult to slice. As a general rule, Molly and Emilia recommend slicing harder cheeses in advance to get ahead of cheese board prep. Keep backup portions in the fridge to quickly replenish the board as the night goes on.

What pairs well with aged Gouda?

Aged Gouda pairs well with sweeter fruit jams, chocolate, candied pecans and even tropical fruits like mango. Fruit-and-nut studded crackers work just as well with aged Gouda as they do with butterkase. For dessert, try pairing the cheese with brownies or caramelly stroopwafels. Drink pairings range from red wine to spiced rum.

While there are guidelines for pairing, Emilia encourages people to step out of their comfort zone and explore out-of-the-box options. “There’s no wrong answer to pairing,” she says. “People tend to think that they have to only pair fancy things with cheese, and honestly, some of the best pairings I’ve had have just been snacks or things I love that are lying around the house.” Take a cue from Emilia’s cheese competition days: Try the cheese with whatever you have in the kitchen; you may discover an unexpected favorite. “Get weird with it,” says Emilia.

item.title: The Safest Way to Handle a Kitchen Grease Fire
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful kitchen safety information

The Safest Way to Handle a Kitchen Grease Fire

A grease fire is one kitchen emergency in which instinct can work against you. Here's how to handle one safely.

One of the most valuable things I learned in culinary school was how to work with fire without losing control of it. So much of cooking depends on knowing how far we can push the heat—getting a pan hot enough to sear steak or bringing oil just to the right temperature for a batch of fried chicken. I’ve yet to lose the little thrill of flambéing a steak au poivre or a rum-laced bananas Foster, but after years in kitchens, I have a healthy respect for high heat.

That respect is particularly warranted around the holidays, when every burner on the stove seems to be occupied, and our attention is divided between the cooking and the guests milling about in the kitchen. According to the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA), Thanksgiving, Christmas Day and Christmas Eve are the three peak days of the year for home cooking fires.

What makes a grease fire especially dangerous is that many of the things we’d instinctively do to put out a fire can actually cause it to spread. Fortunately, handling a grease fire safely is a fairly simple matter of knowing what to reach for and what to leave alone.

What causes a grease fire?

Whether you’re sauteing vegetables in a little olive oil or frying chicken in a Dutch oven, it’s important to recognize when your cooking fat is getting too hot. Different oils have different smoke points (the temperatures at which they begin to smoke) but if an oil continues to heat well beyond that point, it can eventually ignite without ever coming into direct contact with a flame. Overheating isn’t the only culprit, though. Oil that splashes onto a hot burner or an open flame can also catch fire, as can grease that has accumulated around the burners.

I find a thermometer invaluable when I’m deep-frying, but it’s important to keep an eye on the pan even when sauteing. It’s frighteningly easy to get distracted chopping the next ingredient or chatting with your dinner guests. If you notice smoke rising from your pan, turn off the burner immediately.

Should the oil catch fire, leave the pan where it is. As instinctive as it may be to move it to the sink, carrying burning oil through the kitchen is a serious burn hazard, and risks spreading the fire.

The most important thing to remember about a grease fire is that water will only make it worse. Most of us are familiar with the rather unpleasant sensation of hot oil spattering onto our hands when moisture finds its way into a sizzling pan. The science behind that reaction is the same here: Water sinks and turns rapidly to steam, agitating the oil. When the oil is burning, that sudden expansion can send flames and droplets of burning oil well beyond the stovetop.

How to Safely Put Out a Grease Fire

A fire extinguisher may seem like the obvious thing to reach for, but not all extinguishers are suited for grease fires. Class K extinguishers are designed specifically for fires involving cooking oils and fats, and they can be useful if you have one and know how to use it safely. For a small grease fire contained within a pan, though, there’s a simpler (and considerably less expensive) piece of kitchen equipment that can do the job: a metal lid.

Both the NFPA and the U.S. Fire Administration recommend keeping one nearby when cooking. A small, contained grease fire can often be extinguished simply by depriving it of oxygen. Provided the flames haven’t spread beyond the pan, and you can approach it safely, here’s what to do:

- Carefully slide a metal lid or baking sheet over the pan, taking care not to reach over the flames.

- Turn off the burner if you can safely reach the controls.

- Leave the pan covered until it has cooled completely. Resist the temptation to lift the lid; even if you think the fire is out, reintroducing oxygen can cause it to reignite.

If covering the pan doesn’t extinguish the flames, it’s important to recognize that the situation is beyond your control. Get everyone outside and call 911.

Source: Taste of Home | Published: 2026-11-25 19:46 UTC | Difficulty: 40/100

item.title: Why Pizza Has Become an Unofficial Thanksgiving Tradition

Why it is here: interesting cultural trend, detailed analysis

Why Pizza Has Become an Unofficial Thanksgiving Tradition

It’s Thanksgiving Eve. The turkey is hogging an entire fridge shelf, every baking dish is spoken for and the cousins just pulled into the driveway. Then somebody asks what’s for dinner, and the only reasonable answer comes in a cardboard box.

If that sounds familiar, you’re in excellent company. As it turns out, the night before the big feast is one of the busiest times of the year for pizza orders, and our collective craving for a good slice is practically a holiday tradition of its own.

How popular is pizza on Thanksgiving Eve?

Ridiculously popular. According to DoorDash’s latest trends report, pizza was the No. 1 pick this time last year, with orders jumping more than 50% compared with other Wednesdays in November. And the ‘za of choice? Plain cheese, up a whopping 70%.

The craze isn’t limited to the couch, either. Toast data shows that pizza orders at sit-down restaurants and bars spiked 48% that evening. Salads, meanwhile, dipped 5%, which sounds about right.

National chains feel the rush, too. “Across the industry, it consistently lands in the top handful alongside Halloween and the Super Bowl,” Greg Hamilton, chief marketing officer at Little Caesars, said in a statement.

Why the Kitchen Closes Early

There’s a certain satisfaction in wiping down the counters the day before, knowing the casseroles are assembled and you’re as ready for tomorrow as you’ll ever be. The last thing anyone wants to do is pull another pan out of the cupboard.

“Thanksgiving Eve is about making life easier,” Hamilton said. “The kitchen is already prepped for Thursday, the house is filling up and nobody wants to cook twice.”

But there’s more to it than giving the dishwasher a break. College kids are back in their hometowns, and childhood friends are making plans to reunite. Even siblings who usually communicate via memes in the family group chat are finally in the same room.

With AAA expecting 81.5 million Americans to travel this week, plenty of those reunions kick off a day before anyone carves anything. Order pizza, and whoever’s hosting actually hears the surprise engagement announcement instead of yelling “Wait, WHAT?” over a sizzling skillet.

What’s worth ordering tonight?

Most customers “tend to go with the classics,” Hamilton noted, but if you’re looking to shake up your usual order (or feed a small army without spending a fortune), several pizza chains have specials running right now:

- Little Caesars: The new Cheesy Garlic Pepperoni pairs pepperoni and mozzarella with a white sauce, then finishes the crust with toasted garlic, Parmesan and Asiago. It’s $6.99 through Dec. 27 and waiting Hot-N-Ready from 4 to 8 p.m.

- Domino’s: The limited-edition Sweet Heat Smokehouse Specialty Pizza layers honey barbecue sauce, Italian sausage, smoked bacon, jalapeños, pineapple and onions under provolone and mozzarella. Mediums are $9.99 each when you order two or more qualifying items through the Mix & Match deal.

- Pizza Hut: The Triple Treat Box is back with two medium one-topping pizzas, breadsticks and cinnamon sticks starting at $21.99 through Dec. 28. For households where every air mattress is already claimed, five large one-topping pizzas will run you $50.

- Casey’s: Through Black Friday, any pan pizza is $12 with the code HOLIDAY in the Casey’s app.

Prices and participation vary by location, and given how busy tonight is shaping up to be, ordering ahead isn’t a bad idea.

Is your crew ordering in before turkey day or cooking two nights in a row? Let us know in the comments below!
