item.title: Smithsonian Head Assures Staff of Independence After Glimpse of White House Overhaul Plan
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: In-depth reporting on institutional independence and political influence in the arts, with clear and structured prose.

Outgoing Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie G. Bunch III reasserted the institution’s independence in a letter to his staff after a leaked document from a Trump aide laid out a sweeping overhaul of its programming and personnel.

“The intended use of this list is unclear,” Bunch wrote in the letter, which the New York Times reviewed and first reported. “What remains clear is that the Smithsonian is an independent institution with the responsibility and privilege to present accurate information to millions of visitors through our scholarship and educational programs.”

The document, titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan,” was photographed on a laptop that a Trump aide was using on the Washington Metro. As first reported by ProPublica, its 25-item action list includes plans to dismiss top curators and administrators, among them Anthea M. Hartig, director of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, whom the White House has accused of promoting “radical activist ideology.”

The plan also calls for a new permanent exhibit, “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance,” and another on “Great Families of American History.” It envisions a “Colossus Statue” of George Washington at the museum’s entrance, which would fulfill a request Trump made in September.

The plan appears to be a work in progress: Photos show the aide brainstorming additions in a notebook. One handwritten entry seems to read “No X-rated exhibition policy,” an apparent callback to a particularly contentious stretch of Hartig’s testimony, when lawmakers questioned her about images of bondage wear in an LGBTQ history exhibition. On Monday, ProPublica identified the staffer as an associate policy adviser with the Domestic Policy Council, the White House office behind a 162-page report that accused the Smithsonian of “extreme political activism that seeks to transform our country.”

A central complaint of the report was what its authors characterized as anti-white bias at the museum, which they said showed in its promotion of diversity, equity, and inclusion. The report accused one exhibition, “Many Voices, One Nation,” of trying “to convince visitors that illegal aliens are entitled to citizenship, voting rights and ‘belonging’ in America.” (Two weeks after the report’s release, Trump signed an executive order directing that signs be installed outside the museum warning visitors of its “ideological capture.”)

The document glimpsed on the staffer’s laptop laid out new interpretive guidelines for exhibits, including an explicit end to the Smithsonian’s use of a diversity style guide. The Smithsonian’s strategy for traveling exhibitions would be reviewed, and one show now on tour, “The Bias Inside Us,” would be halted. Grants to “woke third parties,” such as the American Alliance of Museums, would also be reviewed.

The Smithsonian’s online K-12 curriculum would be overhauled to “realign educational materials with patriotism, not ideology.” The “Becoming US” module on immigration, for example, would be deleted and replaced with a “Founders-focused curriculum titled something like Architects of Liberty: The Heroic Journey of America’s Founders OR Profiles in Liberty: Washington and America’s Heroic Men of Courage.”

The Smithsonian, a network of 21 museums, is structured to operate independently of the White House. It’s governed by a 17-member Board of Regents: the Chief Justice of the United States, John G. Roberts Jr.; the Vice President, JD Vance; six members of Congress from both parties; and nine private citizens. Legally, the Smithsonian answers to Congress, not the White House, but federal money makes up about 60 percent of its budget. Trump proposed cutting that funding by roughly 12 percent for fiscal year 2026, a threat that ultimately went unrealized.

Bunch, who became secretary in 2019, has repeatedly asserted the institution’s legal independence as pressure from the White House has mounted. The administration has demanded that the Smithsonian turn over internal materials and pushed for the firing of Kim Sajet, the director of the National Portrait Gallery, whom Trump had called “highly partisan.” Sajet ultimately resigned. Bunch has drawn similar attacks: a White House aide reportedly called him a “rabid partisan.”

In a May interview with the New York Times, Bunch seemed to acknowledge that recent vacancies on the Board of Regents had weakened his position, though he still appeared to have the support of a majority of the board. In September, he announced that he would retire at the end of the year.

In his letter to staff on Tuesday, Bunch wrote, “As I have said before, we welcome scrutiny of our work, and even disagreement. The Smithsonian will continue to be driven by scholarship, research and reflection, free from outside influence and in service to the American people.”

Source: ARTnews | Published: 2026-11-25 20:44 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Tate Liverpool will reopen in fall 2027 after a £30 million transformation with the exhibition “Surrealism: Staging Dream Worlds,” a nod to the museum’s inaugural Surrealist show in 1988.

The surrealism exhibition will run from fall 2027 to spring 2028 and include works by Salvador Dalí, Eileen Agar and Man Ray. According to Tate Liverpool, the show will also explore the “important role of surrealism in the history of theater and dance” through the movement’s major commissions for stage sets and costumes. Also on view will be Dorothea Tanning’s costume designs for the ballet The Witch, photographs of Sheila Legge performing as the “Surrealist Phantom of Sex Appeal” at the opening of the 1936 International Surrealist Exhibition in London, and material from the archive of Ted Joans.

“Surrealism invites us to see the world differently and what better way to reopen Tate Liverpool. This exhibition will spark imaginations, surprise visitors and reward curiosity, offering a fresh perspective on one of art’s most celebrated movements. It also brings a wonderful echo of the surrealist exhibition that opened our gallery in 1988, while taking visitors on an exciting new journey,” said Jemima Pyne, interim director of the Tate Liverpool, in a statement.

Tate Liverpool closed in October 2023 and was scheduled to reopen in 2025, but fundraising difficulties pushed the date back to 2027. The architecture firm 6a architects is redesigning the gallery’s home, an 1846 warehouse on the Royal Albert Dock, as part of a £35 million ($46.5 million) renovation.

Why it is here: Engaging photography and narrative that provides a deep dive into the cultural significance of a specific horse breed, with useful vocabulary.

Run with the Semi-Wild Yilki Horses of Anatolia in Nur Tucker’s Captivating Photos

Around the dusty plains and otherworldly volcanic rock formations of the historical region of Cappadocia, a millennia-old tradition continues. Here in Central Anatolia, Turkey, horses have been a part of daily life, civic programs, and military campaigns since prehistory. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse, photographer Nur Tucker captures a portrait of the region’s living heritage.

Published by Hemeria, the title delves into the beauty and tenacity of the semi-wild horses while also highlighting the lifestyles of those who herd them through rugged landscapes. Tucker, who is a British-Turkish photographer based in the U.K., has long been drawn to the vigor and elegance of horses, and the yilki breed that populates Anatolia have a particularly resonant history.

“Yilki” comes from the Turkish verb yılmak, which means “to flee” or “to be set loose.” The name “has come to describe the condition of these herds that live between liberation and loss, between domestic heritage and wild abandon,” says a statement.

In a place where horses have been bred for agriculture, transportation, battle, and more for thousands of years, their role forever changed within just the past century due to mechanization and industrialization. With motorized tractors, trucks, and cars to work the fields and provide transportation, horses essentially became redundant. Released to fend for themselves, they survived harsh winters, bred on their own, and grew into sizable herds. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse, Tucker composes a love letter to these striking animals, celebrating their resilience through more than 100 images.

The book is available for purchase directly from Hemeria, and it’s slated for worldwide release next October. See more on Tucker’s Instagram.

A Sculptural Playground in Shanghai Is Designed for Human-Powered Play

In Shanghai’s Jing’an Sculpture Park, a monumental new installation by Brooklyn’s Wade and Leta has a clear goal: to get people up and moving in the same space. Titled “Catching Feelings,” the interactive artwork doubles as an all-ages playground with the artists’ signature sculptures and geometric forms. A central tower holds a quartet of slides, while other spinning and writhing elements are designed for more unstructured interaction.

“Catching Feelings” is one of 36 projects in the ninth edition of the Jing’an International Sculpture Project, an annual project helmed by the UCCA Center for Contemporary Art. In comparison to the artists’ earlier works, the bold, kinetic playground is decidedly analog, with any movement powered by the people interacting with its components rather than embedded motors or motion generated by the wind.

“We’re interested in the life and activity around our work—the behaviors it causes, the elations it brings,” the artists say in a statement. “We watched the same grandfather return with his granddaughter to play hide and seek; an 84-year-old and his partner used the space as the backdrop for their video recordings; new friends were made on our ground spinners; we even glimpsed a man in a business suit having a go on the slide.”

“Catching Feelings” is presented alongside monumental works by Olafur Eliasson, Marshmallow Laser Feast, and many others on view through December 31. Find more from Wade and Leta on their Instagram.

item.title: Shahzia Sikander Sculpture in St. Louis Generates Protests and Counterprotests
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Article explores the public reaction to a contemporary sculpture, offering a glimpse into the intersection of art and social issues.

Activists against women’s right to choose in relation to their reproductive rights protested a sculpture by Shahzia Sikander in St. Louis this week, calling for the removal of the 18-foot-tall work titled Witness (2023).

As the organization describes itself on its website, “Too many women are unfulfilled, unhappy, and underpaid in their jobs, but afraid to take the leap into the unknown. We designed a program to guide motivated women through a process to start working in exciting careers and get paid what they’re worth.”

First Alert 4 quoted an activist with a group called Students for Life America associating Sikander’s sculpture with the overturning of Roe v. Wade in 2022. “Her skirt spells Hava, which is Eve, the first female rebel, to breathe life,” said Reagan Barklage, who related the work to the late US Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg. “It’s just, you do not need to kill your children in order to breathe life. That’s actually the exact opposite of what that means.”

She continued: “We’re alarmed that this is what they’re choosing to use to represent our city. We do not stand for these pro-abortion rights. And we’re trying to stand for women and true empowerment.”

A counterprotester thought otherwise. “We’re here because this organization that’s located on this block has every right to display whatever artwork they want on their own property,” said Leslie Zacks, who spoke of the protest in the context of a recently failed amendment that would have reinstated a near-total abortion ban. “The reality of the situation is that the people in Missouri have twice had the opportunity to voice their preferences with regards to the abortion issue and have made it very, very clear with increasing majority where their preferences are.”

Rung for Women issued a statement saying the organization “respects the right of individuals to express their views about art, including those that differ from our own. We recognize that Witness has prompted strong reactions and respect the sincerely held beliefs of those who have expressed concern. We remain proud to host this work by Shahzia Sikander at Rung for Women.”

The same sculpture by Sikander was the subject of heated protest in Texas in 2024, when it was decried by a group that called it “satanic” before it was to go on view at the University of Houston. After an opening and artist talk related to the work were subsequently canceled, Sikander said, “Art should be about discourse and not censorship. Shame on those that silence artists.”

An attempt by ARTnews to reach the artist was not immediately successful.

item.title: Dead Man Is Accused of Stealing Art from Michigan Museums
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Detailed reporting on an art theft case, with clear descriptions and context for the reader.

The FBI is seeking a warrant to search electronic devices belonging to a Grand Rapids man accused of stealing art from two Michigan art museums.

According to a federal affidavit, Mikolai Augustine Stasiulewicz, 27, allegedly stole a color lithograph by artist Ellsworth Kelly, from Western Michigan University’s (WMU) Richmond Center for the Visual Arts on June 23. A worker notified WMU police that the work was missing, and Stasiulewicz, who was caught on surveillance video carrying the framed print, was identified through facial-recognition analysis by Michigan State Police.

Stasiulewicz is also alleged to have stolen a 16th-century Albrecht Dürer print from the Grand Rapids Art Museum (GRAM) on July 2. According to the FBI, he had been seen at the museum on June 17, “in what appeared to be a pre-theft surveillance visit.” Between the two thefts, he is accused of entering nonpublic areas at the Muskegon Museum of Art on June 25; however, Muskegon police said he didn’t take anything.

The FBI, which eventually took over the case, learned during its investigations that Stasiulewicz had met with a man on July 8 at the Gun Lake Casino Resort in Wayland, Michigan. Surveillance video shows him leaving with an unknown amount of cash.

Stasiulewicz was found dead in his home on July 30. According to the Kent County Medical Examiner’s Office, he died of a morphine overdose on July 26. Although the office’s autopsy report rules the death an accident, it also notes that “the decedent is currently under investigation by the FBI for involvement in an art gallery theft,” and that a brother had told police that may have played a part in his death.

Four artworks, including the Kelly, valued at $10,000 and the Dürer, valued at $10,000–$20,000, were found at the home the next day.

On Monday, November 23, the FBI sought a warrant to search Stasiulewicz’s cellphone and laptop computer to determine if any others were involved in the thefts. “In my training and experience, and that of the Art Crime Team, phones and computers like the devices will often be used to communicate with co-conspirators,” FBI Special Agent Evan Alkema wrote in the federal affidavit. “They may contain evidence of communications about what art pieces to steal, negotiations for sale prices, and arrangements to transfer and ‘fence’ the stolen works.”

Since its inception in 2004, the FBI’s Art Crime Team, which handles cases involving the theft, forgery, and trafficking of art and cultural artifacts, has recovered more than 20,000 objects valued at $1 billion.

Stasiulewicz was an amateur artist who studied at the Interlochen Center of the Arts, the FBI said.

item.title: London’s New Museum Needs a Better Reason to Exist
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Analysis of a new museum's design and its impact on the community, with clear prose and useful context.

The new London Museum has been a humongous undertaking: 10 years in the making, costing £437 million in total against a budget of £337 million, and yet, after all that time and money, it’s hard to know where any of it went.

From 1976 to 2022, the city’s museum, then called the Museum of London, occupied a site on London Wall at next to the Barbican complex. It moved to Farringdon, a grittier neighbor of the City’s financial district, because the old building was hard for visitors to find and too small to display the full collection.

The new space is bright and airy, closer to an Erewhon café than a museum lobby. An on-site café, open around the clock from Thursday to Sunday, serves hot chocolate and ginger beer. The furnishings, though, feel random in such a pristine setting: a flock of large plastic sheep meant for sitting on, and shop signs from London fixtures like the Odeon cinema and Morley’s, the fried chicken chain. When was the last time any Londoner saw a sheep in the city? In theory, all of this should appeal to Londoners who have taken up early-morning run clubs, traded pints for matcha lattes and aren’t above a gimmicky bit of decor.

“People are looking for community, and they will have it in the museum,” Sharon Ament, the museum’s director, told ARTnews.

The architects, Asif Khan and Stanton Williams, working with the conservation specialists Julian Harrap Architects, have designed a space that’s inviting.

“It took people until the 21st century to realize that cultural institutions are for everyone, and that’s what we strive to make here,” Khan told ARTnews at the press preview. He wants visitors to dip in and out of the story of London without feeling as if they’re in a museum. “When we look at audiences outside of the regular museum visitors, many find it challenging and don’t feel welcome. This is a welcome for those people,” Khan said. Entry is free, there are three separate entrances, and built-in sofas with reading lights invite passersby to stop in, though few people pass through Farringdon unless they’re waiting for the nightclub Fabric or the cocktail bar Space Talk to open.

Still, London is a city of 9.1 million people and a global center for art, film, music, finance and fashion. Finding stories that capture its quirks shouldn’t be that hard.

The museum is divided into three sections. Real Time, at the main entrance, represents London today and includes Banksy’s Piranhas sentry box. (What could be more London than Banksy?) In the Linbury Hall, Our Time attempts to tie the city together through objects like the Lord Mayor’s State Coach from 1757, the Buckingham Palace switchboard and Syd’s Coffee Stall, an East End food cart that operated from 1919 to 2019. Downstairs is Past Time, perhaps the only part of the museum that feels like a museum. It’s the most educational section, with small rooms on the women’s suffrage movement and the Great Fire of London. The rest of the floor is scattered with a piece of a fatberg, Tom Daley’s diving trunks from the London 2012 Olympics, a chair owned by Charles Dickens, a 2,000-year-old Roman wall painting, Anna Pavlova’s tutu for The Dying Swan and more.

The London Museum is a work in progress and until it figures out what sets it apart from the city’s other museums, it will remain a large crèche, where parents can bring their children to roam freely. But there’s still some hope: in 2028, the museum will open two temporary exhibition spaces, perhaps the museum will finally lean into its London-ness and celebrate the cornerstones that makes the city so glamorous and gritty, from the Teddy Boys of 1950s, Mods and Rockers of the 1960s to the Sloane Rangers of the late 1970s and 1980s.

Until the London Museum gets it right, the city has the Bayeux Tapestry, on view at the British Museum through July 11, 2027, with tickets topping out at £33 ($44). At the preview, word went around that one journalist had skipped it in favor of the 950-year-old cloth. In hindsight, I should have done the same, or stayed home to play Grand Theft Auto VI.

Source: ARTnews | Published: 2026-11-25 19:24 UTC | Difficulty: 50/100

item.description:

Why it is here: In-depth coverage of Adobe's Creative Agent, with clear prose and useful vocabulary for an English learner.

Adobe’s Creative Agent transforms Creative Cloud tools and Firefly workflows

Adobe has rolled out its Creative Agent across the Creative Cloud, providing users with agentic workflows across its platforms to give creatives “more time for their craft”.

Unveiled at the Adobe MAX conference in Miami Beach on 10 November, the update spans the brand’s flagship Creative Cloud tools.

Photoshop now features generative restyle and relight, Premiere has a new colour mode, and InDesign now supports co-editing (beta).

Adobe is also bringing the Creative Agent to Firefly – its AI creative studio – through the Firefly AI Assistant, which is currently in beta.

Users can direct the assistant in plain language, with Adobe stating it has already been used for everything from batch retouching portraits to turning product shots into short-form social videos.

The aim is to help creators take on projects that may previously have required more time, resources or technical complexity.

Adobe has also launched Firefly Design in beta, a single workspace that combines raster and vector graphics with motion, 3D and print design.

Available as part of Creative Cloud, Firefly Design allows designers to build, review, and hand over projects without leaving the platform.

Topaz Labs, now part of Adobe, has released two new image-enhancement models, Wonder 4 and Image HDR, which are sold separately through Topaz.

Adobe said the Creative Cloud updates respond to the way creatives are increasingly working – juggling more formats, apps and mediums while being asked to turn projects around faster.

The brand’s latest approach aims to tackle this by bringing “AI assistance and collaboration directly into the Adobe tools they rely on”.

Deepa Subramaniam, vice president of product marketing for Creative Cloud at Adobe, said the aim is to protect what makes a creative’s work distinctive.

“The ideas, taste, style and vision that creative professionals bring to their work are what make their work stand out,” said Subramaniam.

“Our latest Creative Cloud innovations transform our trusted creative tools into agentic, intelligent workflows that give pros the precision, control and flexibility to explore their ideas, streamline their work and stay focused on the creative decisions that make their work uniquely theirs.”

The Creative Agent – which Adobe describes as a creative partner – now powers AI Assistants (currently in beta) across Premiere, Illustrator, InDesign, After Effects and Frame.io. In Photoshop, the assistant is available only in the Photoshop beta app.

The agent handles multi-step tasks behind the scenes, letting professionals delegate work and increase their creative velocity while remaining “in the director’s chair”.

In Premiere, the agent now supports new capabilities, including applying an effect to every clip in a sequence, tracking a masked subject through a frame, and adjusting colour and exposure across a whole sequence at once.

Adobe is also previewing local MCP integrations, which allow external AI agents to connect with its software.

The integrations will let users instruct third-party agents of their choice to work inside Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere and After Effects, editing project files directly on their own computer.

Layers, vectors and sequences stay fully editable throughout the process, so users can “step in at any moment to refine the work by hand”. The local MCP integrations will be available in private beta in early 2027.

If a user’s chosen third-party agent is also connected to other MCP-capable tools, such as Google Drive or Slack, it can bring them into the same workflow. For example, it could pull in a brief from Google Docs, work on the project using Adobe’s tools and share the result with colleagues in Slack.

Adobe has also added several updates that give Firefly users more say over how the AI assistant works. Creatives are now able to save their preferred formats, colours, brand guidelines, characters and products to be applied consistently in future projects.

A new plan mode lets users review, edit and approve the agent’s plan before it starts, or leave the agent to run on its own. Adobe explained that creators remain in control, “guiding the work and making creative decisions as their projects evolve”.

Users can also choose which AI model the agent works with, or let the agent select the best fit for the task.

In Firefly Boards, the agent can help develop mood boards, storyboards and concepts through conversation as they take shape in real time, “guided by human taste and direction”.

Adobe also introduced a preview of always-on agents to carry out routine jobs, such as sorting new files or preparing content for different platforms, “even when the customer steps away”.

Firefly’s video, design and image editors have also been updated, with the aim of taking projects from initial idea to finished work in a single workflow.

Among the other additions are a gallery of ready-made, quick actions, visual boards, and node-bases workflows through Firefly Graph (beta), which lets users build repeatable workflows of their own.

Adobe’s examples include turning a video storyboard into a finished cut and, in Firefly Design, carrying a brand identity from initial concept through client review within a single design workspace.

To learn more about the updates, visit Adobe’s website.

item.title: Desai Chia designs Bethesda Residence to balance "openness and discretion"
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Balances openness and discretion in design, with clear and detailed description, suitable for an English learner.

Desai Chia designs Bethesda Residence to balance “openness and discretion”

A large light well brings daylight deep into this private home that was designed by Desai Chia Architecture for a tight site in a dense Maryland neighbourhood.

The project takes its name from its location in Bethesda, a city located northwest of Washington DC.

The house is set within a suburban neighbourhood near the downtown district, where residential lots are about one-fifth of an acre (647 square metres). Because the houses here are close together, the architects needed to be very mindful of privacy concerns.

“The clients sought a house that would feel open and light-filled without sacrificing privacy,” said New York-based Desai Chia Architecture.

“Its compact lot and the close proximity of neighbouring houses required a careful response balancing both openness and discretion.”

The architects intended the house to “rethink suburban-urban hybrid living through a modern lens”.

Roughly rectangular in plan, it has three levels and a basement. Setbacks help break up the mass, particularly on the street-facing elevation.

The building appears “as a two-storey building from several vantage points,” the team said.

“The home is carefully scaled to blend with neighbouring houses, balancing a strong architectural identity with sensitivity to its suburban context,” the team said.

Facades are clad in grey fibre-cement panels made to last for a century. The material is known for protecting against fire, pests and extreme weather, according to the team.

“A durable, low-maintenance exterior with a strong architectural presence was a key client priority from the outset,” the architects said.

“Glass-fibre-reinforced concrete (GRFC) panels were selected to create a crisp, sculptural facade that captures texture and shifting light throughout the day.”

A modern-style bay window adds dimension and visual interest to the front and back facades.

Within the home, public spaces are located on the ground level. The rear portion opens into a yard with a lap pool.

The upper levels contain bedrooms and two offices, and the top floor has a rooftop terrace. The basement holds a gym, ping-pong area and media room.

A limited number of windows helps ensure privacy. To provide natural illumination, the team created a three-storey light well, which is positioned along a central staircase and brings daylight deep into the dwelling.

“This vertical, faceted volume allows sunlight to cascade downward, distributing diffuse light from a small skylight across circulation spaces on multiple levels while minimising solar heat gain,” Desai Chia Architecture said.

The all-electric house has a geothermal heating and cooling system. To enable the homeowners to age in place, the house has a shaft where an ADA-compliant elevator could be added in the future.

The homeowners are physicians, one of whom can walk to his practice in downtown Bethesda.

“When needed, the dedicated home offices allow both physicians to work from home in spaces with calming natural light,” the studio said.

“Its location – easily walkable to downtown amenities and robust public transit – supports a connected pattern of work and family life.”

Other homes in Maryland include a restored carriage house by Colleen Healey Architecture that features colourful facade panels and a family home by Ziger Snead clad in stone shingles, charred wood and weathering steel.

Project credits:

Design architect: Desai Chia Architecture

Architect of record: Thomson & Cooke Architects

item.title: Wine bar informs rich colour palette for Yorkshire home renovation by Tuckey Design Studio
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Rich description of a home renovation with a wine bar-inspired color palette, suitable for an English learner.

Wine bar informs rich colour palette for Yorkshire home renovation by Tuckey Design Studio

London architecture practice Tuckey Design Studio has renovated and extended Bay House in rural Yorkshire, using a rich, moody palette intended to evoke the feeling of a wine bar.

The project involved reconfiguring and expanding the country house dating from the early 2000s, while introducing a garden spa and sauna.

Tuckey Design Studio was tasked by the clients to recreate the feeling of their favourite wine bar, which informed a palette of dark timber carpentry, terracotta-painted walls and a bespoke wine storage cabinet alongside a tasting area.

“The ambition was clear from the beginning: to bring the atmosphere of a much-loved London wine bar into the home,” project lead Fraser Biggins told Dezeen.

“The clients’ enthusiasm for wine and music became important touchstones for the design, informing both the arrangement of the spaces and the character of the interiors,” he added.

The home’s previously cramped interiors are now centred on a large, double-height atrium, which serves as both a point of arrival and a gathering and tasting space with a bespoke timber “wine wall”.

This hall is finished with dark timber panelling, terrazzo floors and terracotta paintwork, with a wall alongside an arched composite stone staircase punctured by small square openings.

This central space leads through into the social spaces, with a kitchen and dining space finished using similar dark timber panelling and concrete countertops.

The stairs lead up to the first floor via a landing with a built-in bench, where a balcony connecting the bedrooms enjoys views of the hall below. It also looks across the garden through windows in a new bay window extension.

“The central hall forms the organising principle of the house, providing a shared space from which the surrounding family rooms and activities unfold,” Biggins told Dezeen.

“A series of interconnected spaces, galleries and overlooking balconies create visual connections across different levels, allowing the house to feel both connected and varied,” he added.

On the first floor, two of the existing bedrooms have been converted into a games room and bar space, finished in dark shades of green and grey.

Alongside them are four ensuite bedrooms finished in warmer shades of pale pink and yellow, with each featuring a hand-painted mural designed to “reflect the character of each occupant”.

“Material choices were guided by a desire for honesty, durability and longevity,” Biggins told Dezeen.

“We wanted the spaces to feel timeless and comfortable, without relying too heavily on traditional materials or references.”

“Instead, the palette brings together robust, tactile finishes that feel natural and lived-in, allowing the character of the materials to speak for themselves,” he added.

The exterior of the extension has been finished in composite stone and dark accoya wood, and looks across the home’s garden to the standalone spa and sauna, which was designed as a “complementary counterpoint” to the main home.

Previous projects by Tuckey Design Studio include a home in Wiltshire constructed using walls of unstabilised rammed earth and a residence within a converted chapel in Devon.

Photography by Fran Mart

item.title: Meet Laerke Ryom, Patricia Urquiola's pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Interview with an influential designer, providing insight into the design field, useful for an English learner.

Meet Laerke Ryom, Patricia Urquiola’s pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years

In this interview, Ryom discusses her innovative work and how it’s rooted in Danish design traditions.

Ryom, who is based in Copenhagen, first came to many people’s attention as one of the co-founders of the design community Ukurant.

Together with fellow founders Josefine Krabbe Munck, Kamma Rosa Schytte and Kasper Kyster, Ryom showed her work as part of its first exhibition at Danish design week 3 Days of Design in 2020, and Ukurant quickly became a recurring highlight of the design event.

Since graduating from the Royal Academy of Fine Art in Copenhagen’s master’s program in furniture and object in 2022, Ryom’s tactile designs have continued to evolve, and she has worked with a range of materials and products.

For her collection Blå, she made handwoven denim upholstery out of worn-out jeans, while the Buckle chair, made with furniture brand Fredericia, resembles a leather jacket.

“I find very interesting the way she moves naturally between furniture and textiles, starting from discarded materials and giving them a new logic through simple gestures,” Urquiola said of why she chose Ryom.

“There is something light in the way she works. Her work feels open and still very much in evolution.”

This experimentation has become something of a signature for Ryom, whose latest exhibition, Raiments, was a sleek exploration of how upholstery could almost become a furniture piece in itself.

To the designer, her work now is in some ways a continuation of the projects she worked on during her time at the Royal Academy.

“During my studies, I was investigating different materials and different typologies, which I actually still think I’m kind of doing – I don’t see myself as limited to one material,” Ryom told Dezeen.

While she “really strongly identifies as a furniture designer”, Ryom has also designed smaller products, such as metal bowls for the Bread & Butter exhibition in Copenhagen and quilted lamps.

To her, function is always at the forefront, and Ryom believes that even details that appear to be purely decorative have a function if they tell a story.

“Even when I’m doing collectible things for galleries, I’m always thinking of the functionality of the pieces,” she explained.

“Even if you can say, ‘[what’s functional] about doing a little skirt on a chair’, as on the Raiments chair, it tells a story; a story of the cover being loose, something that is its own thing, [separate] from the frame. For me, that’s still a function or a means to an end.”

Her aim is to create pieces that straddle the line between collectible and functional design; something that is artistic and yet commercial enough to someday go into production.

“I want it to be something where the distance between the categories disappears, and they become a shared thing,” Ryom explained.

“That’s something I think a lot about, that the collectible design and the artistic work I do should have a little sprinkle of something that you could see in production.”

The collectible design and artistic work I do should have a little sprinkle of something that you could see in production

The idea of giving beauty to everyday objects, rather than creating pieces that are purely functional or purely aesthetic, is one that has deep roots in the Scandinavian design tradition.

While Ryom’s pieces might not be the pale-wood designs usually associated with Danish design – though she has worked in wood, using offcut wooden pieces to design furniture for Ukurant in 2023 – she sees herself as part of this tradition.

“Even if people don’t think that what I do looks like typical Danish design, I feel like it’s completely rooted and very fundamentally based on the principles of the Danish design tradition,” she explained.

“I view myself as someone who is not in opposition, but who is developing or following along [with it].”

While her own pieces in the past have so far mostly been made in smaller quantities, Ryom sees positively on the current trend of big brands, such as IKEA and Disney, working with younger designers and mass-producing their work.

She believes it helps to spread knowledge about designers to a public that isn’t always aware of the people behind the products.

“I think it’s an important thing because what we see, at least here in Denmark, is that the knowledge about designers today, for the general public, is crazy small for a nation that kind of brands itself as a design nation,” Ryom said.

“Talking to my parents, even with them having a designer for a daughter, they’re still trying to figure out ‘what is it that you actually do’?

Inspiration can only take you so far – at some point you need to get working on it, interpret it and experiment with it

Ryom herself, meanwhile, says she sees a big difference between her current work and that of a few years ago. She thinks it comes from “starting to believe in yourself and your intuition, and getting more skilled in your craft”.

But, she also consciously works on developing her ideas and taking them from the initial inspiration stage to the final product.

“Inspiration is something that I stumble upon in my everyday life, but at the same time, it only becomes interesting when I sit down and work with it,” she said.

“Inspiration can only take you so far – at some point you need to get working on it, interpret it and experiment with it and investigate what the substance of the inspiration actually is.”

As someone who’s constantly exploring new materials and ways of designing, Ryom also highlights the importance of collaboration. She says that while she likes doing a lot of the work on her furniture herself, she has also gotten better at reaching out to experts to get input for some of her pieces, including her Enfold chair.…

Five key projects by Dezeen Awards emerging designer of the year Simon Skinner

This year Simon Skinner was named emerging designer of the year at the Dezeen Awards. Here, he selects five projects that showcase his work.

Swedish designer Skinner set up his studio in 2020 and has rapidly become known for his sculptural furniture and installations that explore rethinking and reusing found materials.

“My practice is centred around material culture, exploring the relationship between objects, meaning and everyday life,” Skinner told Dezeen.

“What connects my work is an interest in how forms carry associations and how these can be reshaped to offer new perspectives on things we know and take for granted.”

Skinner finds that the things that excite him about design are also “the same things that make me suffer”.

“You never quite know what’s coming next when running your own practice, but there’s also something exciting about that uncertainty,” he said.

“A material or an object you’ve overlooked for years can suddenly become the starting point for a whole body of work.”

Over the coming year, along with creating new collections and public installations, Skinner hopes to dedicate more time to research.

“I want to make more room for research and experimentation, and give myself time to follow an interest before knowing exactly where it might lead,” he said.

“When I started researching Afro combs at Konstfack, I became aware of how much history and symbolism an everyday tool can hold. That experience still informs how I work,” he continued.

“I want to keep exploring the objects and forms we take for granted, looking at the meanings they’ve inherited and what happens when you change their material, scale or context.”

Read on to find out five key projects by Dezeen Award-winning Skinner, as described by the designer:

“An ongoing project in which vintage glass sourced from flea markets and second-hand shops is brought together in sculptural lighting compositions.

“Drawing on the memories and associations embedded in these found objects, the work explores the relationship between material, memory and light.”

“Crafted in my studio, these combs celebrate rituals and traditions surrounding textured hair.

“Informed by historical references and personal experiences, they reimagine an everyday object through distinctive forms and symbols.”

Vanity Table

“Extending the exploration of beauty rituals within the Syntax collection, the Vanity Table offers an alternative reading of an object associated with personal grooming.”

Upholstered furniture

“These one-of-a-kind pieces, a daybed and an armchair, are upholstered in hand-dyed canvas in deep magenta hues.

“Combining traditional upholstery techniques with an experimental approach to colour and detail, the pieces embrace the irregularities of the dyeing process, making them an integral part of their character.”

Aluminium stool/side table

“This piece of furniture explores our relationship to the mechanical lock. The lock is integrated into the leg, with keys used to secure the connection between the leg and the seat.

“The keys can also serve as hooks for keychains and personal belongings, inviting individual expression.”

Photography by Peter Hansen unless stated

item.title: Are trees on buildings more than a greenwashing gimmick?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Discussion on the trend of trees on buildings, with clear reporting and useful vocabulary, suitable for an English learner.

Are trees on buildings more than a greenwashing gimmick?

For more than a decade, buildings bearing trees have been sprouting up all over the world, from New York to Paris to Shanghai to Sydney.

It has arguably become one of the defining architectural trends of our era, taken up enthusiastically by top studios including BIG, MVRDV, MAD and Ateliers Jean Nouvel.

And yet, not everyone is a fan. Almost every time Dezeen publishes an arboreal structure, a volley of comments crying greenwashing and gimmickry soon follows.

So, are the haters right on this one? Or do the arguments stack up in favour of wooded buildings?

The root of the issue

To proponents of the approach, some of the benefits of putting trees on buildings are indisputable.

“I’m totally in favor of not only trees on buildings, but any type of natural habitats on buildings wherever it’s possible,” said Fernando Scherner, an associate director in the nature and biodiversity team at engineering firm Buro Happold. “There are a few things that I think we can’t even argue about anymore.”

There is, Scherner told Dezeen, strong evidence that vegetation on buildings bolsters biodiversity. And, he says, “there’s no discussion” that done right, shade and evapotranspiration from leaves can effectively keep homes cooler in hot weather, reducing the need for air conditioning – and therefore energy use.

But this second point gestures towards the crux of the debate about trees on buildings.

Such buildings require extra structural material to support the weight of the trees and soil, increasing the carbon cost by more than what the trees themselves will be able to sequester. Critics therefore argue that any carbon savings from reduced energy use are a red herring, because a similar benefit could be achieved through much simpler passive cooling measures such as awnings and shutters.

“I think that criticism is entirely legitimate, particularly if carbon sequestration is being used as the main justification,” said World Green Building Council technical lead for sustainable buildings Carolina Montano Owen.

“Trees do sequester carbon, but relatively slowly compared with the upfront emissions that can arise from additional reinforced concrete or steel needed for large planters, supporting structure and associated systems.”

Even Dutch architecture studio MVRDV, one of the most fervent incorporators of trees on buildings, admitted in its Carbon Confessions exhibition held earlier this year that it would take hundreds of years to offset the climate impact of its La Serre project in Paris, currently under construction. MVRDV declined to contribute to this article.

A place to grow

While the phenomenon of trees on buildings goes back hundreds of years, to the Guinigi Tower in Tuscany, the undisputed poster child for the current movement stands at the other end of Italy.

Bosco Verticale in Milan is a pair of residential high-rises covered in 21,000 plants, including 800 trees up to 20 metres tall. It caused a sensation upon its completion in 2014, and was later selected by Dezeen as that year’s most significant building in the world.

The architect behind Bosco Verticale, Stefano Boeri, has since delivered other “vertical forests” in Eindhoven, Huanggang, Tirana and Utrecht, with several more on the way.

As you’d expect, he is bullish about the benefits of putting trees on buildings. He points to analysis by Arup, which concluded that the embodied carbon of Bosco Verticale is just one per cent greater than a comparable building with balconies of the same depth without vegetation.

“The load of the greenery, including the soil, trees and so on, really only slightly exceeds the variable loads that, in any case, must necessarily be taken into account in the structural design of cantilevered space,” he told Dezeen.

Boeri argues that changes to the construction process – such as the use of prefabrication methods or mass timber – promise to cut the embodied cost further in future vertical forest projects.

Even so, Philip Oldfield, head of the University of New South Wales’ School of Built Environment, is not convinced.

“I think the equation is pretty challenging to make the case that trees on buildings are beneficial from a greenhouse-gas emissions perspective,” he told Dezeen.

However, Oldfield points out, that’s not to say that architects adorning their buildings with trees are necessarily acting in bad faith.

“I’m a fan of Bosco Verticale,” he said. “I think it’s a really inspiring building, but not from a carbon perspective.”

“What inspires me about Bosco Verticale is it says, ‘hey, look: you can have a hint of suburban lifestyle in a high-rise urban building,’ which could make high-density living more attractive to a greater socio-economic spectrum, and then that may be more sustainable in the long run.”

Though harder to measure than carbon, it’s generally acknowledged that incorporating greenery into dense urban settings has positives for human wellbeing.

For instance, when Oldfield helped to conduct a post-occupancy study of the social housing development Pinnacle@Duxton in Singapore, he witnessed children sitting under trees to do their homework 50 storeys in the sky.

“Singapore’s been able to add trees and green across its built environment, and it has fundamentally changed the experience of the city, I think for the better,” he said.

Branching out

With a very high-rise urban landscape, year-round hot weather, lots of rain and low wind speeds, Singapore is the perfect setting for buildings bearing trees, and the construction industry here has become adept at making it work.

But in other parts of the world, things have gone less successfully. Jean Nouvel’s One Central Park in Sydney, for example, had to undergo emergency repairs after one of its heavy planter boxes fell to the ground in 2022.…

item.title: Staff at Edinburgh College of Art criticise "financially-driven" closure of design courses
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: News article on the closure of design courses, with clear reporting and useful vocabulary, suitable for an English learner.

Staff at Edinburgh College of Art criticise “financially-driven” closure of design courses

Over one hundred staff at Edinburgh College of Art have signed an open letter addressed to the university, calling on the institution to reverse its decision to cut three craft-focussed design courses from its programme.

Open letter states “deep concern”

The open letter was signed by 109 unnamed staff members of Edinburgh College of Art, which announced on 15 September that it would stop admitting students for its undergraduate courses in jewellery and silversmithing, textiles and performance costume from 2027.

The move is part of a wider decision by the University of Edinburgh, which the art college merged with in 2011, to make £140 million’s worth of cuts to arts and humanities courses.

“We the undersigned are writing to mark our deep concern about the University of Edinburgh’s current financially-driven restructuring,” states the letter, which was written by an unnamed senior lecturer in the school of design and published yesterday.

“As staff who collectively provide and deliver the teaching, research, technical expertise and administration of design, we assert that there is irreparable harm being done to the core values of our subject area, school, and to the art, craft and design professions in Scotland at large,” it continues.

The open letter also asks the university to retract its decision to close the courses and requests better communication between the university and its employees.

Signatories describe an “alienating” period during which the decision to close the courses was “made without prior consultation with [the university] staff”.

“Rash decision-making based on unsubstantiated and opaque data seems to be characterising the announcements of closures and cuts, and there has been no dialogue with students and staff that can be understood as meaningful or considered consultation,” they state.

“We feel that the area’s staff have been treated callously or with very little regard by senior management, and we are writing, in part, to warn you of the damage this has created and ask you to make effort to repair it.”

Courses part of “wider ecosystem”

The letter goes on to emphasise the importance of “individual programmes as valuable parts of [a] wider ecosystem”, and particularly stresses the urgency of craft-based undergraduate courses in the creative sphere.

“Looking specifically at jewellery and silversmithing, textiles, and performance costume, these are subjects that teach, in different and inherently valuable ways, specialised material knowledge and sensibilities, innovative critiques, and developments of systems of production and consumption, great capacities to research-through-making, and the ability to speak to a society’s needs through aesthetic form, the power of narrative, and the arts of material, chemical and technological mastery and manipulation,” it states.

The letter is addressed to the University of Edinburgh Court, the university’s governing body, which is scheduled to meet on 7 December to review the decision.

The open letter is the most recent statement issued by a collective against the decision to cut the courses. It follows a live petition led by arts organisation Craft Scotland calling for the urgent reinstatement of “the only undergraduate craft courses offered by Edinburgh College of Art” amidst public backlash.

Dezeen has approached Edinburgh College of Art for comment.

Photo by Colin Hattersley

item.title: David Rockwell Takes Us Inside the Design of Skywalker Grill
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Article on the design of Skywalker Grill, with clear reporting and useful vocabulary, suitable for an English learner.

Designing a restaurant for George Lucas might seem like an invitation to draw from the filmmaker’s extensive cinematic universe. But when David Rockwell and his team began developing Skywalker Grill, the signature restaurant at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles, the conversation went in a different direction.

Rather than referencing the Star Wars franchise or any of Lucas’s other films, the restaurant would take its cues from something more personal: Skywalker Ranch, the filmmaker’s creative retreat in Northern California. Lucas and his wife, Mellody Hobson, envisioned a space that felt warm, intimate, and welcoming, a deliberate contrast to the futuristic architecture of the museum designed by Ma Yansong of MAD Architects.

In the latest episode of Once Upon a Project, Rockwell joins host AJ Paron to discuss how that vision took shape, from the unconventional fabrication techniques behind the restaurant’s sculptural wood interior to the decisions that shaped its relationship with the surrounding museum.

“They wanted to start the conversation around warmth and the kind of warmth of Skywalker Ranch in many facets, not only material palette but also custom furniture,” Rockwell explains.

That direction ultimately led to an interior defined by rich cherry wood, curved banquettes, custom furnishings, and carefully integrated lighting. One of its most striking features is a continuous wood shell that wraps from ceiling to walls, creating an almost cocoon-like environment. According to Rockwell, there isn’t a single right angle in the restaurant.

Achieving that effect was considerably more complicated than it appears. Each cherry wood panel was individually fabricated using a combination of traditional woodworking and technology-enabled techniques. Behind the seamless surfaces, the team also had to accommodate seismic requirements, mechanical systems, lighting, and acoustics.

When Paron asks what proved most challenging during the project, Rockwell points to the engineering behind the wood shell. “If I had to pinpoint one element, it would be developing the system to mount and support the cherry wood panels in such an organic design,” he recalls.

The conversation also explores how the team approached the restaurant’s relationship with the surrounding museum. While the building’s sweeping forms and futuristic character could have encouraged a more theatrical interior, Rockwell and his clients were interested in something subtler.

Instead of incorporating recognizable cinematic imagery, the design borrows from filmmaking’s use of light, movement, and framing. A curved bar directs attention toward panoramic views of Los Angeles, while the lighting was carefully designed to avoid reflections in the expansive glass walls.

Even the furniture placement was considered from an unusually cinematic perspective: Rockwell Group created renderings from every seat in the restaurant. “We’ve never had anyone ask us to look at that from that specific point of view,” Rockwell shares.

Throughout the episode, Rockwell offers a behind-the-scenes look at his collaboration with Lucas and Hobson, who were closely involved in the design process, reviewing mockups, testing furniture, and helping shape the restaurant’s many details.

Listen to the latest episode of Once Upon a Project to hear the full conversation between host AJ Paron and David Rockwell.

item.title: What I’m thankful for, literarily.
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: personal reflection, literary appreciation

What I’m thankful for, literarily.

– Listening to a poem while doing my little stretches. The Library of Congress and Poetry Archive collections, to be specific.

– And I’m thankful in advance to the programmer who builds me a little widget or website that streams a random poem from these archives.

– The new Marlon James. I’m late to the party, but damn.

– Finding something cool in a pile of books someone is giving away.

– The major book awards no longer being afraid of support for Palestine, and Paradiso 17 and Huna winning NBAs.

– A really good pen. I’ve had two instances recently where I had a small bookstore coupon that I spent on luxe pens. Highly recommend treating yourself to a fine writing instrument.

– Funny novels with funny first person narrators.

– The tide continuing to turn against AI. I’m thankful we may see AI’s high water mark very soon.

– Getting to interview Adam Peterson for the release of his story collection.

– Booksellers, who are in the middle of their most hectic season. I’m thankful for everyone who treats them reasonably this time of year.

– Peanuts, a Perfect Snack For Reading.

– Librarians, who are always in the middle of hectic season.

– Flaming Hydra, and especially Luke O’Neil’s recent New England Week which I’m revisiting as I pack up to go to Boston for the holiday.

– Connecting with a stranger over a book, especially that thing where someone points at your book from a distance, and you close it and hold up the cover, and they give you a thumbs up. Really good stuff.

– Small presses, and all the cool and weird things they’re taking a chance on.

– Marilynne Robinson. Her middle name is Summers, but she’s an autumn writer.

– My sweet seven month old showing preferences for books. And I also chew on the books that I like, so I’m thankful that he inherited that trait from me.

– Trying to explain Gene Wolfe’s deal to someone for the first time.

– A small book you can read in an afternoon. Also having an afternoon free to read.

– Olga Ravn’s gift guide, which includes Ibuprofen and haunted dolls.

– Reading an author who is really going for it and trying something new. I appreciate someone taking a risk, regardless of the outcome. (Usually.)

– A friend asking for a book recommendation, and then actually reading your recommendation, and then telling you they liked your recommendation. No better feeling in the world.

James Folta

James Folta is a staff writer at Lit Hub and the managing editor of Points in Case. He co-writes the weekly Newsletter of Humorous Writing. More at www.jamesfolta.com, or you can reach me at jfolta@lithub.com.

item.title: Mourning is a Tide in “Flee”
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original narrative, exploration of themes

Set in the foggy aftermath of the pandemic, the debut novel Flee by Tim Raymond introduces readers to an alternate world dissolved by the rapid spread of Novel Aquatica, a virus with the capability of transforming infected individuals into beluga whales. The plot follows former ESL instructor Jensen Fisher, a person with autism in his late thirties, as he is forced out of the comfort of his apartment in South Korea and into the responsibility of caring for one of his students, Min-kyoung, after she loses her mother to the virus. Simultaneously urgent, funny, and heartbreakingly reflective in its memories, Flee is about the everchanging landscape of loss and how to rediscover peace within oneself.

The plot strings together elements of autofiction, climate fiction, and something akin to a post-apocalyptic survival journal, all while maintaining a feeling of reminiscence, love, and mourning. Raymond identifies as an autistic, nonbinary writer based in South Korea, and they sincerely reflect aspects of their identity into our narrator, such as the concept of social masking, stims, and thought patterns associated with what a person with autism can experience. The story opens with a hark to Herman Melville as Jensen states his name and the intent for why he sets out to tell his journey. As Jensen and Min-kyoung quickly realize they cannot stay in Jensen’s apartment, the two set out with Jensen’s cat Ori on a roaming quest to find a means to keep living.

Memory and forms of coping are peppered throughout the novel. A love for videogames helps both Jensen and Min-kyoung navigate the turmoil of a world plunged into demise. Jensen references characters from games like Zelda: Breath of the Wild and Hades as the two search for food in abandoned malls or consider routes of survival along the mountainside. As the group encounters survivors, Jensen flashes to experiences with family members he has lost connection with or moments with his wife Yoon, who passed away prior to the events of the novel. Interacting with strangers throughout their travel has Jensen recounting how he was sometimes misperceived in his autism with talking to people prior to the spread of the virus. And yet, Raymond excels in showing the beauty and creativity and resourcefulness abundant in people with autism. In one leg of the journey, both Jensen and Min-kyoung talk to and care for a woman who is infected and mutating into a whale. As the woman loses speech and terrestrial mobility, Min-kyoung reassures her and helps her move to a nearby river.

The organic nature by which the memories ebb and flow feels akin to our reality, wherein the thoughts of the past are sometimes used to inform our present or, alternatively, how memory can intrude, harm, or distract us entirely from goals we set out to achieve. Often, chapters begin with a recollection of a time before the pandemic or find themselves slipping in between Jensen and Min-kyoung’s conversations. Mostly effective, the direction was temporarily lost and disoriented a few times until Jensen is pulled back to the present through means of the plot.

Romanticization of Korean culture is touched upon, but could have been fleshed out more in Jensen’s reflections of his time in the country. On rare occasions, Jensen may generalize or discuss elements of the Korean language in a manner that feels glamourized. At one point in which the author Raymond counters this, Min-kyoung cautiously points out to Jensen how a cluster of survivors intentionally chose foreign representatives to lead the two around their encampment. She believes the survivors do this to convince Jensen, the perceived adult and foreigner in the situation, of the encampment’s safety. Less attuned to the nuances within Korean culture, Jensen is brought to this observation by his former student.

Like memory, themes of isolation, familial dynamics, and placelessness shift and come in and out of focus across Flee. What does home mean when someone finds themselves in a lifestyle of constant relocation? How does grief both connect and separate us from one another? As people form relationships or pull away from our lives, how do our siblings and children and lovers move with them? Raymond’s storytelling—whether it be of sailors sharing their travels, people surviving and describing illness, or immortal videogame characters trudging through the afterlife—can help represent alternate or marginalized perspectives and reveal how what appears to be a stable ground of self-understanding may actually be an unfathomable sea of learning and relearning.

FICTION

by Tim Raymond

Button Poetry

Published on November 24, 2026

Danny Rivera (he/they) is a Chicago-based reader, writer, and reference librarian at both Truman College and DePaul University. They completed their Masters in Library Science through the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign in 2025. When not working in the stacks or assisting students with research, their head always rolls to queer horror, fantasy, and science fiction. They live with their partner, Ry, and their two black cats, Pan and Grim. They are currently working on a dark little fairytale novel.

item.title: The Fire-Hose Style of Journalism: A Dirge for Salon
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: historical context, analysis of journalism

Document

In the dying days of 1995, I was a freelance journalist in Portland, Oregon, who spent most of my time seated at a rickety particle-board desk, a gift from my father-in-law. The desk was covered in faux-walnut laminate and swayed from side to side as I wrote. I had already finished my main financial gusher for that year, a history book for fifth graders, and I needed more work.

In this respect I was no different than any freelancer in literary history. In fact, the technology involved in my trade, and the speed at which it functioned—its industrial metabolism—had hardly changed in the preceding century. Of course, I had a computer. But it hardly seemed to be much more than a glorified typewriter. And of course I had an email account, courtesy of the nerd Valhalla known as CompuServe. But the business of freelance journalism was still built largely around stuffing wads of paper into envelopes and sending them to editors, who would then transform the contents into other wads of paper: newspapers, magazines, books. The product, whatever you thought of it, was palpable.

Into this cozy Victorian setting came an online publication called Salon. It had been launched that same fall by a crew of ex-staffers from the San Francisco Examiner, traditional journalists trying to break the mold. I don’t remember which Salon editor contacted me in the first place. I do remember reading the website in my chilly little office, steadying the stupid desk with one leg and feeling an almost metaphysical puzzlement. Salon wasn’t some programmer’s hobby, whipped up in creaky old COBOL. It looked like a magazine, with zippy graphics and respectable fonts. The prose was smart, stylish, and amusingly contrarian.

All of this made a kind of sense to me. What was tricky was that it was free. That first afternoon, I printed out one of the articles, about The Beatles Anthology, which was just then airing on TV. I suppose I was turning back the technological clock—transubstantiating the product back into paper. Reading Salon gratis made me feel as if I were doing something furtive, as though I were a shoplifter, but it represented a kind of post-Gutenberg freedom.

Over the next year, I would write many pieces for Salon. I started out with book reviews that were assigned to me by Dwight Garner. (He had previously edited a few things of mine at Vogue, in terms of ethos the absolute inverse of Salon and, eventually, in terms of finances too.) Dwight sent me books by the bushel, or so it felt. I wrote very short pieces for him very quickly; they appeared online almost immediately. This, for the journalist, was unprecedented and nearly beggared belief. No more waiting for your piece to come out, pacing the equivalent of a widow’s walk. Sometimes I was even instructed to send the piece straight to the copy editor so we could cut a few more minutes out of the process.

Speediness of reflexes was part of the value proposition for Salon. Within months, the “smart tabloid,” as its founder David Talbot called it, was posting daily rather than weekly. In this way it inaugurated a fire-hose style of journalism that would in time become universal. The new norm was not waiting, not allowing stories to lose their heat in the cooling saucer of classic media.

Salon’s politics were similarly nontraditional: left-leaning, libertarian-adjacent (as per its Bay Area digs), but without an obvious party line. It doubtless helped that the magazine was not a subsidiary of a larger corporation, which was the case with Slate (part of Microsoft) and the earlier, cruder Mr. Showbiz (part of Starwave, a short-lived multimedia platform founded by Microsoft’s Paul Allen). Yes, Salon’s seed funding had come from Apple—a mingy $60,000—followed by a more substantial disbursement to the tune of $2 million from the Adobe cofounder John Warnock and various other investors. But it was an independent entity, unconstrained by the need to tiptoe around the feelings of a corporate proprietor.

In any case, I wasn’t writing about politics. I was writing about culture: the magazine’s strong suit. From books I branched into music—I believe it was Joyce Millman, Salon’s television critic, who assigned me pieces about Prince, Los Lobos, Bill Frisell, Cassandra Wilson. These were my enthusiasms, not the sort of dutiful, indiscriminate coverage that a film-critic friend of mine once likened to servicing a vending machine. I was allowed to venture further still when I pitched a piece about Martin Scorsese’s use of music. (The Casino soundtrack, I wrote, struck me as what the director might listen to “if he were shipwrecked with nothing but a polyester suit and a bank of slot machines.”)

It wasn’t long before I was writing short personal essays. I wrote one about being hoaxed by the founder of the Church of Kurt Cobain, which turned out to be nonexistent, although certainly plausible in the drizzling, grunge-friendly atmosphere of Portland. I wrote another about becoming addicted to All My Children during a serious family health crisis in the midst of which I found myself strangely inspired by the surreal resiliency of the characters, who never died unless their respective actor’s contracts with the show expired. I’m not making any extreme claims for these pieces. They were written at the madcap pace dictated by Salon and sandwiched between other freelance explorations—of dental malocclusion or aluminum smelting, say. For me, though, they still evoke the adrenaline feel of the period, the wild sense of participating in something new and transformative.…

Source: The Paris Review | Published: 2026-11-25 13:00 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100

item.title: The Green Elf
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original short story, exploration of relationships

When Kyle finally told Lucy the truth, he hid under the covers. They’d been on the sofa, his head in her lap as she touched his hair, coaxing him, telling him he could just say what was bothering him, whatever it was. No sooner had he told her than he sprang to his feet, ran to the bedroom, and pulled the duvet over his head. She coaxed him again, robotically now, to come out.

“Of course you’re not bad,” her voice replied to his muffled question.

He’d been working up to this, she realized, for weeks or months. Like on that night, walking home through Union Square, when he’d told her there were things he wanted to do—things he’d hoped he would no longer want now that he was with her, but that he found he still wanted. She remembered then, as she watched the sidewalk glitter beneath her steps the way sidewalks do in New York under the streetlamps, how he’d told her early in their relationship that she’d miraculously eliminated his snoring. Spooning her, he believed, had been the cure. Now his cavernous snores filled their room each night, his great, heavy arm pinning her in place. She often found herself awake under its weight, scootching her body an inch at a time, attempting to shift positions without waking him. In those moments, the world seemed to gape at her with its darkness.

She hadn’t worried on that night walking home. She’d felt special. She knew she was exceptional—the only girl, out of so many, he’d ever given a key to. From the first time they met, she’d felt chosen by him. His compliments, the way he cleared his schedule for her, the dinners and theater tickets. It was she who’d hesitated. She’d found his eyes beady, his skin sallow and cold, his mouth in a permanent downward curl. But the dating history he relayed made it clear hers was the minority opinion, and he was tall and had two Ivy Leagues on his resumé and his jokes were cutting. One morning lying in bed, six weeks after she’d graduated college and three weeks after she’d first messaged him (she liked the app where only women could initiate), he asked if that night at Sean’s, he could introduce her as his girlfriend. She felt a twinge of revulsion, of panic. She said not yet. No. She left his apartment. But later that day, he called her while she was in the park with her friend Jesse. Was it okay, he asked, if he slept with his ex-girlfriend?

“What?” she said.

“She’s coming over to pick up her stuff. Since you said you don’t want to be my girlfriend, is it okay if I sleep with her?”

She was angry, furious. At the end of the call, she agreed to be his girlfriend.

After his confession that day on the couch, the childlike refrain stuck. You’re good, she’d tell him when he grew insecure. She’d pet his forearm from elbow to wrist, going with the grain of his hair, soothing, until he stopped bucking and turned soft and pliable, like a willing child. She liked exercising this ability, a talent she might not otherwise have discovered.

That phrase was the only trace of what he’d told her that was ever mentioned between them, a sort of oblique reference; beyond that, the matter was set aside. He was not active, and so she agreed not to tell anyone.

“Even your therapist,” he said after coming out from below the duvet.

“Okay,” she replied, but she told her therapist anyway.

Afterwards, she panicked that Kyle would find out she’d told, but of course he didn’t. She was comforted by her therapist’s response that consenting adults were consenting adults. As time passed, she nearly forgot about it. There was the time she opened her old laptop, which had been in a corner of their apartment collecting dust for over a year, and several windows opened automatically that made her worry. She was proud she’d closed the browser without reading, but she asked him about it. Were they pop-ups?

“Yeah,” he said, “must’ve been.” She figured he’d just been watching porn on it. And then there was that smudge on his cheek, the one he said was his colleague Tanya’s mauve lipstick. When they went to dinner at Tanya and her husband’s, Lucy noted with relief that her lipstick was in fact mauve.

Of course, now and then—rarely at first, more often as their first couple years went by—he made a joke about it. The week she moved in, after they painted a misguided accent wall that would lurk in her peripheral vision for years like a square, mustard bruise, he asked her to try it just once, to celebrate the occasion. She said it’s not funny, and he said no, it is, and that night when he slept, she pushed his arm off her without caring if he woke, which he didn’t. Around his birthday or the holidays—Christmas was the worst time for him, despite his professed love of it and his insistence that they perform every tradition, tree trimming parties and mulled wine and old cartoons—he kidded about what he wanted for his present. She’d purse her lips and turn away, and he’d touch and pinch her and pretend they were flirting, and she’d think about how long and ugly his face could be, how his smile could be so joyless.

The first time she did it was on his birthday in their third year together. Thirty, still far in the future for Lucy, seemed like the age of an adult to her. He brought it up while they were having dinner at his favorite restaurant, Squid. In the months leading up to this, she’d felt his growing frustration. It was a darkness that lapped at the edges of his voice, his hulking shoulders, sometimes overflowing and swallowing them both. One night he crumbled to the floor, drunk and naked, like an oversized fetus with a vortex of despair swirling around him, and she stood over him, unmoving, perched on the precipice of a black hole. Afterwards, her memory of the occasion was hazy, but still it left its mark on her, like a thumbprint in a newly opened container of Play-Doh.

But on his birthday, at the restaurant, he approached her like a lawyer with his deal points outlined, ready to negotiate yet optimistic about his prospects.…

Source: The Rumpus | Published: 2026-11-25 13:05 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100
