item.title: Revenue Shares and a Seat at the Table: Mamdani Reimagines Tech Transfer
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

In October, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the New York City Economic Development Corporation (NYCEDC) awarded New York University $29.2 million to help establish a 23,000-square-foot quantum lab near the institution’s Washington Square campus. NYU will invest an additional $255 million to establish the Quantum Fabrication Facility—known as QFab—where researchers, students, start-ups and businesses can turn quantum research into commercially viable technologies.

Representatives from the city will be on QFab’s executive board, and the city will share in revenues from the new technologies that emerge from the space. “This first-of-its-kind agreement will give the city board seats to shape the future of the quantum industry and a stake in the new technologies that emerge from the lab, making sure that all New Yorkers see the profits and progress from quantum technology, not just the wealthy few,” Mamdani said in a statement about the investment. “We are building a city where economic justice doesn’t come at the expense of innovation.”

Last week at the New York Times DealBook Summit, Mamdani and NYCEDC announced a second investment: a $15.8 million capital commitment to Vanderbilt University to establish two advanced engineering research laboratories on its new campus in Manhattan.

Vanderbilt will match the city’s investment to establish the Visualization and Testing Environment for Medical Devices (VISE-MED) and the Vanderbilt Center for Intelligent Mobility (V-CITY), which will focus on transportation and energy technologies. The deal also includes a revenue share for any IP developed by V-CITY and VISE-MED during the 10-year period of the agreement.

Public investment in research and innovation ecosystems—Boston’s Kendall Square, Raleigh-Durham’s Research Triangle Park and even NYCEDC’s Roosevelt Island project are all examples—is a hallmark of the country’s research might. Still, most collaborations center on tax incentives or real estate deals, not the possibility of returns on the research itself. And while revenue sharing is common in university partnerships with philanthropies, private donors or state-backed agencies, such as the Cancer Prevention and Research Institute of Texas, this is the first time, several innovation experts say, they’ve seen a city strike such a deal.

New York City’s model represents a new frontier for public-private partnerships, where cities have more say in how academic research is conducted within their municipalities and how it brings economic value to their communities.

“This is absolutely a new model and a creative one in a lot of ways, because they’re putting significant money into the buildout of these spaces,” Daniel Goetzel, a practitioner in residence at the Harvard Kennedy School and the former director of strategic partnerships for the National Science Foundation’s Technology, Innovation and Partnerships Directorate, told Inside Higher Ed. “Historically, all that value was captured through retention of companies or additional tax revenue for the city, but there wasn’t anything captured from the actual companies that were created.”

The arrangement puts the taxpayer in a new role.

“A city asking for a direct financial return treats the public as an investor rather than a donor,” Jeffrey Schell, a patent lawyer and managing partner at Whiteford, said in an email to Inside Higher Ed. “Cities also control land use and local capital dollars, which research universities in dense markets increasingly need, and that gives a city leverage a philanthropy does not have.”

Both projects were selected through an open request-for-proposal process. NYU was selected out of 25 applications “based on its demonstrated leadership in quantum, its ability to leverage significant public and private funding and its partnerships with CUNY and NYC Public Schools,” an NYCEDC spokesperson wrote in an email to Inside Higher Ed.

The Vanderbilt investment is tied to “specific capabilities and public needs and their track record of success and leadership teams,” the spokesperson added. The labs will focus on advancements in surgical robotics, wearable technology, urban transit optimization and clean energy.

Small Slice of the Pie

Although the revenue-sharing proposition is novel, the deals aren’t likely to add much to the city’s bottom line, and if they do, it will be far into the future. That’s because any revenue will come from each university’s central administration cut of profit, the smallest slice of the tech-transfer pie, typically between 10 and 15 percent. Most proceeds from successful research commercialization go toward patent costs, the inventor’s share and school and department shares.

New York will receive 50 percent of Vanderbilt’s central administration share on the first $100,000 of annual revenue from any intellectual property created at VISE-MED and V-CITY, the NYCEDC spokesperson said. On any revenue over $100,000, the city will receive 27 percent, along with a portion of school and department proceeds.

When intellectual property is created at NYU’s QFab, scheduled to open in 2030, the city will receive 15 percent of the central administration’s proceeds. NYCEDC said it intends to work closely with City Hall to determine uses for any money it earns.

“I would describe the revenue share as a low-cost option for the city and a statement of principle, not a budget line,” Schell said. “Quantum hardware licensing revenue at any scale is likely many years out.”

The history of tech transfer also shows that the odds of a windfall from any new discovery are low.…

Source: Inside Higher Ed | Published: 2026-11-25 08:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.insidehighered.com/news/tech-innovation/2026/11/25/mamdani-unveils-new-model-tech-transfer

item.title: McMahon Eyes Potential Settlement with ‘Ring Boys’
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Smiley N. Pool/The Dallas Morning News/Getty Images

After two years of protracted litigation, Education Secretary Linda McMahon has agreed to private mediation with the “Ring Boys” who alleged they were abused during her time as a World Wrestling Entertainment executive. They accused her of overlooking sexual misconduct.

The sudden move, detailed in court filings released Wednesday, raises the prospect that McMahon could settle and avoid a trial.

McMahon, who led the wrestling company alongside her husband, Vince McMahon, served in various executive roles in WWE from 1980 until she stepped down in 2009 to run for the Senate. Multiple plaintiffs allegedly abused by former WWE ring crew chief, Mel Phillips, sued both McMahons, WWE, and its parent company, TKO Group Holdings, in late 2024.

Phillips, who died in 2012, was accused of sexually abusing young boys and teens he recruited to work on the ring crew, allegations that became an open secret among industry insiders and a punchline on WWE programming with various commentators referencing the allegations on TV.

McMahon has denied wrongdoing and downplayed her responsibility in supervising Phillips. She also challenged the constitutionality of the Maryland Child Victims Act, a recent state law that allowed the plaintiffs to bring the case. Last month, Judge James Bredar rejected that challenge, which allowed the legal proceedings to move forward.

Attorneys for plaintiffs and defendants met for a telephone conference Tuesday to discuss a potential schedule for discovery as the litigation moved toward a trial. Instead, the parties agreed to enter private mediation. Bredar put the case on hold until February amid the discussions.

Of the eight anonymous plaintiffs, the court allowed only two to move forward with litigation against McMahon. However, others continue to pursue claims against WWE and its parent company.

Neither McMahon's attorneys nor the plaintiffs’ immediately responded to requests for comment.

As McMahon has quietly defended herself against allegations that she knew about and ignored multiple instances of child sex abuse, she has become increasingly vocal about failures by public school systems to safeguard students from child abuse. In a Fox News interview and in multiple social media posts, the education secretary blasted missteps by administrators at Albemarle County Public Schools in Virginia who failed to screen employees for child abuse. The school division shut down for five days, through Thanksgiving, to process outstanding background checks. The U.S. Department of Education has also placed the Virginia Department of Education on high-risk status for allegedly failing to enforce state and federal laws, and directed it to withhold funds from the school division until it corrects issues with its employee screening processes. ED also launched a civil rights investigation into ACPS this week.

“The failure of Albemarle County Public Schools to take basic steps to protect its students is deeply upsetting,” McMahon wrote in a Tuesday social media post. “Conducting required background checks is not optional—it is a legal obligation. The Trump Administration is keeping its promise to parents by holding schools and states accountable for the safety of their children.”

Source: Inside Higher Ed | Published: 2026-11-25 19:03 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Times Higher Education

At last week’s annual Student Success US conference, four student ambassadors had an opportunity to weigh in on those conversations, drawing on their own experiences navigating higher education.

The conference—a collaboration between Inside Higher Ed and our parent company, Times Higher Education, in partnership with the University of Utah—featured four student ambassadors who introduced speakers, emceed sessions and helped ensure student voices were represented throughout the event.

As the conference came to a close, the four ambassadors took the stage for a discussion moderated by Inside Higher Ed Editor in Chief Sara Custer, reflecting on which conversations resonated with them, what they felt was missing and what gave them hope for meaningful change on their own campuses.

Here are four key takeaways from the conversation.

- Look beyond retention and graduation rates.

Devin Duncan, a third-year student at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill who served as the academic support ambassador, emphasized the need for colleges and universities to reconsider how they measure student success to better capture the experiences of students as they progress toward their degrees.

“What I hear a lot about at UNC is the retention rate and the graduation rate. Those are great metrics of success, but I think they’re a bit outdated,” Duncan said. “People want a college degree, I believe that to be true, and we see that students are staying … but they’re also struggling at levels that we’ve never seen before, so the retention rate is only one picture of the success of your initiatives.”

For Duncan, part of that shift involves assessing the effectiveness of individual student success initiatives rather than relying primarily on institutionwide outcomes.

“What I didn’t notice as much of in some of the conversations is, how do we actually zoom in on what those metrics of success are?” he said. He pointed to the need for institutions to better understand how students engage with campus resources and whether barriers such as inflexible operating hours prevent them from accessing support.

“It’s one thing to have the resources,” he added. “It’s another for the students who need them to be able to use them.”

- Student success is a shared responsibility.

Israah Ansari, a recent graduate of Johns Hopkins University and Howard Community College who served as the health and wellness ambassador to the conference, noted that the panels she participated in addressed a range of issues, from faculty and staff burnout to housing insecurity among students. Those conversations underscored how supporting students requires attending to the needs of those who play a role in their success, she said.

“Student success requires the success of everyone else,” Ansari said. “It requires the success of students but also administrators, faculty, staff, families.”

While institutions have made progress in recognizing the challenges facing their campus communities, Ansari said, they have more work to do in translating that awareness into action.

“What universities are getting right pretty consistently is that acknowledgment piece,” she said. “They’re acknowledging where problems may be, they’re acknowledging what solutions could possibly be, but the action part is still not fully complete.”

Joshua Jones, a fourth-year student at Louisiana State University who served as the college experience ambassador, similarly emphasized the importance of engaging students directly in identifying challenges and informing institutional efforts to address them.

“Have those conversations with students about, ‘Hey, what are some pain points that you’re experiencing that we can be able to identify, so that way we can support your success along the way?’” Jones said. “Everybody plays a role in student success.”

- Move beyond a one-size-fits-all approach.

Laurel Tushbant, a third-year student at the University of Utah who served as the life-beyond-college ambassador, noted that many conversations about supporting students throughout their academic journeys revolved around early intervention. While she acknowledged the importance of those efforts, she emphasized that institutions also need to consider transfer students and those who may have fallen through the cracks and missed out on support early in their college experiences.

She stressed the importance of recognizing that students bring different aspirations to higher education and may define success differently.

“There’s this domino effect about if you feel like you belong, you’re going to be retained in the university, and then hopefully … you’ll be successful in your own way,” Tushbant said. “Maybe a first-gen student sees success as graduating, but I see success as going to grad school. We all have different levels of what we think that success might be.”

Duncan added that institutions need to be more responsive to the evolving needs of students, particularly amid rapid technological advancements such as artificial intelligence.

“I don’t think we’re at a point where we can say higher education is not valuable, or we need to be scrambling through these crises on what to do with higher education at this time,” Duncan said. “Institutions need to move more nimbly; shared governance is great, but being caught up in one particular problem for years to get something down to the finish line may not be the best thing in this day and age.

“Today’s learner is so different from the learner four years ago, and it will be different from the learner four years from now,” he added. “So let’s lean into that as an opportunity, not as a crisis.”

- Put trust at the heart of student success.…

item.title: Tennessee University Fires Transgender Professor Over Restroom Use
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Photo illustration by Justin Morrison/Inside Higher Ed | rustamank/iStock/Getty Images

An assistant professor and information media librarian at the University of Tennessee at Martin was fired last month for using the women’s restroom, the institution’s student newspaper, The Pacer, reported.

Johnnie LaDue told the paper last week that she had been confronted by the library’s dean after someone filed a complaint about her use of a staff-only women’s restroom in the library. She later received a written warning citing the Riley Gaines Women’s Safety and Protection Act, a Tennessee state law that went into effect in July that requires people to use the restroom that corresponds with their sex assigned at birth.

But LaDue declined to use an alternative restroom, noting that the only single-occupancy restroom available was farther away than the women’s room and was located in a room where her co-workers ate and socialized, making it awkward to use.

“I decided to stay principled,” she told The Pacer. “I’m a woman. I’m going to use the women’s room, and if you’re going to fire me for that, that’s on you. But I’m not going to change who I am or diminish who I am.”

LaDue, who said she was the only transgender employee at the university, was ultimately terminated a week later on Oct. 13. A campus police officer delivered the letter of termination, which The Pacer has published in full, to her home. In response to The Pacer’s request for comment, Bud Grime, vice chancellor of communications and marketing, replied, “I’m advised by the university to decline commenting or being interviewed regarding this personnel matter.” An article by the LGBTQ+ news site Them reported that a university representative also declined their request for comment.

item.title: Naval Academy Professor Sues Over Civilian Tenure Cuts
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images

The complaint, filed last week, comes about two months after Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth directed all military academies to “cease appointing civilian employees to tenured positions,” arguing without evidence that the institutions have allowed “civilian academic norms to dilute our focus on lethality.”

Referred to in the complaint as “Professor Doe 1,” the faculty member challenging the new policy had been on the tenure track and was expecting a review in spring 2027. But that all came to a halt Nov. 2, when the academy provost issued a directive that “removed all policy, procedures, and reporting requirements concerning academic tenure … and provided no identified transition procedure for incumbent tenure-track faculty,” according to the complaint. Meanwhile, the Academy’s Faculty Handbook still allowed tenure consideration.

The complaint argues that the change in policy violates administrative procedure law, explaining that “where an agency’s own rules impose binding procedural requirements intended to protect individuals, the agency must follow them unless and until they are lawfully amended or rescinded.”

The professor is not seeking an order that automatically awards them tenure. Rather, they ask for injunctive relief that protects their tenure eligibility while a final ruling is decided and, ultimately, the opportunity to undergo “lawful consideration” for tenure under the existing review framework.

The professor is one of roughly 300 civilian faculty members at the Academy, according to web posts from the Academy and the U.S. Naval Institute.

item.title: Mott Community College Removes President
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Photo illustration by Justin Morrison/Inside Higher Ed | Ivan-balvan/iStock/Getty Images

Following a controversial two-and-a-half-year run, President Shaunda Richardson-Snell is out at Mott Community College.

Mott’s Board of Trustees voted 4 to 0 on Monday to place Richardson-Snell on paid leave and terminate her contract. The discussion about terminating her contract was largely held behind closed doors at Monday’s meeting, and the board offered no explanation for the decision to remove Richardson-Snell from the helm of the Michigan college.

Although trustees did not explain their actions, they terminated the president’s contract without cause. Compensation details have not yet been made public, though Richardson-Snell signed a three-year contract in May 2025 that set her annual base salary at $255,000. The college has a head count of nearly 10,000 students.

Mott Community College officials did not respond to emailed questions from Inside Higher Ed but sent a news release announcing the termination of Richardson-Snell’s contract and the appointment of Marcus Matthews as acting president. Matthews, who was elevated from his role as associate vice president and chief of staff, has worked at the college for almost eight years.

(Richardson-Snell did not respond to a request for comment from Inside Higher Ed sent via LinkedIn.)

Richardson-Snell was originally hired as interim president in July 2024, a move that prompted pushback from faculty and staff given her lack of higher education experience and the board’s decision to lead the search themselves. The seven-member board—which has frequently split on decisions involving her employment—lifted the interim tag in December 2024.

As president, Richardson-Snell clashed with faculty over collective bargaining, prompting employees to protest over the stalled negotiations on the first day of classes this fall. She was also criticized for allegedly proselytizing on campus, discussing her religious views in response to student questions about artificial intelligence and telling faculty that “God was on her side” during a discussion of grievances raised by the faculty union over collective bargaining.

The Mott College Education Association welcomed the move in a social media post.

“This transition is not about personal grievances; it is about the health and future of our college,” faculty union president Brian Littleton wrote in the posted statement. “For too long, our campus has been distracted by avoidance controversies, broken promises of transparency, and a departure from standard governance practices. Today, we have the chance to start over and restore the professional, collaborative environment that our students and faculty deserve.”

The union also called on the trustees to use the presidential transition to “rebuild campus morale, restore ethical governance, and chart a new course for the college.” Faculty are also seeking a seat at the table as the board looks for its next president following the highly contentious process used to hire Richardson-Snell, which bypassed a national search.

“We are ready to work with the Board, but the days of unilateral appointments must end,” Littleton added.

item.title: PEN America Splinter Group Forms Amid Tensions Over Gaza War
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Andrew Lichtenstein/Corbis via Getty Images

More than 100 writers, translators, artists, editors, agents and booksellers disappointed by PEN America’s response to Israel’s war in Gaza have formed a free expression splinter group called PEN Writes US.

“Guided by the PEN Charter’s vision of ‘one humanity, living in peace and equality in one world,’” the new group says it’s working toward “mobilizing writers at every stage of their career to defend free expression, support writers and artists at risk, and champion reading, translation, and literature,” according to its website.

The formation of PEN Writes US comes after three years of mounting tension within PEN America—which has long advocated for academic freedom—over its response to the Gaza war. Some PEN America members have criticized its stated opposition to “academic and cultural boycotts,” as well as its perceived lack of advocacy for writers from Palestine and inadequate criticism of Israel’s role in the war.

In 2024, fallout over PEN’s response to Gaza-related free expression issues pushed so many performers to drop out of the group’s annual awards show and “World Voices” festival that organizers canceled the events, though they resumed the following year. In July, PEN America President Dinaw Mengestu—a founding member of PEN Writes US—resigned after the organization published a report on the “rising isolation and exclusion” of Israeli and Jewish writers since the war began.

On Monday, novelist Maaza Mengiste told the Associated Press that while both groups share many of the same goals of fighting censorship and encouraging dialogue among writers, PEN Writes US will be an organization where “sustained and equal advocacy for all writers guides principles rather than institutional caution.”

But the new group isn’t official yet.

According to its website, PEN Writes US is working with PEN International to become a recognized PEN Center, with the goal of being formally admitted at PEN International’s annual Congress in September 2027.

item.title: Students Say They Don’t Use AI in ‘Harmful’ Ways, but Their Peers Do
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Photo illustration by Justin Morrison/Inside Higher Ed | AndyL, Kirillm, and leolintang/iStock/Getty Images

A minority of college students say they use artificial intelligence in “potentially harmful” ways—such as writing essays, solving problem sets or summarizing assigned readings—but most students say they know peers who use AI tools for these tasks, according to a new working paper from the National Bureau of Economic Research.

Only 23 percent of surveyed U.S. college students said they used AI to draft essays, but 54 percent reported their peers do so, the data shows. Thirty-nine percent of students said they use AI to summarize readings, but 60 percent claimed their peers do so. Eleven percent said they use AI to solve answers in a problem set “without taking time to understand the answer,” but 49 percent said their peers do. Only 8 percent of students admitted to copying and pasting text responses from AI into assignments with little editing or reflection, but 50 percent said they believed their peers do this.

“There are, of course, several possible interpretations for this finding. One is simply that cheating is rampant and students will not admit to it themselves but will volunteer that their peers are guilty. Undoubtedly, this is part of the story,” wrote co-authors Bruce Sacerdote, an economics professor at Dartmouth College, and Mason Parris-Bacon, an economics research specialist there. “However, it could also be that students overestimate the degree to which their peers are cheating frequently on many assignments.”

Between June and September, the researchers surveyed three groups—Dartmouth undergraduates (n=1,201), incoming Dartmouth first-years (n=332) and a representative sample of U.S. college students (n=1,003)—via the market research and survey company College Pulse. Findings for each group were reported separately. In both undergraduate samples, more women responded than men. Four percent of students in the U.S. colleges sample were studying arts and humanities, 48 percent were studying sciences, 31 percent were studying social sciences and 18 percent were pursuing another major or had yet to decide on one.

Given the large gap between students’ own reported AI use and how they believe their peers are using AI, it’s possible that students are “reporting the single worst observed behavior across many peers as opposed to the typical peer behavior,” the authors wrote. “We can’t rule this out, but we would note that for other questions about peer versus self-behavior, the own versus peer rates match up quite nicely.”

This is true for several of the potentially “helpful” uses of AI; larger shares of students reported that they and their peers use AI for these tasks. Thirty-five percent of U.S. college students said they used AI to create outlines for papers or projects, and 50 percent reported their peers did this. About 61 percent said they used AI to explain difficult concepts, and only 58 percent said their peers did the same. Forty-six percent reported using AI to create practice quizzes or study aids, while half of students respondents said their peers did so, and 17 percent said they used AI to write or debug code, while 33 percent said their peers used AI for this task.

About one in five students (22 percent) said they paid for a premium version of an AI tool, and 48 percent said they think their peers pay for AI.

The findings jibe with other surveys of college students’ AI use, including a Lumina Foundation and Gallup poll earlier this year that showed 57 percent of U.S. college students use AI in their coursework on a daily or weekly basis. A report from the Higher Education Policy Institute, also from this year, showed that 95 percent of college students use AI in at least some way. Inside Higher Ed’s most recent Student Voice survey showed that eight in 10 students use generative or agentic AI routinely.

Fewer students reported using AI for problem-solving in other parts of life. Over half (55 percent) of college students said they would never trust AI with personal or social decisions, and 63 percent said the same about medical or health decisions. Fifty-two percent of college students said they would never trust AI with “anything that genuinely matters.”

Dartmouth students were far more likely than American college students generally to trust AI with these types of decision-making; 50 percent said they’d never trust AI with personal decisions, 23 percent said they’d never trust AI with medical or health decisions and 27 percent said they’d never trust AI with “anything that genuinely matters.”

The researchers also asked students about AI’s impact on the job market. More than half (56 percent) of students said they believed AI “is reducing the number of job opportunities in my desired field,” and 55 percent agreed that “having strong AI skills will be important for success in my career.” About three in 10 students (32 percent) said AI is “creating jobs in the fields that interest me because it makes humans more productive” and 53 percent said they are “competitive in the job market when it comes to AI knowledge and skills.”

Source: Inside Higher Ed | Published: 2026-11-25 08:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: MP calls for action after her likeness used for AI porn deepfakes
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear and impactful

MP calls for action after her likeness used for AI porn deepfakes

A member of parliament whose name and image were used in AI content on porn sites said the issue could make women less likely to want to enter public life.

Mims Davies, the shadow Welsh Secretary, said she received an email in her parliamentary inbox which said "her likeness was found on forums in abusive and pornographic content".

The Conservative frontbencher said people making money from deepfakes was "grotesque", urging people to report it if it happens to them so that "culprits can be held to account".

"It's completely unacceptable, it's a violation and an outrage," she told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast.

Deepfakes are videos, pictures or audio clips made with artificial intelligence to look real.

It is illegal, external to share or threaten to share intimate photos or videos of someone without their consent, including through deepfake images.

Davies said she had waived her right to anonymity to call for more resources to find and prosecute culprits.

Ofcom, the communications regulator, said "significant action is being taken to tackle intimate image abuse" but added there was "more to do".

Davies, MP for East Grinstead and Uckfield in East Sussex, said: "There are things you expect to be dealing with these days in public life and frankly this is not it.

"This could be any woman. This could be anyone in politics, in business, or down in your high street.

"We need to be able to protect ourselves from deepfakes."

She added: "This is going to have an effect on our daily lives, on our lifestyles. We need an answer to this.

"There's a problem, a new frontier which we need to battle."

She previously told the BBC she was spiked on a night out in 2019.

Mims Davies: My likeness was found in abusive and pornographic content

Shadow Welsh Secretary Mims Davies says her name and image were used on porn sites without her consent, and warns it's putting women off entering politics.

Davies, who studied politics and international relations at Swansea University before embarking on a career in journalism in Wales, said the issue was likely to make women "feel less likely to want to enter public life".

"It doesn't just affect you personally, it affects families. You never know when you're walking into a room what people might be thinking.

"We need more women in public life at every single level, from councillors, to Westminster and to the Senedd. It's tough out there.

"We need those kinds of voices in the room."

Her office confirmed reports have been made to the Metropolitan Police and parliamentary authorities.

An Ofcom spokesperson said: "Nobody should have to experience the trauma of having an explicit deepfake created or shared without their consent.

"Under the Online Safety Act, tech firms must assess and mitigate the risk of UK users encountering illegal content like this on their sites and apps, and remove it quickly when they become aware of it.

"We've laid down clear expectations for how platforms should do this â including by using automated technology to deal with illegal intimate images â and we've driven some of the strongest changes of any online safety regulation in the world.

"We've also shown we'll take action if evidence suggests companies are falling short."

In January, Ofcom launched an investigation into X over concerns its AI tool Grok was being used to create sexualised images.

The regulator gave platforms until the end of September this year to take effective steps to stop illegal intimate images and deepfakes from spreading.

At the time, it warned that any firms which breached their duties would face fines of up to 10% of their global annual revenue.

item.title: Farage helps launch new campaign against the UK rejoining the EU
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, significant political impact

Farage helps launch new campaign against the UK rejoining the EU

Nigel Farage has helped launch a new campaign against the UK rejoining the European Union.

The Reform UK leader offered his support to Keep Britain Out, which sees him reunite with his Brexit-supporting ally Arron Banks - who co-founded the Leave.EU campaign during the 2016 referendum.

Farage was the first MP to sign the campaign's "Pledge for Britain". This contains "10 commitments" for elected officials to abide by, including opposing rejoining the EU, its single market or customs union.

The campaign was launched as Prime Minister Andy Burnham explores closer ties with the EU, after he agreed a deal with the bloc covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

Burnham has argued that Brexit has done "more harm than good" and has suggested potential options for the future could include rejoining the customs union, the single market or a fresh referendum on full EU membership.

But he has ruled out major changes to the UK-EU relationship before the next general election, saying he will stick to Labour's 2024 manifesto pledge not to return to the single market, customs union or freedom of movement.

On Monday, Burnham said there was "no fixed destination" on the talks with the EU, adding it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.

Speaking at a press conference on Wednesday, Farage said the 2016 referendum was the "most divisive thing I have seen in families, in communities" and he hopes the next general election "kills this stone dead".

He told reporters: "I didn't pick this fight, the prime minister has picked this fight. As far as I was concerned it was done and dusted.

"But if battle has to be joined I will join it gleefully. What he's doing is madness, it's not necessary."

Farage said Keep Britain Out would be a "forward-looking, positive campaign about how Britain can be richer, more productive" outside the EU.

There are 10 issues listed on the pledge card, including asking signatories to "oppose mass migration" and support the country's farming and fishing industries.

Farage suggested he expects other Reform MPs and candidates to sign the pledges.

Banks said he wants pro-leave MPs to support them, adding: "We hope some Labour MPs will see sense and sign it and even Conservatives."

Asked if he is funding the campaign and to what extent, Banks said a "whole series of donors" have been "back in touch".

He added: "The last campaign was also funded by the British public, so I'm not going to go into who's donating what at this stage."

The launch of Keep Britain Out follows the formation of another anti-EU campaign called Stay Out, which has received support from Lord Gove - the chairman of the Vote Leave campaign in 2016.

Meanwhile, the European Movement is helping launch a rival campaign to rejoin the EU, called Get In.

item.title: The Contract Was the Easy Part: How Accelerator Day Put the Pentagon on the Clock
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, technical detail, strategic insight

go beyond the headlines.

November 25, 2026

Cara Teeter and Bonnie Evangelista

The Pentagon demands urgency from industry while allowing its own decisions to drift. On July 24, we ran an accelerator day to put the government under a deadline and make it responsible for what followed. We led the inaugural event for the Office of the Assistant Secretary of Defense for Special Operations and Low-Intensity Conflict, assembling the process in less than two months and executing $650,000 in legally binding awards over eight hours.

Each of the 15 finalists received $10,000 for its technical “pitch” to the government assessment team. 10 received an additional $50,000 in seed funding to advance toward operational assessment, the subsequent phase of activity called “Gate 2.” Those amounts support an initial commitment to the next phase. The total cost of a useful assessment would depend on the technology, mission, and operating environment. We also assigned each advancing company a government project manager responsible for scoping the work, arranging funds, and bringing end users and potential adopters into it.

We started small so we could learn before committing substantially more money, then modify or end investment as evidence warranted. That portfolio approach preserves options as threats and technologies change. Its credibility depends on the government’s willingness to carry those decisions through assessment, and where justified, into fielding and sustainment.

Pentagon news and Breaking Defense covered the event and its ambition to accelerate contracting. Three months later, we can describe the decisions made after the awards and what work remains. Our experience exposes a harder test for acquisition transformation: whether the government can sustain its urgency once the event ends and the coordination becomes difficult.

In its 2026 annual assessment, the Government Accountability Office reported that the average time for major defense acquisition programs to deliver capability had exceeded 12 years and was likely to increase. It also found continued shortfalls in applying iterative development practices. Those timelines encompass requirements, development, testing, and production decisions far beyond the scope of our prototype awards. However, those timelines establish the institutional context for why the department needs faster ways to assess mature commercial technologies.

Our contribution to this problem will depend on bringing operational learning forward and finding organizations prepared to act on it. An assessment can expose a technical limitation, reveal a better application, or show that a proposed solution deserves no further funding. Reaching those judgments early gives acquisition leaders room to change course before a program’s commitments become difficult to unwind.

As one of us argued previously in these pages, acquisition incentives often make visible failure more consequential than delay. Another review can feel safer than authorizing an assessment that would answer an unresolved question. We designed accelerator day to force a decision while the operational need was immediate, with leaders, funding, and contracting support available to act. The same demand for a timely decision should now follow every project beyond its initial award. If not, operators bear the cost of waiting while responsibility disperses across the organizations processing the request.

We worked with operational partners to frame nine challenge areas, issued a call for solutions, reviewed nearly 700 submissions, and selected 15 finalists for accelerator day. We transferred funding to Army Contracting Command-Rock Island and assembled multi-disciplinary assessment teams before the pitches began. Industry received operational problems and room to propose applications of technology that companies had already built. Advancement depended on whether there was sufficient operational demand to justify a proposed solution.

We used One Nation Innovation’s Open National Innovation Exchange other transaction vehicle, a flexible agreement mechanism for prototype work. One Nation Innovation serves as an acquisition intermediary connecting government and industry through a digital marketplace. The instrument let us tailor the initial business arrangement to the limited work and modest commitment involved while preserving flexibility for subsequent investment. We kept the terms simple and proportional to that stage, avoiding lengthy negotiations and complexity that the initial awards did not require.

Giving industry that latitude has a basis beyond this event. A 2025 study in the Journal of Political Economy compared Air Force research competitions that allowed firms to propose ideas to competitions that prescribed desired products. The researchers found that awards under the open approach increased commercial innovation and military technology adoption. Although those findings support seeking industry proposals for operational needs, our particular model still should establish its value through results.

Our assessment teams combined operational users, technical and acquisition experts, allied-partner representatives, and strategic stakeholders. Participants came from the Army and Navy, the department’s research and engineering organization, Cyber Command, special operations organizations, and the Department of Homeland Security and Veterans Affairs. Every evaluator signed a nondisclosure agreement and was required to disclose actual or potential conflicts before assessing vendor pitches.…

item.title: Does Congress Really Want Its War Powers Back?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, legal and political analysis

go beyond the headlines.

Elizabeth Beavers

November 25, 2026

Congress wants its war powers back. At least, that is the message that the legislature has communicated to the public numerous times over the past decade. Members of Congress have forced an astonishing number of votes on resolutions challenging unauthorized presidential warmaking, with some achieving historically unprecedented success in one or both chambers of Congress. But soon, it will become time for Congress to put its money where its mouth is.

In its flurry of Vietnam War-era reforms in the 1970s, Congress enacted the War Powers Resolution as a framework to manage the divided war powers that the Constitution gives to both the legislature and the commander in chief. The law was enacted over President Richard Nixon’s veto, and sought to clarify and limit the circumstances under which presidents could utilize military force without congressional acquiescence. Further, it enacted requirements to increase presidential reporting to and consultation with Congress. Post-Nixon presidents have expressed doubts about and outright opposition to various aspects of these provisions’ constitutionality.

In addition to those features, this statutory scheme reserved to Congress the power to pass resolutions overriding presidents when they deployed military force without congressional authorization. These resolutions were “privileged,” meaning any member of Congress could force a debate and vote on them.

Originally, war powers resolutions were meant to become binding upon passage through Congress. However, in 1983, the Supreme Court ruled in its landmark case INS v. Chadha that so-called “legislative vetoes” were unconstitutional unless they were presented to the president for signature. But, of course, this tool was created for Congress to oppose the president, and so any passed resolutions presented to the president would inevitably be vetoed. Thus, it appeared that unless Congress could muster the two-thirds supermajority required to overcome a presidential veto, they would amount to nothing more than press releases.

Yet members of Congress keep introducing and voting on them. In a forthcoming study, I track congressional use of resolutions eligible for expedited procedures, either as a concurrent resolution under section 5(c) of the House of Representatives or as a joint resolution in the Senate utilizing the post-Chadha amended procedures represented in Section 601(b) of the International Security Assistance and Arms Export Control Act of 1976.

According to my calculations, members of Congress have introduced 89 of these resolutions and forced votes on 45 of them since Chadha. This number tabulates how many privileged war powers resolutions have been considered on the floor of Congress in any manner, including procedural votes. Far and away, the Trump administration’s unauthorized military actions in Iran have prompted the most resolutions, to the tune of 39 introduced and 15 receiving votes thus far. In a historic development earlier this year, one passed both the House and the Senate in its original form as a concurrent resolution that section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution sought to make binding on the president without his signature pre-Chadha. Although two others have passed the House of Representatives, the Senate has since declined to adopt further Iran war powers resolutions in any form, with reporting indicating the Trump administration has exerted pressure on Senate Republicans to oppose them. Just last week, the Senate again voted down a concurrent resolution on the Iran war, with Sen. Thom Tillis stating, “this one doesn’t go to the president, so it’s just a statement from Congress. I’ve made that statement.”

Much of the commentary around these resolutions has framed Congress as fighting to claw back its constitutionally-envisioned powers through the only mechanism available in a Republican-led Congress. Those who have introduced their own Iran war powers resolutions — and there are many — have spoken of their desires to “reassert Congress’ constitutional authority,” and have Congress do “its job under the Constitution.”

But do they really mean this? In addition to the power to declare war, the Constitution also gives Congress the power of the purse. Upon taking the majority in the 120th Congress, Democratic leaders could insert provisions into appropriations bills that prohibit the use of funds for continued warfare in Iran. That is certainly not without precedent: Prior excursions became so unpopular that Congress utilized its power of the purse to force termination, as it did regarding Vietnam and Cambodia in 1973, Angola in 1976, and Somalia in 1993. Of course, Congress could also simply refuse either in the lame duck or new Congress to approve the supplemental war funding President Donald Trump has requested.

The new Democratic majority could also explore a court challenge against Trump’s defiance of its successfully passed Iran war powers resolution. After all, federal courts have never explicitly said that Chadha’s ruling applies to the War Powers Resolution, and there is an intriguing argument that, as distinct from other unconstitutional legislative vetoes that delegate statutory authority, the War Powers Resolution simply enforces what the Constitution already makes clear.…

Source: War on the Rocks | Published: 2026-11-25 08:30 UTC | Difficulty: 80/100

item.title: Bangladesh’s Government Battles Unrest on Multiple Fronts
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, political and social unrest

On November 18, Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rahman asked his rivals in parliament to stand together as they had in 2024, when a student uprising ousted Sheikh Hasina from power. He also invited the opposition leader, Shafiqur Rahman of the Jamaat-e-Islami (JI), Bangladesh’s largest Islamist party, to his parliamentary office for tea. The two spoke alone.

Five days later, Rahman met a delegation from the National Citizen Party (NCP), founded by student leaders of the uprising. His government also planned formal talks with JI.

Elsewhere in Dhaka, garment workers gathered outside their factories and demanded a rise in wages.

In February, Rahman’s Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) won more than a two-thirds majority in parliament. He is in a position to get legislation passed in parliament without the support of the opposition.

So why is he seeking his rivals’ help now?

On November 17, the day before his speech, a crowd stormed and set fire to a police station in Gopalganj, Hasina’s home district. Wage protests across the country halted production at nearly 450 garment factories that day. Rahman accused Hasina’s Awami League (AL) of encouraging violence in the factories.

Hasina’s possible return from India to Bangladesh came up even during a prayer in parliament. On November 9, after parliamentarians stood in silence to mourn former lawmakers, prominent figures, and accident victims, State Minister for Religious Affairs Mohammad Shamim Kaiser prayed to God for strength to resist any attempts to bring back “fascism.”

He meant Hasina and her party. That day, her lawyers applied for a passport at Bangladesh’s mission in New Delhi. She had fled to India on August 5, 2024.

However, Dhaka refused Hasina’s passport request. The AL, whose political activities remain banned, called a nationwide shutdown for November 19. The disruption was greatest in the party’s southern strongholds. In Gopalganj, a crowd stormed Tungipara Police Station on November 17. Witnesses said the attackers freed detained members of the AL’s student wing, and set part of the building on fire. The home of one BNP lawmaker was torched later that evening. Two days later attackers set fire to Muksudpur Police Station and the home of another BNP lawmaker.

In the southern district of Pirojpur, a 25-year-old bus assistant named Mohammad Siam died when someone set fire to the parked bus where he was sleeping. Police said they did not know who torched the bus. Nationwide, police have recorded 83 arson attacks on vehicles and crude bomb blasts at 87 sites over the past two weeks.

Grameen Bank reported attacks, including attempted arson, at 72 of its offices across 40 districts this month. Its founder, Muhammad Yunus, led the interim government after Hasina’s government fell. Rahman’s government accused AL leaders abroad of encouraging the violence.

On November 24, Hasina again asked Dhaka to fly her home from Delhi on Biman Bangladesh Airlines on December 16, which Bangladesh marks as Victory Day — the day Bangladesh’s war of independence from Pakistan ended in 1971. Hasina says she wants to surrender.

A Bangladeshi tribunal sentenced her to death in absentia last year for ordering the crackdown on protesters in July-August 2024. She denies the charges. Rahman’s government has refused the flight request, saying India would have to extradite her.

The country has also tightened security along its border with India ahead of December. Border Guards Bangladesh had stepped up patrols and installed floodlights. A commander said his force was on alert for AL supporters, who might try to enter illegally. The police chief also asked officers in border districts to watch for attempts to bring weapons or explosives into Bangladesh.

The JI and NCP share Rahman’s opposition to an AL comeback. They also want him to honor constitutional reforms voters backed in a referendum in February.

After meeting Rahman, NCP leader Nahid Islam said the current situation is not an overnight development. It was the outcome of the government’s failure to act on the deteriorating law and order situation in the country over several months.

Moreover, along with the garment sector unrest and AL-related unrest, some of the violence came from the ruling party. A Bangladeshi rights group recorded nine deaths in 35 clashes between BNP factions in October.

The Home Ministry reported fewer murder cases nationwide in the first nine months of this year than in the same period last year. In Khulna, a southern division, however, six people were killed in just over three weeks. One was a brick and sand merchant, who was shot in his shop. Local BNP leaders, including lawmakers and the city administrator, have expressed concern over the killings and extortion and called for stronger police action.

Bangladesh has deployed 101 platoons of border guards across eight districts. The Ansar paramilitary force said it had deployed 57 platoons in nine districts.

Meanwhile, garment industry workers are on strike. A sewing machine operator earning 13,500 taka a month told Human Rights Watch that rent took 6,000 and cooking gas another 2,300. The family could no longer afford the children’s schooling. “Tell me, what’s left for food?” the worker asked.

In August, a federation of garment unions asked the labor minister for a wage review. The monthly minimum wage of 12,500 taka (about $100) dates back to an agreement in 2023. The BNP had campaigned on a promise to link wages to inflation.

Workers began returning to factories after the government promised a raise from December. When a wage board meeting was postponed, they walked out again. At the end of the talks on November 23, owners were offering 15,800 taka a month. Workers’ representatives had lowered their demand from 32,000 to 22,000. The Center for Policy Dialogue, a Dhaka-based research institute, estimates it would take 16,351 taka just to buy what the minimum wage bought in 2023.…

Source: The Diplomat | Published: 2026-11-25 05:37 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100

Why it is here: original reporting, political negotiation

Badenoch challenges Burnham over university fees for EU students

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has challenged Andy Burnham over whether EU students in the UK could pay lower university tuition fees as part of his deal with the bloc.

The prime minister insisted the issue of tuition fees was "a separate deal", with discussions on this continuing.

Asked whether he could rule out EU students paying the same fees as British students, Burnham said this was "the European negotiating position" and "won't be put on the table".

At a UK-EU summit last Friday, the two sides agreed a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth travel scheme.

A joint statement said they would also work towards a "supplementing" agreement on tuition fees for EU students in the UK and British students in the EU, with negotiations concluding within six months.

EU sources had earlier suggested the bloc might hold up applying the wider deal until it was agreed that EU students who wanted to study in the UK would pay the same fees as British students.

But the UK has insisted the wider deal will come into force regardless of whether the two sides can reach an agreement on tuition fees.

- Deal with EU not dependent on tuition fees agreement, Miliband says

- Published5 days ago

At the moment, EU students at UK universities generally pay the same fees as international students, ranging from Â£11,400 to Â£38,000.

For British undergraduate students tuition fees are currently capped at Â£9,790 a year.

Universities have raised concerns that capping EU student fees at the same level could cost hundreds of millions a year, at a time when the sector is struggling financially.

At Prime Minister's Questions, Badenoch asked Burnham who would pick up the bill if EU and British students paid the same fees, "cash-strapped universities or cash-strapped taxpayers?"

In response, the PM said "the deal on tuition fees is not done", adding: "We will take that conversation forward always rightfully mindful of the challenges faced by higher education."

Pressed over whether the EU would still sign his wider deal if he refused to cut fees for European students, Burnham said legislation introduced in Parliament on Thursday would set a date for the implementation of deals on food, emissions and a youth experience scheme.

He added: "We will continue discussions with the European Union on the question of tuition fees."

Asked if he would rule out EU students paying the same tuition fees as British students, Burnham replied: "She is referring to the European negotiating position, which is not the British negotiating position.

"That has not been put on the table. It won't be put on the table."

Asked if Burnham was saying EU students would not pay domestic fees, the prime minister minister's official spokesman told reporters he would not get ahead of the outcome of ongoing talks.

item.title: EU offers UK fresh deal on 'Made in Europe' scheme
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, trade and economic policy

EU offers UK fresh deal on 'Made in Europe' scheme

The UK could be included in the EU's proposed scheme to protect car manufacturing in Europe without Britain having to impose import taxes on Chinese electric cars, under draft plans.

The proposal has been drawn up by Ireland, which currently holds the EU's rotating presidency, and will be discussed by EU governments.

It comes after previous suggestions the EU would demand the UK align its tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles as a condition of joining the scheme.

Senior figures in the British government have been talking increasingly positively about the potential to join on terms London would be willing to sign up to, and are cautiously optimistic about this latest move.

The "Made in Europe" scheme, known formally as the Industrial Accelerator Act, aims to protect EU manufacturing with restrictions on goods from outside countries, with a particular focus on both China and the car industry.

The idea is potentially dangerous to the UK, as being outside the EU would mean being exposed to restrictions principally intended for others.

Germany and France had previously agreed a joint position under which UK involvement would have been conditional on matching EU import restrictions and tariffs on imports of Chinese electric cars and hybrids.

Alignment in this area with the EU would increase the price of increasingly popular Chinese cars in the UK, as well as raising the prospect of a potential Chinese retaliation with its own tariffs imposed on British-made cars.

'Real concern'

Now Ireland, as first reported by the Financial Times, external, is suggesting the UK could join Made in Europe without the need to match the EU's tariffs.

The argument made in favour of this is the UK and EU car industries are so heavily integrated and interdependent.

The proposal, which would also apply to Switzerland and countries in the European Economic Area (EEA) such as Norway, would depend on the non-EU countries granting the EU access to their subsidy and procurement schemes.

However, the idea is still at its early stages. It will first be discussed by EU ambassadors, before it is considered by competition ministers from the EU's member states at a meeting next month.

The proposal would also have to be accepted by the European Commission and the European Parliament.

Andy Burnham has previously pushed for UK inclusion in the scheme to avoid "collateral damage" to British industry.

Speaking at Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, he claimed the government had successfully "removed the threat" from the Made in Europe scheme as part of talks over the EU deals he agreed last week.

Pressed later whether he had overstated how advanced talks were on the EU side, the prime minister's spokesman said: "We continue to engage on these issues with Europe in a genuine spirit of cooperation."

A spokesperson for the Irish presidency said it had proposed a "pragmatic and balanced way forward" on the scheme, having "listened closely to all member states".

Source: BBC Politics | Published: 2026-11-25 16:45 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100

item.title: Reality TV star backs extending sex education to 18
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, social policy, cultural impact

Reality TV star backs extending sex education to 18

TV celebrity and "revenge porn" victim Georgia Harrison has urged MPs to back a new law that would extend compulsory relationships and sex education (RSE) up to the age of 18.

The Only Way Is Essex and Love Island star led a protest outside Parliament to call for the change, telling the BBC it was needed to combat the "poison" young people were being exposed to online.

The demonstration comes ahead of a debate and vote next week on a draft law that would legally require all further education providers in England to teach RSE to under-18s.

The Department for Education (DfE) said it was exploring how RSE could be extended to colleges.

Compulsory relationships and sex education currently stops at age 16 in England, meaning sixth forms and colleges are not required to teach the subject.

Speaking in Westminster, Harrison said: "Between 16 and 18 is the age that people first start having sex.

"It doesn't make sense that we're abandoning them at that time."

Harrison said "misogynists" had "sold our young people advice, but really, it's poison".

"We need to undo it and the only way to undo it is through education," Harrison said.

Harrison was a victim of so-called revenge porn. Fellow reality TV performer Stephen Bear was jailed for posting intimate footage of the pair online, which he had filmed at his home in Loughton in Essex.

She said making RSE mandatory to age 18 could help prevent intimate image abuse of the kind she suffered.

The campaign outside Parliament was organised by media organisation LADbible.

The Relationships and Sex Education (Further Education Sector) Bill has been put forward by Alistair Strathern, the Labour MP for the Hitchin constituency in Bedfordshire and Hertfordshire.

It is a private members' bill, which are only debated on Fridays and rarely become law.

However, Strathern told the BBC he had "a good chance of making real change".

"I've been really encouraged by the response we've got from ministers so far," he said.

A DfE spokesperson said: "Supporting children and young people to grow up happy and healthy whilst safeguarding them from harm on and offline is a job for us all.

"We're determined that across our education system, schools and colleges play their part.

"That's why we have rolled out mandatory RHSE [relationships, sex and health education] in schools and we are exploring how we can extend this to colleges too."

The bill follows a petition by the survivor-led campaign group Make it Mandatory, which called for sex education to be mandated to 18.

Faustine Petron said she founded the campaign after surviving a coercive and abusive relationship when she was under 18.

"I thought back to the lack of education I had about the signs of abusive behaviour, grooming and coercive control," Petron said.

"I was shocked in my research to find out that sex education ends at 16. I thought 'how nonsensical'.

"I got into the relationship at 16. Why stop and have this dangerous loophole in the law?"

item.title: Shamash Alidina: Gratitude with Room for Everything Else
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: essential for this reader

Gratitude practices sometimes feel like one more thing to get right, as if we’re supposed to feel thankful on cue no matter what’s happening.

Our guest this week is Shamash Alidina. He offers a gentler approach. You make room for whatever you’re feeling, and then you see whether one small, ordinary thing you appreciate can sit alongside it.

In this meditation, you’ll:

- Acknowledge how life is for you right now

- Hold difficulty and appreciation side by side

- Connect gratitude to what you value, rather than just how you feel

Shamash Alidina: Gratitude with Room for Everything Else

Or listen to the guided audio.

- Find a comfortable position and let your body settle. You can close your eyes or keep them open with a soft, relaxed gaze. There’s nothing to achieve here. You don’t need to feel calm, happy, or grateful. You’re simply giving yourself a little time to be here.

- Notice the places where your body makes contact with what’s beneath you. Feel the gentle movement of your breath. There’s no need to change it. Just notice the body breathing in and breathing out.

- Allow whatever you’re experiencing to be here. Maybe your mind is busy or your body feels restless. That’s fine. There’s nothing you need to fix.

- Bring to mind how life is for you at the moment. Perhaps something is worrying you. Maybe you’re missing someone, feeling lonely, or facing a challenge. Or perhaps things are going reasonably well. Whatever you notice, acknowledge it honestly. You might silently say, This is what I’m experiencing right now.

- Notice any feeling in your body that comes with this experience. It might be tightness, heaviness, or restlessness. You don’t need to make it go away. Imagine making room for it the way you’d make room for a visitor at your door. You don’t have to invite it to stay forever. Just acknowledge that it’s here. For these few moments, there’s no need to talk yourself out of how you feel. Let yourself be a human being with human experiences.

- With the difficulty in the background, look for one small thing you appreciate. It might be someone who cares about you, a place where you feel safe, a warm drink, a comfortable bed, or a memory of laughter. Something quite ordinary is enough. If nothing comes to mind, that’s perfectly fine. Simply notice the support beneath your body or feel your feet on the floor. You don’t have to produce gratitude on demand.

- If you’ve found something, take a little time with it. What about this person, place, or experience matters to you? Maybe it brings warmth, comfort, connection, or relief. Maybe it’s simply pleasant. Don’t force the feeling to be bigger than it is.

- Notice the details. If it’s a memory, recall it gently. If it’s happening now, explore it through your senses. Let yourself receive the experience rather than hurrying on to the next thing.

- Hold both the difficult and the good. You don’t need to get rid of a difficult feeling to appreciate something good. You can feel worried and still enjoy being supported. You can feel sad and remember someone you love. You can feel lonely and appreciate a small, kind interaction. Imagine holding the difficulty in one hand and this small appreciation in the other.

- Consider what this moment of appreciation points toward. Is there something you value in it, such as connection, kindness, friendship, health, creativity, or a little space to stop and breathe? Is there one small action you could take today to bring more of it into your life? You could send someone a message, step outside, take a proper break, or offer yourself a little more patience. If today is hard, the kindest thing may be to allow yourself some rest or support. Gratitude doesn’t require you to pretend everything is fine.

- Return to your surroundings. Notice your breathing, the sounds around you, and the support beneath your body. When you’re ready, gently open your eyes if they’ve been closed, and bring some gentle movement into your body.

- Thank yourself for taking these few minutes. May you find room for both the difficult moments and the small moments of goodness in the days ahead.

Source: Mindful | Published: 2026-11-25 13:00 UTC | Difficulty: 40/100

Original link: https://www.mindful.org/shamash-alidina-gratitude-with-room-for-everything-else/

item.title: You’re Not Too Much Just Because Someone Else Needs Less
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: strong, worth their time

“Being myself doesn’t give me unlimited access to somebody else’s attention.”

I am a talkative person.

Not “occasionally enjoys conversation” talkative. I can answer a question, take three side roads, remember something from 1987, and still believe I gave you the short version.

I’m also a helper. When I care about someone, I want to find exactly the right example to make something click. Unfortunately, I have a habit of continuing long after the click.

For years, I thought being myself meant showing up with all of that enthusiasm. Now I’m learning something so obvious I’m almost embarrassed it took me this long: the other person gets to be themselves too.

I learned that the hard way during my years working with foster children and families. I could get so excited about helping a young person understand something that I’d explain it from six directions. I was giving an excellent presentation, at least according to the person giving it.

On one occasion, a young person I cared about a lot told me I was using too many words.

Well, shit.

I was going full steam down one track with the backstory, the examples, the whole TED Talk. She wanted the movie trailer. She had asked me directly to stop beating around the bush.

My first reaction was confusion. What do you mean? This is good!

Then embarrassment. Then a much less flattering question: Was I still talking to help her, or was I partly entertaining myself?

I realized I had been trying to do everything at once: explain, soften the message, make it interesting, help her feel safe. Some of that was care.

But some of it, honestly, was fear. I didn’t fully trust that I could say something directly and let it be enough.

She had told me exactly what she needed in that moment—fewer words, not more. And caring about her meant honoring what she needed, even if it wasn’t how I naturally communicated.

So I regrouped and tried again. Not with a different personality. Just a different way of showing up for the person in front of me.

I wish I could say I always took that kind of feedback so well.

Other times, I ran the whole spectrum from martyr to victim in my head: Well, that’s the last time I ever try to help you. If I’m too much for you today, I must be too much for you forever. Maybe we shouldn’t even be friends since I can’t truly be me.

It’s quite a leap from “Can you get to the point?” to “Apparently I should retire my entire personality.” But I have made it.

And when I’m not very invested in the person, I’m more likely to just shut down. Pride and ego win, I detach, and I stop talking.

I’m not always known for taking redirection well. I am getting better.

Recently I heard about someone who kept talking to a woman during her workout. She wasn’t there to socialize; she wanted to concentrate on exercising. When the conversation didn’t go well, the response afterward was essentially, “Well, I have to be me.”

Yes. You do. But she gets to be her too.

That sentence has been rattling around in my head ever since. Because “I have to be me” sounds wonderful until being me requires somebody else to stop being themselves.

If I love talking, that doesn’t mean you have to love listening at that moment. If I process things aloud, you aren’t automatically my processing partner.

I can be enthusiastic, curious, funny, and capable of producing a twelve-minute answer to a question that technically required the word “yes.” Those things can all genuinely be me. But they still land somewhere.

Maybe you are tired, distracted, or simply finished with the conversation. I don’t need to decide which explanation is right before I respect it.

Sometimes we treat another person as a charging station. We come away from a long conversation feeling wonderful. We told the story, got the laugh, processed the problem.

Meanwhile, they may have been running on fourteen percent the whole time. Then they say they need quiet, and suddenly we’re the injured party.

Now the quieter person has two jobs. First, manage their own overload. Second, manage our feelings about the fact that they are overloaded.

But being asked for less conversation isn’t necessarily being asked to become less of a person. I can mean well and still overwhelm someone. And being myself doesn’t give me unlimited access to somebody else’s attention.

Maybe somebody really does think you are too much. That can hurt.

But before you turn that into a life sentence, add the missing words: Too much for whom? Too much when? Too much for what?

Maybe you are not too much for your best friend. Maybe you are too much while she is trying to exercise.

Maybe you are not too much for your partner. Maybe you are too much at 6:30 in the morning before coffee.

That is not a moral failure. It is information.

And it works both ways. One person may feel connected by talking everything through. Another may feel connected by sitting together without a word.

Neither one is broken.

These days I still love stories, jokes, metaphors, and the moment when someone’s face says, “I get it.” None of that needs to disappear.

But I’m trying to catch myself sooner when I stop noticing the person who has to receive all my wonderful information.

Sometimes the best thing I can do is ask, “Do you want the short version?”

And then, here’s the radical part: actually give it.

I don’t need to turn myself off. I can turn the volume down. The quieter person gets to be themselves, and I still get to be me.

About Kelly Blakey

Kelly Blakey is a writer, mother, and former social worker with thirty years of experience in behavioral health. Drawing from her professional and personal experiences, she writes about the patterns that shape our relationships, the stories we tell ourselves, and what happens when we begin questioning them. She is the author of Holy Shit, That’s Me and Holy Shit, I Do That Too. Visit her at HelpingHealer.com.

Source: Tiny Buddha | Published: 2026-11-25 16:19 UTC | Difficulty: 40/100
